One of the flashier amateur shortstop defenders of the last couple decades, Cholowsky was a late-first round prospect as an Arizona high schooler who wanted top-of-the-draft money to sign. Enough teams were worried about how much he'd hit that they had him more toward the back of the first round, and though the White Sox are rumored to have made a run at him, he ended up at UCLA. There, Cholowsky took a big enough leap as a sophomore hitter to make himself the odds on favorite to go first in the draft. He cut his strikeout rate to 9.3% and hit 23 homers. When you combine everything Cholowsky participated in in 2025 (the college season, Team USA trials and international play, and fall ball at UCLA), he had an 1.127 OPS. 
Cholowsky's highlight reel defensive ability is the bedrock of his game. His hands, actions and body control are incredible, and make him a potential Gold Glove shortstop despite middling range. For such a great shortstop, Roch is a thicker-in-the-middle athlete, and it's possible his range will depreciate as he ages and make him merely a 55 or 60-grade shortstop in his late 20s. On offense, Cholowsky's ability to tuck his hands inside the baseball and barrel stuff on the inner third has improved a lot since high school, but he's still a little long to some parts of the zone. He identifies and adjusts to breaking stuff and moves the barrel around pretty well, but middling plate discipline and Cholowsky's lever length combine to keep his hit tool projection a little south of average. He should still be able to access pull-side power with regularity because of his style of swing and good (for a shortstop) power. Though Roch is a different physical package, his tools are very similar to what Dansby Swanson's were coming out of Vanderbilt. He'll probably strike out more than most of his shortstop peers, but get to pull power and play awesome defense en route to some seasons with 3-plus WAR.

Cholowsky, the son of former Minor Leaguer and long-time scout Dan Cholowsky, was a top 50 player as a two-sport athlete from the Hamilton High School program in Arizona that produced Cody Bellinger. His commitment to UCLA priced him out and he ended up the highest-ranked player not selected in the 2023 Draft. After a solid freshman year with the Bruins he vaulted himself to the top of 2026 Draft boards by posting a 1.190 OPS with 23 homers as a sophomore. He's considered by some to be the best all-around college shortstop prospect since Troy Tulowitzki and has done nothing to diminish that take with a solid junior season. A 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter, Cholowsky has the chance to have four plus tools when all is said and done. He routinely finds the barrel, doesn't swing and miss or chase with an advanced approach at the plate. When he finds the ball out front, he'll show off 70 raw power to his pull side, and that's where his home run pop showed up in 2025. He's not a runner, though he's smart on the basepaths. That lack of pure speed won't impact him as a defender; he uses what he has in short spaces very well. That, along with his plus instincts, allow him to get to most balls at shortstop, where he profiles as a plus defender with a plus arm. A leader who was a high school quarterback, he serves as the head of his infield in the same manner. His tools and makeup make him look like the kind of player who could be big league ready in a hurry.

Emerson is a well-rounded prospect who is a virtual lock to remain at shortstop for the long haul thanks to plus range, actions, and arm strength. He's a grinder in the box who takes a ton of pitches and spoils borderline offerings until opposing hurlers give in and either give him something to hit or walk him. A twitchy, bottom-hand dominant swing results in all-fields doubles contact. Emerson is of medium build - he's not the second coming of Corey Seager or Bobby Witt Jr. - but skilled high school shortstops like this tend to come off the board within the top 10 picks and eventually become everyday players at the position.

Scouts have a difficult time finding any flaws in Emerson's game, with one noting the worst thing he can say about him is that he's not Bobby Witt Jr. Like Witt, Emerson is a rangy prep shortstop from the Dallas/Fort Worth metroplex with all-around tools, even if his aren't quite as loud. He transferred from Argyle HS to Fort Worth Christian HS to play his senior season under former big leaguer Rusty Greer, who also mentored Witt while he was growing up, and won Gatorade's national high school baseball player of the year award. Emerson's advanced skills stand out as much as his tools, starting with the way he stacks up quality at-bats, making good swing decisions and barreling balls to all fields. He generates impressive exit velocities with a pretty left-handed stroke, and while he doesn't sell out for power, his bat speed and projectable strength portend future 25-homer pop. He presently focuses on just making hard contact in game action but can launch balls in batting practice and finished second at the High School Home Run Derby during All-Star Week. Emerson is an average runner out of the batter's box but pairs solid speed underway with good instincts. The Texas recruit may be a bit underrated with the glove because he's such a fluid defender at shortstop that he makes difficult plays look routine. He has a strong arm, quick hands, sound fundamentals and a finely calibrated internal clock, so he's a lock to stay at short. His makeup is as impressive as the rest of his game.

Lackey is a well-rounded, rapidly-improving catcher prospect who went from having no Division I offers as an underclassman to being a potential top five pick. The best college catcher in any draft class tends to come off the board in the top 10, and Lackey is a good bet to do just that. His game has no obvious holes on either side of the ball. His footwork coming out of his crouch can have inconsistent direction, but when he has a smooth exchange, he'll pop around 1.90, which is plus. He's a skinny 20-year-old (he turns 21 the week before the draft) who still has room for mass and strength on his frame, but already Lackey is a strong pitcher framer and ball-blocker. He's also a good contact hitter with a gorgeous swing. Again, Lackey has no obvious weak point as a hitter, and he's especially good at buttoning fastballs, which he had a 91% contact rate against in 2025. His all-fields approach yields a lot of gap doubles right now but those might turn into home runs as Lackey fills out. This is a good primary catching prospect and an instantaneous Top 100 guy upon entry into pro ball, a potential future All-Star.

A late bloomer as a Georgia high schooler, Lackey didn't receive any NCAA Division I offers until his senior year in 2023, and he didn't draw much attention from scouts because he attended few showcase events. Now he's the best catching prospect in the 2026 Draft and poised to join Jason Varitek, Matt Wieters, Joey Bart and Kevin Parada as first-round backstops out of Georgia Tech. He has dramatically improved each season with the Yellow Jackets, batted .397/.519/.772 as a junior and won't last longer than the top three or four picks. Lackey's right-handed swing can get a little busy, but that doesn't prevent him from making consistent contact to all fields. He's extremely patient, rarely misses fastballs and has the plus raw power to provide 25-30 homers on an annual basis. His flat stroke produces too much groundball contact but he's driving balls harder than ever and in the air a bit more often this spring. Extremely athletic for a 6-foot-2, 215-pound catcher, Lackey isn't quick out of the batter's box but can flash plus run times once he gets going. He's very agile behind the plate and should become a solid receiver and blocker once he improves his focus and consistency. His strong and accurate arm is another asset, and he looked capable at third base while playing 13 errorless games there in 2025.

Flora has an ideal pitcher's build and movement patterns at a loose-armed 6-foot-5. He was able to sustain upper-90s velocity for 75 innings in 2025, 30 more than the prior year. Flora sits 97 and regularly touches 100 with plus extension. His arm speed makes the baseball very difficult to pick up out of his hand and gives Flora's seldom-used changeup huge long-term projection. Right now his fastball and a couple of different sliders make up 95% of his pitch usage. Flora has great feel for locating lateral-action sliders to both sides of the plate, some slower, some as hard as 87-89 mph. His mechanical and athletic foundation are very exciting, as is his arm strength and breaking ball feel, but he has a little more pitch development ahead of him than most top-of-the-class arms.

Dillon Tate was the No. 4 overall pick in the 2015 Draft out of Santa Barbara. Ten years later, UCSB's Tyler Bremner was taken with the No. 2 pick in the 2025 Draft. Flora, who relieved as a freshman and then moved in to join Bremner in the Gauchos rotation in 2025, could be the next in line to be an early pick in the first round. After a solid sophomore season and even better junior campaign, it wouldn't be as much of a surprise as Bremner was. Flora's combination of size and arm strength should intrigue most teams. The 6-foot-5 right-hander already offers premium velocity, with a fastball that sits in the 96-97 mph range and regularly touches triple digits, with good shape, carry and armside ride to it. He'll employ two different sliders, both of which can flash plus. There's a slower 78-81 mph sweeper with a lot of horizontal depth and also a harder, more gyro-like traditional slider, thrown 86-89 mph. He has plus feel to spin and just needs to gain a little bit more consistency with shape. His hard changeup is coming along, a kick change with downer splitter depth that now flashes plus. A solid strike-thrower who maintains his velocity, Flora might not have the same feel to pitch Bremner had, but he's more physical than his predecessor. He's posting every week for the Gauchos and has separated himself more than any college arm in the class, so he should fly off the board early in the first round.

Eric Booth Sr. turned down the Blue Jays as a 34th-round pick in 1993 and became a record-setting kick returner at Southern Mississippi. His son has inherited his speed and athleticism and will use it to forge a future in baseball. He has added polish to his swing and defense this spring, and his combination of tools and skills should land him in the top 10 picks. Booth has an unconventional setup and pumps his hands away from his body, sometimes leaving him with a choppy-looking left-handed stroke. He nevertheless makes consistent contact and barrels balls while displaying a good sense of the strike zone. His bat speed and strength translate into impressive exit velocities and could result in 20-25 homers per year if he smooths out his stroke and launches balls in the air more regularly. He won the home run derby at the Perfect Game All-American Classic last July. One of the fastest runners in the 2026 high school class, Booth can get from home to first in a little over four seconds and ran the quickest 60-yard dash (6.33 seconds) at the East Coast Pro showcase in August. To make the most of his plus-plus speed, the Vanderbilt recruit will need to hone his basestealing instincts and improve his reads and routes in center field, and he's making strides in both areas. He has addressed the biggest weakness in his game, working to improve his arm strength to average.

Lebron is an incredible athlete with ideal athletic projection, and the two traits give him a shot to grow into impact power while remaining an excellent shortstop defender. He's a slender, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 or so, built like an athlete who could play any sport well. Right now that serves to make Lebron a great shortstop defender. He has great range, he bends well, and his hands, actions and arm strength are all plus or better. To be built like he is and move like he does at his size makes it easy to project Lebron at shortstop in perpetuity while also forecasting added strength as he matures. 
Whether Lebron will actually be able to hit enough to get to his power is the big question. His pitch recognition and feel to hit are both incredibly raw, and Lebron struck out at an alarming rate in 2025 (24%, worse than his freshman season) and has concerning chase and miss splits against secondary pitches. College players with such a wide range of outcomes are pretty rare, and Lebron's possible ceiling (if his feel to hit improves) makes him a likely high pick even though he's at risk of hitting too little to matter.

Overshadowed by first-round picks Arjun Nimmala, George Lombard Jr. and Aidan Miller in Florida's high school shortstop class of 2023, Lebron was on scouting radars but went undrafted because he wouldn't have gone high enough to lure him away from an Alabama commitment. By early 2025 he had become the frontrunner to go No. 1 overall in the 2026 Draft, though he was passed by UCLA's Roch Cholowsky later that spring. He still has a chance of matching Joe Vitello (No. 7 in 1991) as the highest pick in Crimson Tide history. The only knock on Lebron is a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, especially breaking balls. He made more contact as a junior but also batted just .229 in Southeastern Conference play as a junior, leading to questions about his long-term hitting ability. He has added 15 pounds and significant bat speed in college, giving him well-above-average raw power from the right side of the plate, and he also has good feel for driving balls in the air. All the rest of Lebron's tools grade as at least plus, as does his makeup, and some evaluators think he's even better than that as a defender despite an uncharacteristically erratic spring. He has a quick first step and ran better than ever this spring, displaying some top-of-the-scale run times while ranking fifth in NCAA Division I with 42 steals in 43 attempts. He can make any throw needed from anywhere at short and would be an asset anywhere on the diamond.

Rojas is a prototypical prep lefty who looks an awful lot like Marlins southpaw Thomas White looked just a few years ago. He is built like a star power pitcher at a fluid 6-foot-4, and Rojas' full-body flexibility and whippy arm are on full display as he pedals home and unwinds. He'll deliver a rise/tail fastball from a low-three-quarters slot, a low enough angle that Rojas can elevate his heater for whiffs. And he does; both Rojas' fastball and frisbee slider generated an elite miss rate on the showcase circuit. His slider is a seamed sickle with ridiculous length, starting from the lefty batter's box and darting all the way across the plate. Though he doesn't have a fully formed changeup right now, Rojas is so limber that it's likely he'll develop one in time. This looks like a potential Andrew Miller sequel.

Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida has produced seven players who have at least touched the big leagues, with Red Sox phenom Roman Anthony the most recent. That list also includes slugger Anthony Rizzo and lefty Jesús Luzardo. Now there’s another elite-level southpaw coming from the program in the form of Rojas, who performed well at a host of summer showcase events like the East Coast Professional Showcase and MLB’s High School All-American Game, not to mention tossing 11 shutout innings for Team USA en route to a gold medal at the WBSC U-18 World Cup. Rojas has positioned himself as one of the top lefties, and best arms overall, available in the class, high school or college. He can crank his fastball up to 98 mph with outstanding riding life, commanding it to both sides of the plate. It’s a better pitch to his arm side, but can get it glove side when he needs to, missing bats when it’s up in the zone. He complements it with a very nasty three-quarters low-80s sweeping slider that is a true out pitch. He doesn’t use his changeup much, but there’s plenty of feel for it to imagine it being a third effective offering. Athletic with outstanding presence on the mound, Rojas can fill up the strike zone, though he occasionally can try to get downhill too quickly and open up his delivery too early, causing a little more scattered command, things that are easily correctable. The Miami recruit has all the makings of a frontline starter and is in line to be Stoneman Douglas’ first first-round pick.

Flukey is a lanky 6-foot-6 righty who held mid-90s velocity across 101 innings in 2025, culminating in a great start against LSU in the College World Series. His 12-to-6 curveball has nearly 20 mph of velocity separation from his fastball, and even though that pitch looks easy to spot out of hand, it has enough depth that it generated a plus-plus miss rate in 2025. Flukey's fastball and curveball represented 83% of his pitch usage as a sophomore, but his slider (which averaged 83 mph) and changeup were both effective when he threw them. Flukey's slider acts as a strike-garnering pitch (he threw both it and his fastball for strikes more than 70% of the time), while his changeup was flashing bat-missing tail late in the season. He has a longer, fairly violent arm action, and there were games when Flukey struggled to get any miss on his fastball because his size imparts hittable downward angle on that pitch. He has mid-rotation ceiling if it turns out this slow curveball can keep playing like an impact pitch.

Flukey finished a strong sophomore season by dueling No. 3 overall pick Kade Anderson in the opening game of the 2025 College World Series finals, taking a 1-0 loss despite striking out nine in six innings. Few college pitchers can get swings and misses with a fastball and chases with a curveball better than he can, which will make him one of the first arms selected and the highest-drafted Coastal Carolina product ever this July. Diagnosed with a rib stress fracture after his first start in 2026, he missed two months but returned with his usual stuff in late April. Flukey maintains mid-90s velocity on his heater deep into games and tops out at 98 mph with armside run and carry. His high three-quarters arm slot allows him to stay on top of his upper-70s curveball, which has so much downer break that it can be hard to keep it in the strike zone, and his feel for spin also extends to a solid 82-85 mph slider. Though both breaking balls were quite effective in college, some scouts question how well they'll play against more advanced hitters. His mid-80s changeup lags behind the rest of his repertoire, though its fade makes it tough to hit when he throws it close to the plate. Because the 6-foot-6 Flukey has a longer arm path and higher release point than normal, it's easier for hitters to see his pitches -- but not to hit them. Despite his size, he has no difficulty repeating his delivery and providing strikes. He could add more strength to his lanky frame, which might mean more power for his already nasty stuff.

Flukey is a lanky 6-foot-6 righty who held mid-90s velocity across 101 innings in 2025, culminating in a great start against LSU in the College World Series. His 12-to-6 curveball has nearly 20 mph of velocity separation from his fastball, and even though that pitch looks easy to spot out of hand, it has enough depth that it generated a plus-plus miss rate in 2025. Helfrick was a highly-regarded high school prospect in Northern California who ventured all the way to the SEC for college. After struggling as a freshman, he had a power-hitting breakout as a sophomore and clubbed 15 homers in 61 games, then struggled with Team USA. Overt physicality, power, and steady catching defense (both receiving and ball blocking) give Helfrick a floor of sorts. It's common for big league catchers to hit around .200, and that's what's likely in the cards for Helfrick, who swings over the top of a lot of soft stuff in the bottom of the zone. He should crush quite a few high fastballs to his pull side and slug even though he will probably strike out 30% of the time in pro ball. 
On defense, his size and strength help make Helfrick a quiet, subtle receiver around the edges of the zone, and he's a skilled, mobile ball-blocker. He has an above-average arm that plays down because his exchange takes too long, and this needs some polish. Luke Stevenson went 35th overall in 2025 after striking out more often than Helfrick did as a sophomore, and Helfrick is a better defender, so his draft stock is just ahead of that area as he enters his junior season.

Helfrick ranked among the best catchers in the 2023 high school class, but an inconsistent senior season and a commitment to Arkansas left him undrafted. He batted .179 as a part-time player as a freshman before tying for the Cape Cod League lead with 11 homers that summer, a prelude to becoming a full-time starter and going deep a combined 33 times as a sophomore and junior. He stood out even more with his defense for the Razorbacks and the U.S. collegiate national team and should become the first backstop in school history to go in the first round. More advanced than most college catchers, Helfrick already calls pitches and excels at running a staff. He shows impressive physical skills behind the plate as well, grading as a quality receiver, framer and blocker. He has a strong arm that will be even more effective if he cleans up his transfer and improves his accuracy. Helfrick's strength and bat speed generate plus raw power from the right side of the plate, with most of his homers traveling to his pull side. He punishes fastballs but will chase pitches out of the zone and struggles to make contact against breaking balls and changeups. Even if he doesn't hit for a high average, he does everything else well enough to profile as a big league regular.

A year ago, Trent Gringlinger was a well-regarded prep catcher out of Huntington Beach HS in California, one who went on to play college ball at Tennessee. Scouts in southern California were abuzz when Trent's younger brother, Jared, reclassified in February from 2027 to be a part of this year's Draft class. The 17-year-old is legitimate two-way player for the Oilers, and evaluators seem to prefer his left-handed ability on the mound. One of the youngest players in the class -- he just turned 17 in April -- Grindlinger is all about projection on the mound. His present stuff doesn't jump off the page, but it's very easy to dream on a lot more to come as he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. His fastball has been clocked up to 95 mph at times -- touching 96 mph last summer -- but he typically sits around 90-93 mph, with good arm speed and strength that some scouts think points to a future plus heater. He's been using an 80-82 mph kick changeup lately, though some favored his feel for a traditional circle change he'd used previously, and he'll occasionally try to throw two brands of slider, with the short, bullet one better than the sweepier version. He tends to be around the plate with his stuff. As a hitter, Grindlinger has a contact-oriented swing, albeit without much impact now, though some feel there is power to come, which would help him fit a likely corner outfield or first base profile better. His name was rushing up Draft boards, but if somehow things didn't work out, he could get the chance to keep playing both ways with his brother at Tennessee next year.

Burress has had two absurd seasons at Georgia Tech and entered his draft year as a career .357/.490/.756 hitter, like a 5-foot-9 Barry Bonds. For an outfielder this size to be a great big leaguer would be mold-breaking. Short of Kirby Puckett (pun intended), righty-hitting outfielders like this don't tend to turn into impact players. While Burress is definitely a good athlete and more explosive than a lot of hitters his size, nothing but his surface-level stats indicate he's an elite player. His contact, chase, and measured power are all closer to the college average, it's just that Burress' ultra-short levers allow him to be on time to pull balls in play straight down the left field line a lot of the time. Burress runs well enough to try and develop in center field, but he's not a lock to stay there. Here he's projected to center not because of enthusiasm that he'll be great there, but because it's the position at which his offense has the best chance of profiling. Burress' performance has been an outlier, but he doesn't pass the visual scouting smell test to that degree, and here he's assessed more as a comp round prospect.

Scouts liked Burress' tools and loved his makeup when he was a Georgia high schooler, but he told teams he'd attend Georgia Tech unless they took him in the first round of the 2023 Draft. He went unpicked and then broke into college baseball with nine homers in his first eight games en route to setting a school record with 60 blasts in three seasons. He should be the first college outfielder selected and crack the top 10 choices. Though he's shorter than his listed 5-foot-9 and lacks projection, Burress has solid or better tools across the board. He has a compact and quick right-handed swing, plenty of strength, a disciplined approach at the plate and plus power that plays to all fields. His stance became very open and led to struggles in his second stint with the U.S. collegiate national team last summer, but he made the necessary adjustments to recover from a slow start this spring. Burress is a quality athlete with a high baseball IQ and a strong work ethic. He uses his solid speed to steal an occasional base and to chase down balls in center field, where most evaluators believe he can remain as a pro. If not, he has the bat and plus arm to profile well in right field, and he set a Yellow Jackets record with 10 outfield assists in 2024.

Reese posted a .901 OPS as a freshman outfielder at Houston, then transferred to Mississippi State (where he mostly played third base) and ripped 40 extra-base hits in 57 games with the Bulldogs despite a bone fragment floating in one of his toes, which was surgered in the autumn. Reese has plus lefty power and bat speed generated by a low-ball swing. He can drop the bat head and drive pitches in the lower third to all fields, with enough power to threaten both foul poles. Reese is rather chase-prone but is otherwise a stable hitting prospect who covers a good bit of the zone. Though he's not a lock to remain at third base, he looked good enough toward the end of 2025 to merit a good long look there in pro ball. If he can remain at third, he'll have a shot to profile as an everyday player even with lesser OBP skills. If he needs to move to first base or an outfield corner, his lack of plate discipline will be more of a problem. Reese is talented enough to be drafted inside the top 10.

Reese began his college career at Houston in 2024 before transferring to Mississippi State and earning Southeastern Conference newcomer of the year honors last spring. He batted .352/.422/.718 with 21 homers while dealing with a loose bone fragment in his left big toe and has produced similar numbers as a junior. After ranking second in the SEC with 12 homers during league play, he should go somewhere in the back half of the first round. Reese's carrying tool is his plus power, which he generates with the strength in his 6-foot-4, 220-pound frame and the bat speed and leverage in his left-handed stroke. He can homer to any part of a ballpark and pounds both lefties and righties. He can get a bit aggressive at times but is making progress with his swing decisions and some evaluators think he could become a solid hitter with 25-30 homers per year. The biggest question with Reese is whether he can handle third base. He's a below-average athlete with limited quickness and range, and his arm is merely average. He has improved since fielding .889 at the hot corner as a sophomore but still could wind up at first base or possibly left field.

Lombard is an imposing physical presence, built like a young tight end and wielding some of the best power in the 2026 high school class, especially among the prospects who can play a valuable defensive position. But his contact rate on the showcase circuit (61% across 824 pitches in 2024 and 2025) is a ruby red flag because there aren't big leaguers with contact rates that low. One would need to project significant improvement in this area for him to be considered a viable big leaguer in any capacity, let alone the sort of star you'd expect a $4 million player to be. If by some miracle he turns into a decent hitter, the ceiling on Lombard is a 35-homer shortstop or third baseman.

Gulliver Prep south of Miami has had more than 20 players drafted over the years, but just two first-rounders. The most recent was George Lombard Jr., now an ascending star in the Yankees system, and now it’s his brother Jacob’s turn. The younger son of former big leaguer George Lombard, Jacob showed off an exciting combination of athleticism and baseball IQ on the summer showcase circuit, putting him in position to come off the board well before his brother did at No. 26 overall in 2023. A 6-foot-3 premium athlete at a premium position, Lombard is a right-handed hitter with plenty of juice in his bat. He has the acumen to be a plus hitter in the future, though he did have some swing-and-miss on fastballs up in the zone over the summer, with a bat path that wasn’t matching the velocity he was facing. He’s already added strength, and speed, of late, with potential plus power. His main weakness might be that he’s a people-pleaser and listened to too much advice on the showcase circuit, with most evaluators believing he’ll be just fine once he lets his athleticism play. He’s an easily plus runner who should be a threat to run at the next level. Lombard will be able to play shortstop for a very long time, with outstanding range, feet, hands and action. Some might have questions about his arm strength, but he has plenty when he needs it. All of this adds up to him being a potential top of the first round pick.

Peterson was one of the best unsigned high school pitchers from the 2023 class, and had two walk-prone underclass seasons at Florida. He has the stuff of a top 10 pick, with a riding fastball in the mid-to-upper 90s, a power breaking ball in the mid-80s, and a plus-flashing changeup in the 84-87 mph range. His delivery is stiff, especially Peterson's landing leg, and he has some head and shoulder violence through release. Florida hasn't always developed their pitchers in the best way, and it's possible a pro team will be able to polish Peterson's mechanics and command quickly after drafting him. He'll be an impact starter if someone can.

In 2023, Peterson was a Top 100 prospect, not to mention a two-way player, from the Florida high school ranks, but some inconsistencies during his senior year likely priced him out of the range where he would have considered signing instead of heading to Gainesville and the University of Florida. He earned a spot in the Gators’ rotation as a freshman and has never relinquished it. He’ll front that staff in 2026 and if he can continue to iron out some things, has the stuff to be the first college arm to come off the board in July. The 6-foot-5 Peterson presents an exciting combination of now stuff and projection. His fastball sat in the mid-90s as a sophomore and he’s shown the ability to reach back for 98-99 mph, both last spring and in short looks this fall. The pitch can show good carry at times, though it can flatten out occasionally and get hit more than it should. Florida calls a lot of sliders and Peterson’s mid-80s breaker has improved into a solid out pitch, though there are some scouts who think his 12-to-6 hammer curve is a better, but not utilized, offering. His changeup has also improved with solid fade and depth. Peterson’s slot has returned to a higher three-quarters slot, similar to where he was in high school, that could serve him well. He can get a little over-aggressive in his mode of operation on the mound, leading to some command issues. There aren’t many college arms with better pure stuff in this class and if he can take another step forward in terms of execution, he could show up in top of the Draft conversations.

Gracia is a strapping, broad-shouldered 6-foot-3 center fielder with big league physicality and a great two-year track record of hitting at Duke prior to his draft year transfer to Virginia. A gorgeous low-ball lefty swing produces nearly average all-fields power for Gracia, who likely isn't done growing into raw thump. He will hit the baseball where it's pitched and do damage to all fields. Gracia's selectivity and hand-eye coordination allow him to move the bat around the hitting zone with uncommon feel for such a big, long-levered hitter, and he posted a comfortably plus contact rate in 2025. 
Gracia isn't a burner, but his feel for center field is good. He's comfortable going back on balls hit over his head and looks smooth at the catch point. There's a chance he outgrows center field, but for now, his skills out there are suitable for continued development. He's one of the most well-rounded hitters in the 2026 draft class and has a shot to go first overall if he's added sufficient strength without sacrificing the speed that would allow him to continue developing in center field.

A solid player during his New Jersey high school days, Gracia got off to a very good start at Duke, earning freshman All-American honors by finishing with a 1.000 OPS in 2024. Gracia got off to a very rough start in his sophomore year as he tried to incorporate a swing change, but he got hot once he abandoned that switch, allowing him to finish with 15 homers and an OPS of 1.007. He followed coach Chris Pollard to the University of Virginia and missed the fall due to an undisclosed illness but returned to have a productive junior season with the Cavaliers. When he's locked in, Gracia looks like one of the better college bats in the class. Swinging from the left side of the plate, he makes excellent swing decisions and shows off plus contact skills. His advanced approach led to a Blue Devils-record 57 walks as a sophomore, and he really limits his swing-and-miss. That gives more confidence that he should continue getting to his solid raw power at the next level, and there's definitely the chance he can keep adding strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. Though he's a fringy runner, scouts give Gracia a chance to stick in center field because of his excellent instincts and efficient routes. If a move to a corner is necessary, left would be a more likely landing spot because his arm is a little short for the prototypical right fielder. His continued consistent production in a year light on college bats hasn't hurt his stock.

Gracia got off to a very rough start in his sophomore year as he tried to incorporate a swing change, but he got hot once he abandoned that switch, allowing him to finish with 15 homers and an OPS of 1.007. He followed coach Chris Pollard to the University of Virginia and missed the fall due to an undisclosed illness but returned to have a productive junior season with the Cavaliers. When he's locked in, Gracia looks like one of the better college bats in the class. Swinging from the left side of the plate, he makes excellent swing decisions and shows off plus contact skills. His advanced approach led to a Blue Devils-record 57 walks as a sophomore, and he really limits his swing-and-miss. That gives more confidence that he should continue getting to his solid raw power at the next level, and there's definitely the chance he can keep adding strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. Though he's a fringy runner, scouts give Gracia a chance to stick in center field because of his excellent instincts and efficient routes. If a move to a corner is necessary, left would be a more likely landing spot because his arm is a little short for the prototypical right fielder. His continued consistent production in a year light on college bats hasn't hurt his stock.

Condon is an explosive athlete whose skill set is like a lot of recent undersized speedsters (like Slater de Brun and Slade Caldwell) except that it comes in a more traditional 5-foot-11 package. Condon's front side often bails toward first base when he swings, which leaves him vulnerable to sliders away from him, but his ability to swing really hard and generate some power at his size is remarkable. Plus-plus speed allows for comfortable center field projection. This is one of the twitchier, more athletic players in the 2026 draft and a classic late first or comp round prospect.

Etowah HS (Woodstock, Ga.) features three seniors drawing attention from scouts in Condon, right-hander Matthew Sharman and outfielder Deion Cole, who helped the Eagles win the state 6-A championship in 2024 and 2026. Condon is the star attraction, drawing comparisons to Pete Crow-Armstrong. Gatorade's Georgia high school player of the year, he may have the best combination of hitting ability and speed in this high school crop. Though Condon has an unconventional left-handed stroke with an upright barrel, he makes good swing decisions and regular contact to all fields. He has enough bat speed and strength to get to average power, though it shows up more in batting practice than in games at this point. He hits balls hard but has yet to pull them in the air consistently. Condon has double-plus speed and likes to use it, playing with constant intensity as he tries to make things happen on the bases and runs down balls in the gaps. He's a quality center fielder who will stay there at the next level, with the added bonus of solid arm strength. A Tennessee recruit, he's reminiscent of former Volunteers star Drew Gilbert with his 5-foot-11 frame, tools and flair.

A .347/.465/.614 career hitter in two years at Maryland before transferring to Texas A&M for his draft spring, Hacopian has a ridiculous TrackMan readout (95% contact rate versus fastballs in 2025, including on Cape Cod, 57% hard-hit rate during his sophomore season with the Terps). He is less toolsy to the eye, however, as his kind of odd, high-effort swing, medium frame, and realistic 2B/3B fit on defense make him look more like a contact-oriented utilityman. Hacopian didn't really hit for power with wood on Cape Cod (he slugged .364), which is more in line with the expectations set by his look as a hitter (middling size, strength and a lot of effort needed to swing hard). He has more of a late-second or third round feel from a visual scouting standpoint, but might be someone's data darling.

Derek Hacopian won the Atlantic Coast Conference triple crown and Player of the Year Award at Maryland in 1992, and his sons Chris and Eddie teamed up with the Terrapins in 2024-25. After Chris slashed .375/.502/.656 with 14 homers and more than twice as many walks (40) as strikeouts (19), and his older brother graduated last spring, he transferred to Texas A&M. His hitting ability and strike-zone judgment rank among the best in the 2026 Draft, though he hasn’t been at his best while dealing with lower-back issues that cost him nearly a month this spring. Hacopian can make hitting look easy because he has advanced feel for the barrel and control of the strike zone, and some clubs believe he has the best bat in the college ranks. Though he has a busy setup, his right-handed stroke always seems to be on time and produces consistent hard contact, especially against fastballs. While his hitting prowess overshadows his power, the latter is at least average and could be more if he drove balls in the air more often. Hacopian played third base as a freshman before shifting to shortstop as a sophomore, and the Aggies originally committed to playing him there in 2026. He's a below-average runner with average arm strength and a lack of lateral range, so he wound up at second base. It's not a given that he can stay on the dirt at the next level, so he could wind up in left field.

Bell is an athletic, switch-hitting shortstop who the Rays drafted 66th overall in 2024 but failed to sign. He had a good freshman season at Kentucky - .296/.385/.522, 10 homers - and is an age-eligible sophomore entering 2026, as he turns 21 at the very end of June. Bell is a competent and pretty dangerous hitter from both sides of the dish. His lefty swing has big natural loft, while his righty swing is well-connected from the ground up and lets him generate good bat speed. Though some of Bell's swings are imbalanced, that's not unusual for a switch-hitter this age, and it's impressive that he was able to maintain a 77% contact rate once conference play began in his first season. Bell is very athletic but needs polish on defense, especially his throwing stroke and accuracy. He throws from a lower slot and some of them sail on him. The athletic components to play shortstop (and probably all over the diamond) are here, and Bell's big league projection probably resides in a multi-positional utility role. He's a mid-first round prospect.

The highest unsigned pick in the 2024 Draft, Bell went 66th overall to the Rays as a supplemental second-rounder out of an Illinois high school. He opted to attend Kentucky, where he was the Wildcats' best player as a freshman and became their first member of the U.S. collegiate national team since Zack Thompson in 2018. He's one of the top sophomore-eligible prospects for 2026 and on track to become the school's first first-rounder since Thompson in 2019 despite tearing the labrum in his non-throwing shoulder in his first game this spring. A switch-hitter, Bell is proficient from both sides of the plate. He has the bat speed and strength to generate 20 homers per season once he learns to lift balls in the air more consistently. He has a decent approach at the plate but can get too passive at times and has trouble staying back on changeups. Bell has all of the ingredients to play a solid shortstop. He has average speed but a quick first step, smooth actions, reliable hands and a strong arm capable of making throws from any angle necessary. His defensive instincts and athleticism would allow him to play almost anywhere on the diamond if he ends up in a utility role. He's gritting through the shoulder injury to play for the Wildcats but will require surgery that will sideline him for several months.

Curiel was a high-profile high school underclassman in Southern California because of his tapered, projectable build, speed, and feel for contact. He didn't develop much bat speed or power by the time his senior year arrived and, slated to be a draft eligible sophomore in two years anyway, he matriculated to LSU. In his freshman year, Curiel slashed .345/.470/.519 and posted an incredible 95% in-zone contact rate. That mark is way, way better than anything Curiel was able to muster in high school and, because of the length of his swing, isn't something he projects to do in pro ball. Curiel's swing is mechanically similar to Roman Anthony's, but with just a fraction of Anthony's bat speed. He's late to the contact point against a lot of fastballs and tends to slice them the other way. This is a warning sign that a hitter lacks the bat speed to handle big league velocity, and this risk applies to Curiel. Though he played left field as a freshman, Curiel can really run and should be developed in center field as a pro. He's built like a premium athlete but doesn't have the strength to hit for power right now, and adding muscle will be a priority for him after he signs. If you're willing to take Curiel's freshman year contact performance at face value, then he should be a top 10 prospect in this draft. More likely, he's a speedy extra outfielder.

Curiel projected as a potential first-rounder early in his career at powerhouse Orange (Calif.) Lutheran HS, but he didn't perform as hoped in his final showcase summer or senior season. He withdrew from the 2024 Draft and headed to Louisiana State, where he was the leading hitter (.345/.470/.519) on a College World Series championship team as a freshman and batted .390 in the NCAA tournament. Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2026, he's posting similar numbers and proving that he can play center field. A lean left-handed hitter with excellent bat-to-ball skills, Curiel uses a fluid stroke and mature approach to spray hard line drives all over the field. His swing is somewhat flat and he may not have more than average strength or bat speed, so he might not deliver more than 12-15 homers per season. He resembles Christian Yelich at the same age, though scouts are skeptical that Curiel can match the power gains Yelich made later in his career. While scouts debate how much pop Curiel will have, there are fewer concerns about his ability to stay in center field. Though he played left field as a freshman, he has solid speed and looks more comfortable tracking balls up the middle. His arm is fringy but playable in center.

A product of Arizona high school powerhouse Corona Del Sol, Carlon stayed home to go to college, jumping right into the Arizona State bullpen as a freshman. He took a big step forward results-wise as a sophomore, also as a reliever, before pitching well in brief stops in the Cape Cod League and USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team Training Camp. A move into the Sun Devils' rotation this spring has helped cement him as top-two-round arm talent, even if the jury is still out about his long-term role. Considered to be the top college arm in the area, Carlon could have the chance to start thanks to a potential four-pitch mix coming from his strong 6-foot-5 frame. The lefty can run his fastball up to 98 mph, sitting around 94 mph, though it can get flat with scattered command. He's able to get back in line with his breaking stuff, starting with an 87-88 mph cutter-like short slider he throws as often as his heater that misses a ton of bats. He can manipulate it and make it a bit longer at times, and he also has an average 12-to-6 curve that offers a different look. His changeup is his fourth pitch, but it does have some fade to it. A solid athlete who hit .349 playing both ways in the Alaska Summer League in 2024, Carlon has struggled at times with finding the zone consistently, though he cut his walk rate down as a starter this year. There's some reliever risk, and he could move quickly in that role, but a team taking him in the top two rounds should give him every chance to stick in a rotation.

Dietz was part of a loaded rotation at Calvary Christian HS (Clearwater, Fla.) in 2023, pitching alongside Landen Maroudis (who signed for $1.5 million as a Blue Jays fourth-rounder) and Liam Peterson (now at Florida and a lock first-round pick). Dietz should join Peterson as a first-rounder in July despite totaling just 1 2/3 innings in his first two seasons at Arkansas. He had a stress fracture in his elbow that required surgery in the fall of 2023 and pitched twice the following spring but broke out this year with 131 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings and a Southeastern Conference-best nine quality starts. His performance during fall practice was so spectacular that some evaluators believed Dietz was the best college left-hander in the 2026 Draft and he has cemented that status with a strong and healthy spring. He works at 94-96 mph and reaches 98 with his fastball, displaying impressive backspin and carry at times and natural cut at others. His mid-80s slider and upper-80s cutter play as plus offerings, and his low-80s curveball does as well even if it's less consistent. He barely uses a mid-80s changeup with depth. Dietz presents an unusual look for hitters, delivering pitches from a 6-foot-6 frame with a high three-quarters arm slot. After two years of little activity, he has filled the zone and finished his season with 14 strikeouts against Kansas in an NCAA regional game. He could continue to improve as he gains more experience.

Strosnider was a multi-sport high schooler (baseball, hoops, track) who struggled during the early portion of his freshman year at TCU before getting hot in the middle of the season. The toolshed outfielder slashed .350/.420/.650 and had 34 extra base hits (including 10 triples) in 56 games as a freshman. Strosnider's swing is similar to that of a young Cody Bellinger, featuring a blend of athleticism and effort that leads to big all-fields power, but also a good number of strikeouts. Though his surface stats improved throughout his freshman campaign, his contact rate was actually worse once TCU got into Big 12 play, and was comfortably below the college average. Strosnider runs well but played only right field as a freshman. If it turns out he can develop into a good center field defender, then the strikeouts will be easier to swallow. Strosnider is risky but has big ceiling as a power-hitting center fielder. His more likely outcome is as a strong side corner platoon option.

One of the best all-around athletes in the 2024 high school class, Strosnider starred in basketball and the high jump as well as baseball. After swing-and-miss concerns and a strong commitment to Texas Christian left him undrafted, he starred as a freshman and became just the sixth NCAA Division I player in the past 25 seasons to reach double figures in homers, triples, doubles and steals. Despite a late-season slump as a sophomore, he could surpass Braden Taylor (No. 19 overall in 2023) as the highest-drafted hitter in Horned Frogs history. Strosnider's batting practice display at the 2023 Area Code Games is still legendary -- he shattered a dorm window beyond the right-field fence -- and he continues to impress with his huge raw power as a sophomore-eligible. He has a gorgeous left-handed swing and makes consistent in-zone contact, but questions still persist about his bat because he chases all types of pitches out of the zone, resulting in too many grounders. While he does much more damage against right-handers, he is showing more pop and drawing more walks against southpaws this spring. A quick-twitch athlete, Strosnider is a 6-foot-2, 200-pounder with plus speed once underway. Many evaluators believe he can play center field as a pro, though he mostly mans right field for the Horned Frogs alongside Chase Brunson, who projects to go in the top two rounds in July. Strosnider had a low-90s fastball as a prep pitcher and displayed plus arm strength last spring before having surgery to clean up his throwing shoulder during the summer.

Lowrance's hitting ability has generated a lot of buzz this spring, to the extent that he could go in the first round. He has a similar offensive profile and better secondary tools than fellow South Carolina prep product P.J. Morlando, a Marlins first-rounder two years ago. The top prospect in Virginia's recruiting class, he's unlikely to make it to Charlottesville. Lowrance has a smooth left-handed stroke and a track record of delivering against quality competition on the showcase circuit. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate, making consistent contact to all fields despite naturally long levers with his 6-foot-5 frame and drawing comparisons to Freddie Freeman. He doesn't lift and pull many pitches at this point, so he'll need to add strength and make some adjustments to realize his 25-homer potential. Though Lowrance moves well for his size, his average speed and quickness will dictate a move to third base at the next level. His solid arm strength will work at the hot corner, though there's some question about his ability to stick there in the long term. If he outgrows third base and slows a bit, he could wind up at first base.

Kuhns turned down seven-figure overtures from multiple big league clubs in the 2024 Draft before ultimately going unselected. He tired down the stretch of his freshman season at Tennessee before looking spectacular in three Cape Cod League starts last summer. One of the top sophomore-eligible pitching prospects in the 2026 crop, he's making a push for the first round by heating up after a slow start. Kuhns spins the ball very well, producing good carry on a fastball that parks at 93-96 mph and peaks at 98 and downer break on an upper-70s curveball. Both are plus offerings and they can become more formidable if they add more power as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-3 frame. He has struggled to find a reliable third pitch, scrapping his upper-80s cutter while still struggling to land his mid-80s changeup or low-80s slider for strikes. Kuhns has the ingredients to pitch in the front half of a rotation. He's doing a better of job of repeating his athletic delivery as he gets stronger, which also could help him develop a more dependable third option. He battled his control and command for much of his freshman season but pounded the zone on the Cape and has continued to do so this spring.

Kuhns spins the ball very well, producing good carry on a fastball that parks at 93-96 mph and peaks at 98 and downer break on an upper-70s curveball. Both are plus offerings and they can become more formidable if they add more power as he continues to fill out his 6-foot-3 frame. He has struggled to find a reliable third pitch, scrapping his upper-80s cutter while still struggling to land his mid-80s changeup or low-80s slider for strikes. Kuhns has the ingredients to pitch in the front half of a rotation. He's doing a better of job of repeating his athletic delivery as he gets stronger, which also could help him develop a more dependable third option. He battled his control and command for much of his freshman season but pounded the zone on the Cape and has continued to do so this spring.

Townsend impressed scouts with his feel for spinning the ball and his athleticism as a California high schooler, and he performed well at the 2024 Draft Combine. He fit into the third-fifth round range based on talent but wasn't signable there and went to Mississippi, where he logged a 6.35 ERA as a freshman. He touched 98 mph with his fastball and had an unhittable slider in an electric Southeastern Conference tournament matchup against eventual national champion Louisiana State and has shown similar stuff all spring, positioning himself as one of the top sophomore-eligible pitchers in the 2026 Draft. Townsend usually operates at 94-97 mph with a fastball that features high spin rates and nice carry, though it doesn't have a lot of life and gets hit more than it should. He also ratchets up the rpms on a pair of power breaking balls, with both his low-80s downer curveball and upper-80s slider with nice depth grading as plus offerings, as does his cutter that averages 90 mph. He also flashes some aptitude for throwing a fading upper-80s changeup as well. More athletic than physical, Townsend works with some effort in his high three-quarters delivery. He has improved his control as a sophomore, doing a better job of landing his fastball and cutter while getting a lot of chases with his entire arsenal. He missed a start with mild shoulder inflammation in mid-March but his stuff remained overpowering when he returned.

A physical lefty with a great curveball, Bolemon didn't allow an earned run during his junior year of high school and struck out two batters per inning during varsity play. In 12 showcase outings during the summer, all over the world, Bolemon dominated his elite peers and allowed just an .085 opponent average in 144 batters faced. This is despite not throwing all that hard. Bolemon's fastball averaged just 92 mph on the showcase circuit and touched 96. His arm action is incredibly deceptive and loose; hitters don't seem to pick up the baseball out of Bolemon's hand, it just appears out from behind his head and sneaks past hem. Both his fastball and breaking ball have generated plus-plus swing and miss in an environment with good hitters. Bolemon's quick arm action might eventually yield a good offspeed pitch, but it's tough to turn over a straight changeup from his slot. He might end up adding a splitter or modified cambio down the road. Right now, he's a sturdy-looking strike-thrower who looks like he's going to have at least two 60-grade pitches.

Bolemon didn't allow an earned run as junior while striking out 101 in 42 1/3 innings, winning Gatorade's South Carolina prep player of the year award and leading Southside Christian HS (Simpsonville) to its fourth consecutive state 3-A title with a 19-strikeout no-hitter in the championship. Then he dominated on the showcase circuit as well and was the ace of the U.S. National Team that won the 18-and-under World Cup in Japan in September, fanning 17 in 11 scoreless frames. He entered 2026 as the consensus best pitching prospect in the Draft -- college or high school -- and while he didn't quite live up to that billing, he repeated as a Gatorade honoree and state champion. Bolemon's stuff is beyond reproach, starting with a 91-94 mph fastball that reaches 96, and he can throw it to either side of the plate with carry or downhill plane. He has a pair of plus breaking balls, with evaluators slightly preferring his 78-82 mph downer curveball to his low-80s sweeper. He also does a nice job of killing spin on a mid-80s kick changeup that could become a solid offering with more use. There's much more to Bolemon than just pitch quality. The Wake Forest recruit has a projectable, athletic frame and a clean delivery that allows him to pound the zone with his main three offerings. Scouts love his makeup and mound presence as well. The only blemishes on his résumé are a partial elbow tear in eighth grade that required internal brace surgery and the fact that he'll turn 19 three months before the Draft, but neither is a concern.

Robbins' long track record of performance could land him in the first round. A year ago, he led the Big East Conference in batting (.422) and on-base percentage (.547) at Seton Hall before topping the Cape Cod League in hitting (.307), slugging (.545) and OPS (.936). He has wielded one of the Southeastern Conference's most dangerous bats since transferring to Texas, quadrupling his previous career high with 24 homers this spring. Becoming more aggressive has allowed Robbins to tap into increased power, as he's chasing pitches more often but also driving them in the air much more frequently and hitting them harder and farther than ever before. His quick right-handed swing allows him to catch up to and destroy fastballs, though his new mindset has left him vulnerable to breaking balls and changeups. He holds his hands and back elbow high at the plate and balances briefly on his back leg before unleashing an uppercut stroke, a nontraditional approach that has resulted in his strikeout rate jumping from 13 percent as a sophomore to 32 percent in the Cape League and 23 percent with the Longhorns. While Robbins produces lackluster run times out of the batter's box, he's an average runner with a knack for stealing and taking extra bases. A corner outfielder at Seton Hall and on the Cape, he has played a decent center field for Texas. He'll get a chance to man center in pro ball but likely will wind up back in left or right, and his average arm strength works at all three spots.

Reddemann spent two years at the University of San Diego developing a reputation as a big-time strike-thrower with a real feel for pitching. A move up to UCLA for his junior year has helped him reach another gear completely. Establishing himself as the Friday night ace on the best team in the country, not to mention with top Draft prospect Roch Cholowsky, has allowed the right-hander to be seen by a lot of the scouting industry, where his improved stuff has helped catapult him to early-round status. His momentum was delayed with news of him missing time due to arm fatigue breaking at the end of April. A fall and offseason with the Bruins’ staff has helped Reddemann add strength and velocity, while all of his repertoire has improved. His fastball now sits around 95-96 mph, and he’s touched as high as 99 mph, getting plenty of swings and misses with the pitch. In the past, his best secondary offering had been his changeup, and the 84-85 mph pitch still has the chance to be a plus offering in the future. But his go-to this year has been a hard, 87-91 mph cutter, a pitch he’s shown he can throw to both sides of the plate against both lefties and righties, with an ability to bury it on the corners. He also unveiled a newer, sweepier low-80s slider, and he’ll use an 80-82 mph curve to get ahead early in counts. Even with the uptick in velocity, Reddemann has continued to fill up the strike zone with all of his offerings, and deception in his delivery helps all of it play up. He’s super-competitive on the mound, and scouts who saw him in San Diego have been impressed in the way he’s changed his breaking ball profile and stepped up his game in his Draft year.

Edwards is a Los Angeles area native who attended Palisades High School, earning back-to-back league pitcher of the year honors as well as consecutive first-team all-city nods in 2022 and 2023. After heading just a stone’s throw away to Southern Cal for college, the left-hander served as a swingman type for the Trojans, amassing just over 70 innings combined. A strong fall showing has been followed up by a solid spring leading the weekend rotation, which has kept the scouting industry’s interest piqued. In many ways, Edwards fits the prototype of a college lefty with a feel for pitching. He has a solid three-pitch mix and knows how to use it effectively. While his fastball typically sits in the 91-93 mph range, he can touch 95. There is some carry and “darkness” to his heater, leading to a 30-percent miss rate on the pitch in 2025, according to Synergy, a miss rate he maintained this spring . He’ll throw his slurvy breaking ball around 80 mph, and the curve flashes as a plus pitch with excellent spin. He has good feel for an above-average changeup with good fade that also can miss bats. Teams will like that Edwards will just be turning 21 immediately after the Draft. The fact that his strike-throwing has improved since he got to campus won’t hurt, either, as he showed excellent command during his work this fall. He has all the ingredients needed to be a solid starting pitcher and his ability to maintain his stuff this spring has floated him up into top-two-round consideration.

Becker, whose father played A-ball with Cleveland, is a lefty-hitting shortstop with rare body projection for a college infielder. He has oppo gap power and enough juice to threaten the wall just left of center field and, at a wiry-framed 6-foot-3, he has room to add strength and do even more damage. Becker swings with a naturally vertical bat path; his hands hang over the strike zone as they load and then loop through the zone in a way that evokes Freddie Freeman. Becker doesn't have that kind of bat control, but it does help him lift the ball even when he's making contact at the top of the zone. Because he swings with a stiff, high front side, he can struggle to dip and connect with lower, softer pitches, especially changeups. 
He needs technical refinement on defense (he needs to stay on top of the baseball on deeper throws), but Becker has the range and athleticism to develop at shortstop and hopefully stay lithe enough to remain there for the long haul. There are scouts who think he'll outgrow short, but they're fine with it as long as it comes with more power. If Becker has another season like both of his underclass years (.366/.459/.637 career line entering his draft year), his floor is probably in the middle of the first round.

When New Jersey high school infielder Nick Becker was being evaluated for the 2025 Draft, there was some concern about signability because of his potential desire to play with his older brother, Eric, at the University of Virginia. Nick ended up signing with the Mariners as a second-rounder last July, and in 2026, it will be Eric's turn. And after two strong years with the Cavaliers in the ACC, he has a good chance to come off the board earlier than his brother did. A left-handed hitter, Becker has been a starter since he set foot on campus, and he's hit from day one, carrying a .366 average and an OPS north of 1.000. He's hit over power as of now, with a solid approach, excellent bat-to-ball skills and limited chase. There could be more impact in there, which could raise his profile, though right now he's content to hunt for base hits with a simple swing. A quiet leader with a slow internal clock, Becker is an average runner with an average arm. A team taking him might at least send him out as a shortstop and see if his excellent instincts allow him to stick there. A move to second or third might be in his future -- he manned the hot corner for Team USA over the summer -- and if he starts driving the ball more, he could profile well anywhere.

There have been only two prep left-handed pitchers from Massachusetts to sign out of high school and make it to the big leagues: Bill Travers back in 1970, Hall of Famer Tom Glavine in 1984, while current Marlins prospect Thomas White went in 2023. Bumila hopes to join that select group as he was racing up Draft boards this spring. The 6-foot-9 lefty, who helped lead his Bishop Feehan basketball team to a state championship this winter, has the chance to be just the fourth prep arm from the Bay State to go in the top 40 picks. He was being mentioned frequently in first-round conversations, though news in early July about a UCL injury -- he had internal brace surgery in May 2025 -- was causing teams to reevaluate. All discussions about Bumila start with his elite fastball. Not only can he crank it up to over 100 mph, but Bumila’s extension and low release height are outliers, creating 19-20 inches of inverted vertical break. In the Massachusetts high school ranks, he doesn’t need much more, though he does have a decent slider and changeup. He can vary the shape of his 88-89 mph breaker, and it should translate to pro ball, while he sells his upper-80s cambio with good arm speed, a pitch with some armside fade to it. Bumila’s already-premium stuff could take another leap forward when he gets pro instruction; he likes digging into metrics and pitch design, so access to professional technology should help. He throws strikes, though he’s definitely control over command at this point. Because of his overall athleticism, the Texas recruit does a nice job of keeping all of his large moving parts fairly coordinated in repeating his delivery. Bumila let teams know about the ligament issue with a plan to wait until after the Draft to enable whatever team takes him to have a say in next medical steps.

Prosek isn't as tooled up as fellow Mississippi prep prospect Eric Booth Jr., but he could join him in the first round because he's one of the most advanced bats in the entire high school class. Part of a Magnolia Heights (Senatobia, Miss.) program that has won eight consecutive Midsouth Association of Independent Schools 5-A championships, he homered twice in the 2025 title game and went deep and earned a complete-game victory in the 2026 finale. He also played well on the showcase circuit, winning MVP honors at the Perfect Game All-American Classic in July, and Gatorade named him Mississippi's 2026 high school player of the year. The nephew of Brewers third-base coach Matt Erickson, Prosek has a quick, compact left-handed swing that always seems to be on time. He can chase pitches and get pull-happy on occasion, but his good feel for the barrel allows him to make quality contact. He has the hitting ability, bat speed and strength for at least average power, and some evaluators believe he can become a plus hitter with solid pop. He ranked second nationally with 18 homers in 41 games this spring. Because he's a below-average runner and lacks lateral quickness, Prosek fits better at third base than in the middle infield. He has seen some action at catcher this spring, playing well enough that scouts believe it's a path that may be worth exploring in pro ball -- though it would add to his development time and take a toll on his offensive production. He has solid arm strength and has pushed his fastball to 93 mph on the mound. He'll be 19 on Draft day and eligible again as a sophomore in 2028 if he attends Mississippi.

High school pitchers participating in the grueling pre-draft circuit often have velo swoons at some point during the showcase process as they pitch all summer and get worn out travelling all over the place. It was the opposite for Schmidt, who added a tick-and-a-half throughout the summer and ended it throwing harder than when it began. Schmidt's delivery looks a lot like Yusei Kikuchi's and Gage Jump's, except on a more sizeable individual, creating rise/run life on his fastball and two-plane break (from Schmidt's POV, the 4 o'clock face of a clock) on his nasty breaking ball. He'll occasionally bury a firm changeup, as hard as 89 mph, but that pitch is a distant third offering right now. Schmidt's a little thicker than most high school pitchers, but he throws strikes with two pitches that are easily plus. In Schmidt's case, his fastball and slider are playing like elite pitches, not merely plus ones. We'd like to see him add a pitch that can more obviously help him navigate righty batters.

If teams like high school left-handed pitchers, this might be the Draft for them. Within the first round, they could have their choice of three from different areas of the country: Gio Rojas in South Florida, Carson Bolemon in South Carolina and Schmidt out west in California. Schmidt may have started the summer showcase circuit behind the other southpaws, but after performances at events like the Area Code Games and MLB’s All-American Game, he’s vaulted himself towards the top of the prep lefty list. An uptick in velocity this summer, particularly at the Area Code Games, certainly helped Schmidt’s stock rise. He was typically pitching at 93-94 mph with his fastball, but he was in the 94-97 mph range, and more of that consistently would certainly help him on Draft boards. There isn’t a ton of deception with the pitch right now, so it can get hit at times. He backs up the heater with a 78-81 mph slider that features three-quarters shape to it, a breaker that can disappear, miss a lot of bats and flashes plus. There’s feel for a changeup, too, which he sells well with arm speed out front. Schmidt has shown an ability to repeat his delivery well and fill up the strike zone with all three of his offerings, providing a very nice left-handed starting pitching kit. The LSU recruit reclassified to be done with high school early, so he’ll still be 17 at Draft time, something that will look good in a lot of team models.

He was typically pitching at 93-94 mph with his fastball, but he was in the 94-97 mph range, and more of that consistently would certainly help him on Draft boards. There isn’t a ton of deception with the pitch right now, so it can get hit at times. He backs up the heater with a 78-81 mph slider that features three-quarters shape to it, a breaker that can disappear, miss a lot of bats and flashes plus. There’s feel for a changeup, too, which he sells well with arm speed out front. Schmidt has shown an ability to repeat his delivery well and fill up the strike zone with all three of his offerings, providing a very nice left-handed starting pitching kit. The LSU recruit reclassified to be done with high school early, so he’ll still be 17 at Draft time, something that will look good in a lot of team models.

Sorrell enters his draft spring as one of the higher variance college hitters in the entire class. He might swing and miss as much as he did in 2025 (his contact rate was only 70%) and slide out of the first round, or he might looks good in center field, make slightly more contact, and go inside the top 10. Sorrell certainly has the power to be a top pick, and he showed it in 2025 even though he was dealing with a hamate injury for a stretch of that season. He has big lefty bat speed and power that makes him capable of leaving the yard to all fields. He's a shorter-levered guy who can flatten his bat path to cover fastballs at the belt, which isn't true of many of the other whiff-risk college hitters in the 2026 draft. Sorrell also dealt with a hamstring issue in 2025 and fellow outfielder Jac LaViolette took center field reps from him when Sorrell was healthy. How he looks on defense in 2026 will be important. If his contact ability improves and Sorrell also looks playable in center field, he could be this draft's Colton Cowser.

Both of Sorrell's grandfathers played in the Majors: Billy Sorrell, an outfielder who shared a 1966 Topps rookie card with Ferguson Jenkins, and Tom Griffin, who led the big leagues in strikeout rate (9.6 per nine innings) as an Astros rookie in 1969. Caden's all-around tools could have made him a top-three-rounds pick as a Texas high schooler in 2023, but he went unselected because he wanted to attend Texas A&M. The starting left fielder on the Aggies' 2024 Men's College World Series runners-up as a freshman, he has been one of the most productive sluggers in the Southeastern Conference the last two seasons. Sorrell has the bat speed and strength to provide plenty of power and that's exactly what he tries to do, focusing on launching balls in the air to his pull side. That approach can get him in trouble, as his left-handed stroke becomes too long and uphill at times, but it also could pay off with 25-30 homers per season. He chases too many pitches and swings through more in-zone fastballs than he should, leading to some worries about his hitting ability at the next level. Sorrell displays plus speed when healthy but isn't terribly aggressive on the bases. In his first two college seasons, he played on the outfield corners in deference to 2025 first-rounder Jace LaViolette, but he's getting the job done in center field this spring with his quickness and instincts. If he moves off center in pro ball, his plus arm strength and offensive production will profile nicely in right field.

Brunson was drafted by the Blue Jays out of San Clemente High School in California but ended up at TCU, where he's been the everyday center fielder for two years. He is as well-rounded a college prospect as there is in the 2026 draft. Brunson is a plus runner and center field defender who has great gap-to-gap range and tracks balls hit over his head with ease and comfort. His all-fields contact approach yields mostly singles and doubles, but Brunson has big league physicality at 6-foot-3, 200 pounds, and his exit velocities are comfortably above the college average. His in-zone contact rate, across all of 2025 and during conference play, was above 90%. He has a good fourth outfielder's floor and might yet develop the strength to hit for enough power to be a first division regular out there, as Brunson will be barely 21 on draft day and is still filling out.

The Blue Jays took a flier on Brunson in the 18th round of the 2023 Draft, but the California prep prospect couldn't be dissuaded from attending Texas Christian. He became an immediate starter for the Horned Frogs in center field, displaying average-to-solid tools across the board. His all-around ability should land him in the top two rounds, even if being a right-handed hitter without a true plus tool limits his ceiling. A steady if unspectacular hitter, Brunson reached base in his first 43 games as a sophomore in 2025. He's an aggressive swinger but makes consistent contact and drills line drives from gap to gap. He translates the strength in his 6-foot-3, 200-pound frame into high-end exit velocities and 20-homer power that plays to all fields. Brunson has solid speed and will find spots to steal an occasional base. He doesn't have classic centerfield quickness but his instincts help him to track down balls in the gaps. If he can't remain up the middle in pro ball, his solid arm strength will fit nicely in right field.

Spangler is a very projectable 6-foot-3, lefty-hitting infielder from Northern California. His swing is bottom-hand dominant and has some length, but he still managed an 85% contact rate on the showcase circuit across a multi-year sample. His size makes it possible that, over time, he'll need to move off of shortstop to third base, but if that happens, he'll probably have enough power to profile there. There are scouts who think he'll be tough to sign.

De La Salle High School in Northern California has produced just one big leaguer in left-hander Kyle Harrison and has never had a first-round pick come from its program. The latter will most certainly change in the form of Spangler, a big shortstop with impressive all-around tools that he showcased at events like MLB’s High School All-American Game and the Area Code Games after being named the Metro Player of the Year as a junior by the San Francisco Chronicle. He wasn't able to build off of that as a back issue kept him sidelined for his senior season, though he did attend the Draft Combine to show what he could do. Because of Spangler’s size - he’s at least 6-foot-3 - his instincts and throwback approach to the game, more veteran baseball people have mentioned he reminds them of a young Cal Ripken Jr. type and because he hits left-handed, there are the invariable Corey Seager comparisons. Spangler is more polish than flash with a simple, solid approach at the plate, finding the barrel consistently. While he can be susceptible at times for breaking stuff down, he has excellent zone awareness and shows a willingness to use the middle of the field or go the other way. He can get to his pull side power at times and more thump should come as he fills out his frame and if he starts committing to getting the ball in the air more. An average runner, Spangler’s instincts make him a good baserunner and also give him the chance to stick at shortstop. He has easy actions defensively, with good hands and while he lacks explosive range, he tends to always be in a good position to make all the plays. If he gets too big, third base is always an option for the Stanford recruit.
