Cuvet started establishing his power hitting bona fides during his high school days at ESB Academy south of Fort Lauderdale in Florida, even enticing the Pirates to take a flier on him in the 17th round of the 2023 Draft. He headed a little further south to Miami and immediately showed the pop would play in college, setting a Hurricanes freshman record with 24 home runs. He followed that up with 18 more in 2025, putting him in a tie for seventh all-time at the school heading into his junior year. Cuvet has established himself as a feared member of Miami’s lineup, with perhaps as much raw power as anyone in the class. He can hit the ball out to all fields and even mis-hits balls over the fence. There are some holes in his swing, leading to some strikeout concerns, but he tends to cover the plate and has proven to be a decent two-strike hitter. If he can cut down the chase a bit, some feel he could approach being an average hitter, which means he might get to 70 in-game power. While he’s not a bad athlete, especially for his size - he’s close to an average runner underway - he has a bit of a slow motor at third base. So despite having an easily plus arm that fits at the hot corner, he’s likely destined to move to the other infield corner, though a team could see if he could handle an outfield corner in a Nick Castellanos kind of way. Wherever he lands defensively, it’s the power potential that will have teams calling in the top few rounds.

Because he's one of the older legitimate prospects in the 2026 high school class -- 19 years and five months old on Draft Day -- Bowen creates some mixed opinions among evaluators. Some believe his mix of tools and potential to stay at shortstop could merit a third-round pick if he's signable. In large part because of his age, others would rather see him prove himself for two years at Oklahoma State before making a significant investment. Bowen has a simple right-handed stroke that he repeats well while focusing on producing line drives from gap to gap. He has the bat speed to catch up to quality velocity and makes consistent contact. He doesn't show much present raw power and generates a lot of grounders, so he may top out at 12-15 homers per season. Bowen has plus speed that translates into base-stealing ability and range at shortstop. He has solid arm strength and should be able to remain at short. His athleticism and arm give him the versatility to play almost anywhere on the diamond.

Ken Dugan won 1,137 games and two NAIA national titles in 37 seasons at Lipscomb (Tenn.), which is now an NCAA Division I program that plays at a field bearing his name. His grandson Jack has rebounded from a rough showcase circuit performance to emerge as the best hitter among Tennessee high schoolers with a strong spring. He helped his cause with an opposite-field homer off a 98-mph fastball from possible second-rounder Bo Holloway at a heavily scouted matchup in late March. Dugan uses a quick left-handed stroke to produce hard contact to all fields. He currently focuses on driving the ball from gap to gap but has the bat speed and strength for 20-homer power once he learns to launch more balls in the air to his pull side. He has settled down and made nice adjustments after trying to do too much at the plate last summer, when he struggled to catch up to velocity and couldn't solve secondary pitches. Though Dugan has solid speed and athleticism, he lacks the actions to stick in the middle infield. He has the arm strength and offensive upside to profile at third base, though some scouts believe he's destined for an outfield corner. He draws rave reviews for his makeup and will be Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2028 if he follows through on his commitment to Tennessee.

Skelton impressed last summer at showcase events, performing well at East Coast Pro and the Area Code Games. He has begun to tap into more power in 2026, producing more homers (seven) than strikeouts (six) as a Tennessee high school senior before becoming one of the few prepsters to venture into the Appalachian League, a college summer circuit. He homered five times in his first seven games with wood bats against older competition before hammering balls in batting practice during the MLB Draft Combine. Though he employs a big leg kick at the plate, Skelton manages to stay on time and make a lot of hard contact with a relatively compact stroke. A right-handed hitter, he generates most of his present power to his pull side. He'll need to do a better job of recognizing breaking balls and toning down his aggressive approach at the next level, whether that's at Vanderbilt or in pro ball. Skelton has played shortstop in high school and the Appy League, but his below-average speed will dictate a move to another position. The best-case scenario is third base, though some scouts wonder if he'll wind up in left field. He has the solid arm strength for the hot corner and has been clocked up to 90 mph on the mound.

A legitimate two-way player from the New Jersey high school ranks, Weingartner didn’t register all that much on the summer showcase circuit, playing sparingly at the East Coast Pro Showcase and both pitching and hitting some at the Area Code Games. He started generating some buzz this winter when he broke the record with a 6.24-second 60-yard dash at the Prep Baseball Report Super 60 and continued to build a case for himself, more as a position player than a pitcher, as the top prep player in the Garden State this spring. While he can crank his fastball up to 94-96 mph on the mound at times, it’s Weingartner’s athleticism and tools as a position player that was garnering more attention this spring. He can put on a show in batting practice, with clear raw power from the right side of the plate. He’s shown some feel in games, but there is some length to what looks like a bit of a manufactured swing that some evaluators think might struggle with premium velocity from professional pitching. It’s obvious that Weingartner has plus speed, and the arm that can touch mid-90s as a pitcher works from shortstop. He could be the type of high school athlete who might need a couple of summers in a complex league, and it remains to be seen if a team will be willing to spend to keep him from honoring his commitment to Penn State.

A solid high school prospect from Dunedin, Florida, Beard began his college career in state at Florida Atlantic University, stepping right into the Owls rotation as a freshman. He took a big step forward as their sophomore ace in 2025, earning All American Athletic Conference First Team honors in the process before making a couple of Cape Cod League appearances and participating in USA Baseball’s Collegiate National Training Camp over the summer. A transfer to Florida State and the ACC could help his profile. Tall and lean, Beard is the quintessential pitchability college lefty with a strong feel for his craft and an unusual delivery to help it all play up. Everything comes from a very high slot that creates extension and deception. Velocity-wise, his fastball is fringy, sitting around 90-91 mph and topping out at 94, but he does a nice job of elevating it up and hitters chasing it out of the zone. His best pitch is his 75-77 mph changeup that gets “Bugs Bunny” comments from scouts, sold with outstanding arm speed. He has feel for spinning his breaking stuff with some depth, both a newer low-80s slider and a softer curve he’s had since his prep days, though they trail the cambio so he uses them a bit more strategically. Beard has made excellent strides with his ability to fill up the zone and limit walks. His ceiling might be a bit limited, but he’s reminded some of Guardians lefty Logan Allen, a second rounder out of Florida International in 2020, in terms of the path he could potentially follow.

Bishop Moore High School in the Orlando area has had one player get drafted to become a big leaguer, though long-time backup catcher Drew Butera went on to college first. Davis hopes to be the first from the program to be drafted at all since 2010, putting his name on the map at a number of MLB Develops events, including back-to-back Dream Series in 2024 and 2025, the 2025 Breakthrough Series and Hank Aaron Invitational, as well as the Area Code Games and MLB’s All-American Game. He’s gone on to establish himself as one of the more intriguing and most athletic prep hitters in Florida in this class. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Davis can do a lot of things well on the baseball field. He displays solid bat speed with an ability to get the bat through the zone quickly to make hard contact. While some evaluators are concerned about impact at the plate as he progresses, others have seen some ability to drive the ball with some sneaky raw power to his pull side thanks to a rotational swing. Davis is a plus runner who can use his speed to impact the game on both sides of the ball. He’s a basestealing threat and can go get the ball in center field, where he should be able to stay for a long time, with a chance to develop into a plus defender in time. He’ll head to Louisiana State for college ball if the Draft doesn’t work out.

One of the smallest and least projectable prep pitchers in MLB Pipeline's Draft rankings, Sullivan also has one of the quickest arms and most explosive fastballs. He ran his heater up to 97 while dominating at the Area Code Games, though he struggled at the U.S. 18-and-under national team trials. He also has a pair of promising secondary offerings and his total package could land him a seven-figure bonus. Sullivan's fastball sat at 94-95 mph on the showcase circuit and has parked at 92-94 in the colder Ohio weather this spring, and its carry makes it difficult to hit and to command. His low-80s curveball with downer break shows the potential to become at least a solid weapon, as does his mid-80s changeup with fade and sink. He also has a short mid-80s slider. Sullivan has so much action on his pitches and some effort in his delivery that he sometimes struggles to find the strike zone. His quality athleticism eventually could translate into at least average control, though some scouts wonder if his lack of physicality or smooth mechanics will make it tough to hold up as a starter. Similarly built Jacob Miller hasn't lived up to expectations since the Marlins made him a supplemental first-round pick out of an Ohio high school in 2022, but he also didn't have Sullivan's power. A Tennessee commit, he'll be Draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2028 if he makes it to college.

Nawrocki spent most of his junior season at Aledo (Texas) HS as a DH, helping the Bearcats win the state 5-A Division I title by batting .532 and winning championship game MVP honors by going 4-for-4. But he opened eyes with his pitching during the summer, including a dominant turn at the Area Code Games where he struck out five of the 12 hitters he faced, and dominated on the mound while leading Aledo to another championship this spring. Though his listed height of 5-foot-11 is generous, and he's almost certainly a reliever, his pure stuff could land him in the top three rounds. Nawrocki may have the best slider in the Draft, an 82-85 mph beast that can top 3,200 rpm and can feature either tremendous depth or sweep, depending on what he wants. His four-seam fastball ranges from 91-95 mph with high spin rates that create quality carry. He doesn't use his firm 85-88 mph changeup much, but its fade and his ability to land it for strikes give it the potential to become at least an average offering. While he's small, Nawrocki has a strong, athletic frame. It's impossible to project him as a starter, but it he can throw consistent strikes and maintain the stuff he displayed during the summer, he could become a high-leverage lefty reliever. Clubs may let him prove he can do that in college and he's committed to Louisiana State.

He doesn't use his firm 85-88 mph changeup much, but its fade and his ability to land it for strikes give it the potential to become at least an average offering. While he's small, Nawrocki has a strong, athletic frame. It's impossible to project him as a starter, but it he can throw consistent strikes and maintain the stuff he displayed during the summer, he could become a high-leverage lefty reliever. Clubs may let him prove he can do that in college and he's committed to Louisiana State.

Murdock headed from the Utah high school ranks to UC San Diego, redshirting his freshman year and then spending his first real season on the mound in 2025 making eight Sunday starts and seven other relief outings, with mixed results. He was a Cape Cod League All-Star last summer, racking up eight saves as a closer for Orelans. He returned to the Tritons’ rotation as a redshirt sophomore this spring and has shown glimpses of dominance, creating a buzz by outpitching Santa Barbara’s Jackson Flora with an eight-inning, 17-strikeout masterpiece in early April, but then failed to build on that momentum in his next couple of outings. At his best, Murdock is a strong power pitcher who can maintain his stuff deep into starts, one who could pitch with two plus pitches at the next level. In that start against UCSB, he sat 95 mph and missed bats with the pitch, but while he’s touched as high as 99 mph, he typically sits around 92-94 and it gets squared up. The slider is typically a legit out pitch, an 84-85 mph breaker that gets a ton of swings-and-misses along with chases. There’s a mid-80s changeup in there, but he rarely goes to it, throwing his fastball-breaker almost all of the time. More often than not, Murdock’s lack of command (well over five walks per nine in his college career), not to mention relatively low extension and effort in his delivery, leads to thoughts of reliever risk. A team interested in making him just the second Tritons pitcher to go in the top five rounds in over 50 years, joining Astros prospect Ryan Forcucci, could send him out as a starter while remembering just how good he looked coming out of the pen on the Cape.

Hailing from a Jesuit High School program in Oregon that produced first-round arms Mick Abel and Noble Meyer, Cooney headed south from his Portland area school to attend the University of Oregon for college ball. He was the only true freshman to start on opening day for the Ducks in what turned out to be an up-and-down first collegiate season for the infielder. Things clicked as a sophomore for Cooney, who earned All Big Ten first-team honors while leading Oregon in hitting and stolen bases. It’s been more of the same as the Ducks’ top bat during his junior campaign. If you get just one look at Cooney, he might not jump off the page because he doesn’t possess overly loud individual tools. Watch him for a while, though, and you can’t help but leave liking what he can do. There is some definite bat talent from the right side of the plate, with a good feel for the barrel and an advanced approach that has led to him walking as much as he’s striking out. He has a definite hit-over-power profile, but he has been getting to more damage this year and has been really locked in during conference play. Cooney has above-average speed and knows how to steal a base. He plays with an edge in a Dustin Pedroia kind of way, an aggressiveness scouts like. He initially lost his starting job at short to teammate Maddox Molony, then worked his way back into the starting lineup at second base. He’s a solid defender there, with some evaluators thinking he could still handle the left side of the infield at the next level.

Hill has been a major contributor to Greenwich Country Day since his freshman year at the Connecticut high school. He threw well as an underclassman at events like the Area Code Games in 2024, then after a solid junior season, opened a lot of eyes early in the summer in a Cape Cod League workout game at Fenway Park. That was it in terms of his summer work, however, as he didn’t pitch at the East Coast Professional Showcase or return to the Area Code Games as an incoming senior. At 6-foot-5, Hill is a projectable prep right-hander with a potential four-pitch mix. He can consistently pump his fastball up to 95-96 mph with some sink, with more in the tank to come. His best secondary offering is his hard slider that can miss bats, but he showed at Fenway he also has a distinct curve with big downer action. He can also drop in a solid changeup with some tail, a cambio he turns over well. Committed to Stanford, Hill’s combination of size and pitch mix point to a future starting pitcher at the next level, especially as his command improves. Because he wasn’t seen more over the summer, scouts will be eager for things to warm up in Connecticut and see if Hill can join the likes of Hiro Wyatt and Frank Mozzicato (both of whom were drafted by the Royals) as recent Nutmeggers to go in the top three rounds.

Ferraro began his college career at Texas A&M in the fall of 2023 before leaving for Blinn (Texas) JC and winning a Junior College World Series championship as a freshman in 2024. He batted .376/.497/.733 with 36 homers in two seasons with the Pirates, then transferred to Texas Tech and slashed .374/.481/.604 with eight longballs this spring. He comes with some of the best hitting data in this college crop but doesn't offer much value outside of the batter's box. Few college hitters combine the ability to execute good swing decisions, make consistent contact and generate premium exit velocities as well as Ferraro. A left-handed hitter, he has flipped his profile from power-over-hit at Blinn to hit-over-power with the Red Raiders. He owns plus raw pop but prioritizes drilling line drives from gap to gap rather than trying to crush balls to his pull side. Ferraro is a well-below-average runner who's conservative on the bases. He has spent most of this spring at DH with sporadic starts in right field, where he has limited range. He was a substandard defender at first base in junior college, though he does have average arm strength and displayed an upper-80s fastball when he pitched as a freshman.

One of the more athletic and projectable pitchers in the 2026 high school crop, Putnam got a late start on the diamond this spring because he had to finish the basketball season first. His fastball touched 97 mph in his second outing, and while his breaking ball and control have been inconsistent, his arm talent is undeniable. He could take off once he focuses on baseball full-time and gets pro instruction, and his upside could land him in the top three rounds. When he's on, Putnam can work at 94-96 mph with armside run on his fastball, which has ranged from 88-98 during his senior season. Gatorade's 2026 Missouri high school player of the year, he can flash some solid upper-70s sliders with quality depth, though his breaker lacks reliability and needs more power. His mid-80s changeup has nice fade and is a more dependable offering. Putnam has a quick arm and a 6-foot-5 frame with plenty of room to add strength, so his pitches should gain more velocity in the future. The Tennessee recruit moves down the mound very well, creating extension that allows his stuff to get on hitters quicker than they expect. He'll scatter his pitches at times but has the ingredients for at least average control as he gains more experience.

A high school product from outside of Athens, Georgia, Jones began his college career at Stetson University, opening a lot of eyes by posting a .935 OPS with 23 steals and earning ASUN Conference Freshman of the Year honors. His move to the University of Florida as a sophomore was cut short after just four games by season-ending shoulder surgery. He was swinging the bat well upon his return as a redshirt sophomore with the Gators this spring, though a lack of impact, especially in SEC play, was somewhat hampering his Draft stock. A 6-foot-3 athletic right-handed hitter, Jones had been as advertised for much of the 2026 season. He has a solid approach at the plate with good bat-to-ball skills, walking nearly as often as striking out in his college career. While he hasn’t been driving the ball, being more of a gap-to-gap guy, there is some projection in his frame, and some think he could get to power, at least to his pull side, if he can learn to get behind the ball better. Jones is a premium athlete but wasn’t clocking in plus run times at the start of the spring, though he was showing more effort and stealing more bags as the season unfolded. He also has the ability to play a very good center field, especially when he’s going full throttle. Some of the energy-related issues could have been him just feeling himself out following last year’s left shoulder labrum surgery, and a strong finish to his SEC campaign could help push him up a bit on Draft boards.

Hernandez registered on scouting radars as a Georgia prepster in 2024, but not enough for clubs to consider buying him away from Georgia Tech. He earned Atlantic Coast Conference freshman of the year accolades in 2025, starting games at six different spots (including one as a pitcher) and breaking Matt Wieters' freshman school record with 69 RBIs. Draft-eligible as a sophomore, he could factor in the top three rounds but also has struggled in ACC play and hasn't shown as much power this spring. Hernandez combines strength with good swing decisions to produce impressive exit velocities. But he also comes with some concerns at the plate, most notably his struggles to make contact against breaking balls. There's some arm bar in his right-handed stroke, which can get long and uphill, and he makes too much ground-ball contact while rarely pulling the ball. Though Hernandez has played a variety of positions, he's a below-average runner who's overmatched at second or third base. He's a fringy defender on the outfield corners and average at first. He does possess the arm strength for right field and pushed his fastball to 93 mph last year before concentrating on hitting as a sophomore.

As the spring high school season in Northern California approached, most scouts probably thought that shortstop Tyler Spangler would be the main attraction when they headed to De La Salle High School. While Spangler hasn’t played this season, Schlicht has made the trip worthwhile whenever he’s been on the mound. The big right-hander, who impressed with his feel for pitching at the Area Code Games last summer, has been exceptional during his senior year, not allowing a run over his first five starts to make teams seriously ponder whether he’s signable. At 6-foot-3 and 195 pounds, Schlicht screams projection while showcasing a very solid four-pitch mix. While there was hope he might have more of a velocity jump this spring, he was getting his fastball up to 94 mph early this season -- sitting more 90-91 as the year went on -- and the pitch plays because it has good finish coming from a low release point. He can really spin two breaking balls, both of which could be plus in time. His slider might have a slight edge with super high spin and good tilt to it over his 11-to-5 curve. He has solid feel for an above-average straight changeup. Schlicht is a solid athlete who gets down the mound well. He repeats his delivery consistently and fills up the strike zone with all of his offering while showing a huge competitive streak when he’s on the bump. He could be the type of prep arm a team with multiple picks makes a play at early, though there is a commitment to Stanford to contend with.

Bishop Moore High School in the Orlando area has had one player get drafted to become a big leaguer, though long-time backup catcher Drew Butera went on to college first. Davis hopes to be the first from the program to be drafted at all since 2010, putting his name on the map at a number of MLB Develops events, including back-to-back Dream Series in 2024 and 2025, the 2025 Breakthrough Series and Hank Aaron Invitational, as well as the Area Code Games and MLB’s All-American Game. He’s gone on to establish himself as one of the more intriguing and most athletic prep hitters in Florida in this class. A left-handed hitter and thrower, Davis can do a lot of things well on the baseball field. He displays solid bat speed with an ability to get the bat through the zone quickly to make hard contact. While some evaluators are concerned about impact at the plate as he progresses, others have seen some ability to drive the ball with some sneaky raw power to his pull side thanks to a rotational swing. Davis is a plus runner who can use his speed to impact the game on both sides of the ball. He’s a basestealing threat and can go get the ball in center field, where he should be able to stay for a long time, with a chance to develop into a plus defender in time. He’ll head to Louisiana State for college ball if the Draft doesn’t work out.

Brother Rice High School in Michigan has produced three big leaguers. One, Nick Plummer, signed out of the prep ranks as a first-rounder in 2015. The other two, pitcher Karl Kauffman and its best alum, DJ LeMahieu, went on to college before re-emerging in the Draft. Dowd is following the path of those two, first spending two productive years at Southern California before transferring to Florida State for his junior season, during which he slowed down as ACC play progressed. Dowd is more of a “sum of his parts” kind of outfielder rather than one with loud tools. Scouts do like the way he can handle the bat from the left side of the plate. He repeats his swing well, making a ton of contact and spraying the ball around the whole field. He might never be a huge power guy, but he will take his chances when the opportunity arises, showing the ability to get the ball in the air when he does. He controls the zone very well, drawing more walks than strikeouts, giving him a possible table-setting role in the future. While he’s not a burner, Dowd is very smart on the basepaths, showing the ability to take extra bags, even if he’s never a threat to steal. While patrolling the grass, he’s displayed the ability to get good jumps in center field and has shown he can handle the corners as well. Some see him as a bit of a tweener profile-wise, one who might be more of a fourth outfielder, but his high floor and plus makeup are assets.

Jorgensen tore the ACL in his right knee during a baseball workout, leading to surgery in February 2025 that sidelined him for his junior season at Jesuit Prep (Dallas) as well as the summer showcase circuit. He returned with a strong inning at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October and has been unhittable for much of this spring. He's the grandson of Mike Jorgensen, who spent 17 years as a first baseman in the big leagues before a long post-playing career with the Cardinals that included nine years as farm director and a partial season as interim manager. Jorgensen creates plenty of backspin on his fastball, which sits at 92-94 mph and touches 97 with bat-missing carry. He also generates high spin rates on his upper-70s curveball, which features plenty of downer break. His low-80s changeup with splitter action gives him a solid third pitch, and some scouts believe it's his best offering. With his fastball characteristics and strong 6-foot frame, Jorgensen draws repeated comparisons to Logan Henderson. The Texas recruit gets down the mound well and produces a surprising amount of extension for his size from a high arm slot. Some evaluators worry about his lack of physicality and projection as well as the effort in his delivery, which results in inconsistent control.

Tennessee's top prep prospect in 2023, McElvain went undrafted because he was intent on following in the footsteps of his older brother Chris (now in the Blue Jays system) and attending Vanderbilt. He compiled a 5.33 ERA in two years with the Commodores before transferring to Arkansas and enjoying much more success. He logged a 1.88 ERA and 34 percent strikeout rate while establishing himself as one of the top lefty relievers in the Draft. McElvain is throwing a tick harder this season, working with a 94-96 mph fastball that peaks at 98 and is most effective when he locates it with carry up in the zone. The Razorbacks have had him employ his heater more than ever and mostly shelve the slider and curveball he used at Vanderbilt. He mainly complements his fastball with a cutter that averages 89 mph and touches 92, tying up both lefties and righties. Arkansas has streamlined McElvain's delivery, helping him repeat it more easily while still preserving much of its funk. He has cut his 17 percent walk rate at Vandy in half this spring, though his command still wavers at times. He's purely a reliever but has the stuff and mentality to handle a late-inning role.

Malony is a viable defensive shortstop who has posted two practically identical underclass years at Oregon, with a .968 OPS in both campaigns. He's a strapping 6-foot-1, has authoritative hitting hands, and is often on time to pull. But Malony's style has him pulling off a lot of sliders, and he doesn't always track the baseball well, so his hit tool projection here is a good bit south of what it'd be if one were to take his 2025 data at face value. A viable shortstop fit, Malony projects as a utilityman in the Zack Short mold.

A product of the Oregon high school ranks, Molony stayed in state for college ball. He made an immediate impact at University of Oregon, earning freshman All-American and first-team all-Pac 12 honors after finishing with a .969 OPS. He duplicated that OPS effort as a sophomore, finishing with 15 homers and 10 steals. A rough stint in the Cape Cod League didn’t help his overall profile, but he’s still the best prospect in the Pacific Northwest. While he’s not in the same category as Aiva Arquette, the Oregon State shortstop who was the No. 7 overall pick in the 2025 Draft, Molony has plenty of attributes to like. The right-handed hitter produces plenty of bat speed coming from a strong and athletic 6-foot-2 frame. The power continues to come, especially to his pull side, though his inability to get to it with a wood bat on the Cape concerns some scouts. He rarely swings and misses at in-zone offerings, but not everyone is sold on his pure hit tool to get to that power. Most evaluators give Molony the chance to stick at shortstop. He’s average, maybe a tick above, as a runner, but he has solid range, good hands and more than enough arm for the premium position. He’s unlikely to reach Arquette levels come Draft time, but a strong junior season with the Ducks could vault him into first-round conversations.

Malony is a viable defensive shortstop who has posted two practically identical underclass years at Oregon, with a .968 OPS in both campaigns. He's a strapping 6-foot-1, has authoritative hitting hands, and is often on time to pull. But Malony's style has him pulling off a lot of sliders, and he doesn't always track the baseball well, so his hit tool projection here is a good bit south of what it'd be if one were to take his 2025 data at face value. A viable shortstop fit, Malony projects as a utilityman in the Zack Short mold.

Tiroly spent his first two years of college ball at Rider University in New Jersey, earning Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference Player of the Year honors as a sophomore. He entered the transfer portal and landed at Virginia, but a foot injury suffered at the end of the fall kept him from showing the Cavaliers or scouts checking him out in his new environment for the first time what he could do. A lack of prep time because of the injury, as well as not being 100 percent to start the spring led to a very slow start, but he was growing on evaluators as he heated up in ACC play. After having so much success in the MAAC, it was unclear how Tiroly would perform against a higher level of competition in a top conference. The right-handed hitter literally couldn’t put his best foot forward, not facing live pitching until opening weekend and wearing a boot between games. As he put the injury behind him, he started showing off a much better feel to hit, with more pop in conference play, answering that question about his ability to handle ACC pitching. Tiroly wasn’t a runner before the injury, so that part of his game wasn’t impacted in any real way. He’s a capable defender at both second and third, with enough arm for the hot corner. Some feel that might be his better position because of a lack of overall range, though playing third would put more pressure on him to keep showing an impact bat at the plate.

An all-state pitcher, wide receiver and wrestler as a Missouri high schooler, LaPour flashed mid-90s fastballs but was so raw on the mound that he went undrafted and received minimal recruiting interest. He quickly added polish in college, cracking Wichita State's rotation as a freshman before transferring to Texas Christian for 2025, when he became the first Horned Frog to record six straight quality starts since Nick Lodolo in 2019. He's one of the most physical and hardest-throwing pitchers in the college class, though he missed two and a half months early in the season with elbow soreness. At his best, LaPour works at 95-98 mph and reaches 101 with heavy sink on his fastball, though it's not as dominant as its velocity might indicate because its shape and command are ordinary. His mid-80s slider can be a plus pitch with two-plane depth at its best, though it breaks so much that he struggles to land it for strikes and rarely uses it when behind in the count. His fading upper-80s changeup is a more reliable offering and he also has tinkered with an upper-80s cutter. Built like a linebacker, LaPour has a physical 6-foot-4 frame and has learned to repeat his simple delivery well enough to develop average control. His biggest proponents see a durable three-pitch starter who might have snuck into the first round with a healthy junior season. Other evaluators think he doesn't miss enough bats and may be better suited for the bullpen, where his bulldog mentality would fit nicely.

Ponatoski won Gatorade's Ohio Player of the Year awards in both baseball and football as a junior in 2024-25, joining Joe Mauer and Randy Moss as the only athletes to earn Gatorade honors in two sports in the same academic year. A four-star quarterback recruit committed to Kentucky in both sports, he skipped summer football workouts with the Wildcats. He may not have pitched enough for his signability to align with his ability for most clubs. Ponatoski's most impressive pitching performance was a one-inning stint at the East Coast Pro showcase last August, when he operated at 93-95 mph with carry and armside run on his fastball and displayed a plus curveball with power and downer break in the low 80s. This spring, his heater often settled at 90-92 mph after an inning or two and his curve wasn't as sharp. His mid-80s changeup is too firm and very much a work in progress. While Ponatoski is athletic and provides strikes, he's not particularly projectable at 6-foot-2 and 200 pounds. He totaled about 30 innings between his junior and senior seasons, plus the showcase circuit, and he might take off if he focuses on pitching after preferring to play shortstop in the past. He's a long-term project with upside but won't realize it until he commits to baseball full-time.

When Chris Pollard left Duke to take over as the head coach at the University of Virginia in the summer of 2025, seven players followed him via the transfer portal. The marquee name was first-round candidate AJ Gracia, but it also included Johnson, a two-way player with more upside on the mound. A strong fall had scouts in the area excited about what he might be able to do as a pitcher for the Cavaliers, but he was slowed out of the gate by what was termed a kinetic chain issue, and he didn’t make his first appearance until March 20. As he has throughout his college career, he put up inconsistent numbers on the bump. Despite a less-than-pretty statline, scouts are still bullish on Johnson as an athletic left-hander who has yet to focus on pitching full-time. He has as many as five pitches to work with, starting with a fastball that averaged a touch over 93 mph but topped out at 97-98 mph this spring, and it some ride to it when he’s at the top of the zone. His slider, thrown up to 83-84 mph, can be a 1-to-7, hammer-like breaker with a ton of swing and miss. He has a distinct upper-70s curve and can also throw a harder, 86-88 mph cutter. He used his low-80s changeup more than any other secondary pitch, throwing it downhill with armside sink and run, a cambio he’ll throw to hitters on both sides of the plate. Johnson has never been a consistent strike-thrower, carrying a career 4.6 BB/9 (5.1 per nine in 2026) rate into NCAA Regional play this year. But there are some raw ingredients to work with, and there were teams who felt he was worthy of top five round consideration, with perhaps another gear to reach when he puts the bat down for good.

Harvard-Westlake High School in southern California has produced high-end Draft talent, from first-round quality arms like Lucas Giolito, Max Fried and Jack Flaherty to exciting hitters like Pete Crow-Armstrong and most recently, 2024 first-rounder Bryce Rainer. This year’s entry is Tronstein, whose Draft stock was up in the air after he scuffled some on the summer showcase circuit but turned things around this spring, particularly in front of a lot of eyes at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational. An athletic 5-foot-11 right-handed bat, Tronstein is an aggressive hitter who is looking to do damage at all times. He’s able to hit the ball very hard, like he did with some elite exit velocities at NHSI, and can drive the ball to all fields with some sneaky pop. He had a tendency to chase too much out of the zone over the summer, leading to some swing-and-miss concerns, and he has a penchant for lunging against soft stuff too much, something that will have to be addressed at the next level. Tronstein is an above-average runner, plus underway, and his speed can help him on both sides of the ball. He’s played both shortstop and the outfield, and while he has an average arm, scouts tend to like him better in center, where his athleticism plays well, because his arm might be a bit shy for plays in the hole. The biggest hurdle for teams considering Tronstein might be his commitment to Vanderbilt.

Weinstein spent his first three seasons of high school at powerhouse Huntington Beach, a program that produced players like 2023 first-rounder Ralphy Velazquez and won a pair of National High School Invitational titles. Weinstein moved over to Orange Lutheran -- owner of four NHSI championships and Gerrit Cole's alma mater -- for his senior season so that he could get the chance to play shortstop. Weinstein has hit wherever he's been, whether it’s over the years as a mainstay in the Huntington Beach lineup, this spring for OLu or at showcase events like the Area Code Games and PG National. He has a nice, balanced left-handed swing geared for contact and an advanced approach at the plate, never giving away at-bats. He’s hit-over-power but he does have some ability to drive the ball in the air to his pull side. While the ultra-competitive Weinstein is a below-average runner, he’s shown he has very good range on the dirt. He's looked solid defensively at short this spring, with solid actions and enough arm where scouts feel he should be allowed to begin his pro career at the premium position. He might be best suited eventually as a hit-tool driven second baseman at the next level, but the biggest question surrounding the infielder is if he is signable away from his commitment to Louisiana State.

One of the better sophomore-eligible prospects in the 2026 Draft, Wentz offers power from both sides of the plate and has helped his cause by improving his conditioning and athleticism. But he also has flummoxed scouts with his inability to stop chasing or do much damage against breaking balls and changeups. Viewed as a potential second-round choice entering 2026, he may have to wait a couple of more rounds to hear his name called. Wentz's combination of bat speed and strength gives him at least plus raw power, and he could tap into more of it if he became more selective and pulled more balls in the air. More effective from the left side, he destroys fastballs but scuffles against everything else, and his aggressiveness leaves him especially vulnerable to changeups. He draws his share of walks because pitchers are reticent to challenge him, but he needs to tone down his approach. The 6-foot-2, 215-pound Wentz is moving better as sophomore and displaying fringy speed. He has split his college career between third base and second base, and his limited range and solid arm strength fit better at the hot corner. He's an erratic defender at both positions, so he may wind up on an outfield corner.

Though McCoy recorded a 7.11 ERA in his first two seasons at South Carolina, a brief but dominant stint in the Cape Cod League last summer left some evaluators wondering if he might be the best college left-hander in the 2026 Draft. He struck out 25 of the 54 Cape batters he faced while issuing just three walks in three starts. He has the stuff and metrics to back up that performance and will have to show that he can sustain it, but he won't get the chance to do so this year after blowing out his elbow in January and requiring Tommy John surgery. McCoy's fastball gained a couple of ticks of velocity on the Cape, parking at 94-95 mph and peaking at 98 with natural cutting action. He also threw a nasty mid-80s slider with plenty of sweep and mixed in some true cutters at 87-91 mph. He doesn't have much trust in a fading upper-80s changeup that he struggles to locate. McCoy's low three-quarters arm slot and resulting low release height create pitches with an unusual combination of velocity and shapes that are hard for hitters to deal with. He lacks size, has effort in his delivery and doesn't have much track record of success or strikes, so he might be more reliever than starter. He looked like he could pitch in the front half of a rotation while on the Cape, and he has the arsenal for a high-leverage role if he does wind up in the bullpen.

Rangel grew up pitching and playing quarterback with the assumption that he'd play two sports at the Colony (Texas) HS, where his father Rudy had been the head football coach for two decades. When it became apparent that his future was brighter on the mound, he gave up the gridiron after his freshman year. He has an electric arm but also comes with some reliever risk. Rangel achieves high spin rates on his two best pitches. His 93-96 mph fastball reaches 98 with carry and armside run, and his low-80s curveball combines power and depth at its best. He'll flash a tighter version of his breaking ball and potentially could develop a distinct slider with more velocity. His upper-80s kick changeup is too firm and rarely used, but it does show some sink and promise. Though he's very athletic, Rangel is smaller than most pitchers and lacks physicality. Add in a slingy delivery with some effort that provides deception but hampers his strike-throwing, and the Texas recruit may be better suited for the bullpen than the rotation. Scouts praise his intelligence and competitiveness, and he could become a high-leverage reliever if he's not a starter. Some teams may hold his age (19 years, three months on Draft day) against him, and he’ll be sophomore-eligible for the 2028 Draft if he makes it to college.

Over the past few years, Basic HS has stood out as one of the best programs in the Las Vegas area, with a few legitimate Draft prospects produced over the past five years. The Southisene family has been a major contributor, with Ty a fourth-round pick in 2024 and Tate going in the first round a year ago. There’s another Southisene -- Troy -- in this year's class, but it’s actually Giles who is the top prospect on the team as an outfielder with a little helium following a strong senior season after which he impressed in workouts with clubs. Strong and compact, Giles has the chance to be a solid offensive performer. He shows off hitterish traits from the left side, showing a solid, balanced approach and the ability to make a lot of solid contact. He looks like he’s more of a hit-over-power guy, but he can drive the ball to all fields. He’ll show off the raw power he can keep learning to tap into in BP, the kind of pop that will surely impress in workouts. An average runner, Giles does have the chance to play center field, though not everyone thinks he can stick there. A once easily plus arm that fired mid-90s fastballs from the mound now looks more above-average after he dealt with elbow soreness that forced him into a DH role during last summer’s Area Code Games. It’s still plenty for an outfield corner, though that move will put more pressure on his bat. To some, it gives him a little more of a tweener profile, but those who see every day player potential will consider signing him away from his commitment to Oregon.

A consistent performer who has slashed .345/.432/.634 in three college seasons, one at Mary (N.D.) and two at Indiana State, Beck won Missouri Valley Conference player of the year honors as a junior. He's a favorite of analytically minded teams, who love his contact rates and exit velocities. One of those clubs could take him inside the top three rounds, which would make him the first Sycamores position player selected that high since Jason Frome in 2001. Though Beck's left-handed swing is unorthodox and a bit stiff and his approach is aggressive, they work for him. His quantity and quality of contact are better than those of most college players, and he almost never comes up empty when he swings at strikes. Scouts who like him believe he can become a better hitter and tap into more power if he can become more selective. Beck has solid speed that plays better on the bases than in the field. His reads and routes need improvement in center field, though he'll get the chance to stick there in pro ball. If he can't, his fringy arm strength will land him in left field and put more pressure on his bat.

Lascelles has been establishing himself as the top Canadian position player in the 2026 Draft class for some time now, playing for the Toronto Mets in the Canadian Premier Baseball League and the Canadian Junior National Team, while also displaying his tools at premier events like the Canadian Futures Showcase last fall and Prep Baseball Report’s Super 60 this past winter. But he really gave his Draft stock a boost with visits to both Arizona and Florida this spring, facing almost entirely professional pitchers. The left-handed swinging Lascelles has pretty much hit wherever he’s been. This spring was no different, when he hit a combined .389 with four extra-base hits in 54 at-bats against Minor League arms. It’s a little bit of an unorthodox setup at the plate, with his elbows far apart and a steep bat path when he swings, but he routinely sends line drives up the middle with a left- to-right-center field approach. He doesn’t always get into his legs, leading to some questions about how much power he’ll have. Lascelles also runs track for his high school and he’s a borderline plus runner who knows how to steal a base. Lascelles has been establishing himself as the top Canadian position player in the 2026 Draft class for some time now, playing for the Toronto Mets in the Canadian Premier Baseball League and the Canadian Junior National Team, while also displaying his tools at premier events like the Canadian Futures Showcase last fall and Prep Baseball Report’s Super 60 this past winter. But he really gave his Draft stock a boost with visits to both Arizona and Florida this spring, facing almost entirely professional pitchers. The left-handed swinging Lascelles has pretty much hit wherever he’s been. This spring was no different, when he hit a combined .389 with four extra-base hits in 54 at-bats against Minor League arms. It’s a little bit of an unorthodox setup at the plate, with his elbows far apart and a steep bat path when he swings, but he routinely sends line drives up the middle with a left- to-right-center field approach. He doesn’t always get into his legs, leading to some questions about how much power he’ll have. Lascelles also runs track for his high school and he’s a borderline plus runner who knows how to steal a base. The TNXL Academy was formed in 2014 to provide baseball players in Florida an alternative high school experience that would provide more instruction and better competition. Since then, the program has produced 10 draftees, though none have made it to the big leagues to date. There are a pair of arms at TNXL this year getting plenty of attention in lefty Spencer Evans and Brady, who moved from the Buffalo, New York, area to train in Florida and raise his Draft profile considerably. Brady offers excellent size at 6-foot-5 and projection, showing off a four-pitch mix at summer showcase events like Perfect Game National, the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Games, before putting together a solid senior season. The fastball is average right now, though he commands the heater he can get up to 95 mph well. He has both a low-80s slider with good angle and an upper-70s curve that’s improved. Some scouts like his changeup better and he has very good feel for his 85-mph cambio. The big right-hander uses a cross-fire delivery that creates some deception and adds some quality to his breaking ball. He moves easily down the mound and fills up the strike zone, with upside to all of his offerings and a good chance to be a starter long-term. Teams also like that he’ll still be just 17 years old come Draft time, though they’ll have to contend with his Louisiana State commitment.

Amalbert really jumped on the Draft scene with a huge showing at last summer’s Area Code Games, when several evaluators singled him out as the best hitter at the event. He started cutting his teeth before that at MLB Develops events like the Hank Aaron Invitational, in 2023 and 2024, as well as the 2025 Dream Series. His offensive potential and tools were getting plenty of attention back home in New Jersey, though his performance wasn’t as consistently electric as it was over the summer. Amalbert’s plus bat speed stands out from the right side of the plate. It’s a swing that some long-time scouts in the Northeast say reminds them of the high school version of Manny Ramirez. And at times, Amalbert looks like he could be an outstanding hitter with elite exit velocities, one who will impress with blast numbers in workouts. Then there are times he struggles with breaking stuff and finding the barrel, like he did over his first several games this spring. When he’s locked in, he shows the potential to be an above-average hitter with above-average power. A plus runner, Amalbert didn’t appear to have a true position. Initially a shortstop, that didn’t really fit, but it seems like he’s found a home in center field, where he’s shown pretty good instincts to go along with that speed. After the Area Codes, scouts may have pegged him to easily be a third-rounder, and he’s going to be crosschecked enough for teams to have a better feel whether his tools are worth trying to draft away from his commitment to Oklahoma.

Coming out of the Queens, New York high school ranks, Montesa began his college career with Division II Adelphi in his home state. He earned Northeast 10 Conference Pitcher of the Year honors as a sophomore, catching the attention of Division I programs. The right-hander transferred to West Virginia for his junior season and opened a lot of eyes early in the season to give himself some helium. He wasn’t able to maintain it consistently, especially in Big 12 play, but while he lost his rotation spot late in the year, scouts still liked his pure stuff enough to keep him in Day 2 conversations. Montesa is an athletic 6-foot-1 right-hander who has a four-pitch mix that could give him the chance to start at the next level. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and can touch 98 at times, and it’s a tough pitch to barrel -- with a decent amount of swing-and-miss -- when he’s up in the zone. Command of the pitch was iffy at best, and the heater can get hit when he’s down in the zone with it too much. He does have a very good feel for spin for both his preferred upper-70s curve that he can manipulate the shape of when he’s locked in and his lesser-thrown harder and shorter mid-80s slider, both of which miss plenty of bats. There is a firm upper-80s changeup in there as well, though it’s clearly his fourth pitch. The biggest thing holding Montesa back is his command. His walk rate climbed as the 2026 season wore on, and his 5.98 BB/9 rate in Big 12 play undoubtedly contributed to him being taken out of the rotation as postseason play loomed, though his good raw stuff and age (he’s still only 20 years old come Draft time) were enough for teams to be discussing in the top several rounds.

The best player to ever come out of Butler Area High School north of Pittsburgh is right-hander Matt Clement, a 1993 third-rounder who spent parts of nine years in the big leagues, but there hasn’t been a player drafted from the program since 2003. This year, the Golden Tornado have a pair of right-handed pitchers who have intrigued scouts. The scouting industry might have had Nolan Stefaniak ahead of Casteel entering the spring, but that’s likely flipped as the latter has made some big strides this spring. Casteel’s combination of size, projection and improved pitchability had teams running to western Pennsylvania to get more looks at him.The 6-foot-4 hurler typically sits around 92 mph and tops out at 95 mph, but he can maintain the low-90s velocity deep into starts, and it’s easy to dream about more to come as he fills out his frame. He has a slider that has the chance to be a true out pitch, mostly with three-quarters shape, depth and bite, though he can manipulate it into more of a slurve or a sweeper as he needs it. He doesn’t use his changeup much, but it has the chance to be a solid third offering with some fade. In addition to Casteel’s stuff ticking up, he also showed a better feel for finding the zone, with solid command and control compared to looks from the fall. The feel for pitching and pure arm strength point to some ceiling here, with some evaluators talking about the West Virginia recruit in the top five rounds.

McNeillie was the top high school pitcher in Georgia in 2023, but went undrafted because he was intent on fulfilling his commitment to the University of Florida. He was an intriguing combination of projection and polish when he got to campus and three years later, scouts are still trying to figure out who he is as a pitcher. He’s thrown almost entirely as a reliever, showing off premium stuff at times but not with results that have always matched it. There was hope the 6-foot-3 McNeillie would take to a starting role at some point with the Gators, but while that hasn’t come to pass, some feel he should be given a chance to do so as a pro. His stuff is louder in shorter stints out of the bullpen, starting with a fastball that’s been 96-99 mph this year as a reliever. It can have some carry when it’s at the top of the zone, and there’s some occasional, perhaps unintentional, two-seam action because his delivery pulls him open and he drops his slot, but it’s often too straight and gets hit more than it should. His best and most-frequently thrown pitch is his 86-88 mph slider and it flashes plus, with good downer action to it when it’s on. There is a changeup in there, but he doesn’t use it often. McNeillie’s command in and out of the zone has been spotty at Florida and that, along with a lack of extension or deception, makes it tougher to project what he might be at the next level. He can get caught between trying to be a complete pitcher and attacking with his power stuff. There will be teams interested in his arm strength, with one good at pitching development perhaps working with him on starting long-term.

Harris entered the start of the summer showcase circuit last year considered one of the best high school position players in the country. And he showed off glimpses of his considerable tools at nearly every event possible, including the Perfect Game National, both PG’s and MLB’s High School All-American Games, the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Game. With his skills, however, came some questions about his hit tool. When the Jacksonville, Florida prep standout continued to have swing-and-miss issues during his senior year, his Draft stock took a hit, leaving his status up in the air. At 6-foot-2 and hitting from the right side, he’s reminded some area scouts in Florida of a young Dylan Crews, who played his high school ball in Florida before heading to LSU. There is definite raw power in his game, and he can get to it at times when he keeps his barrel in the zone for a long time and creates leverage. But he has struggled to find consistency at the plate, with strikeouts still plaguing him this spring, especially having difficulty connecting against breaking stuff. Harris does have above-average speed and uses it well on both sides of the ball. When he combines it with his outstanding instincts in center field, he looks like a potentially plus defender up the middle in the future. The arm would play in a corner, and he might have the raw power to profile there if need be, but it might not be until he spends some years in the University of Florida lineup before he moves on to pro ball.

Sosa was a solid high school prospect on the east coast of Florida who was in the top 125 of MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 250 back in 2023. He went undrafted and headed to North Carolina State to begin his college career, spending two years with the Wolfpack before being considered one of the best players, especially behind the plate, in the transfer portal. He came back home, fulfilling a dream to play for Miami for his junior season, putting up excellent numbers for the Hurricanes. There were two big questions surrounding Sosa when he got to Miami: Can he hit for average and can he catch? He’s improved on both fronts this spring to improve his Draft stock. Scouts have some conviction his left-handed swing will play at the next level, with what is now a solid gap-to-gap approach. He has very good raw power to his pull side that he’s been getting to in games, while also showing this season that he can handle left-handed pitching, cutting down his strikeout rate and drawing more walks. Sosa still has work to do in his overall defense behind the dish, but he has made strides in his blocking and does a good job of framing and stealing strikes. He has fringy arm strength which can play up as average at times because of his quick release. He has the floor of being a solid backup or platoon type, with the ceiling of being an every day, bat-first catcher.

Hailing from Oakton High School in Virginia, Lavey stayed in the region to head to George Washington University to extend his baseball career. He made an immediate impact as a freshman, earning second-team All Atlantic 10 honors, repeating the feat again as a junior. In between, he was a Cape Cod League All-Star. His solid showing on the Cape, carrying that over to the 2026 season and constant need for decent all-around catchers had teams considering Lavey in the top several rounds. Lavey checks off an oft-coveted box as a left-handed-hitting catcher. Nothing he does is flashy, but he can do everything pretty well. He has an easy swing, with a line-drive, up the middle approach, and he has the strength to drive the ball at times, with solid exit velocity data to back that up. He doesn’t swing and miss or chase much and walked more than he struck out as a junior. Behind the plate, there’s work to be done, but he has the makings of a solid defensive backstop, one with an above-average arm and pop times under 2.00 seconds. He’d receive better instruction on his glove work on the pro side, so there’s some ceiling to reach there. That and his steady bat had some believing he could go in the top five rounds come Draft time.

Plant City HS, located between Tampa and Lakeland in Florida, has produced two big leaguers over the years. Both were left-handed pitchers: Kenny Rogers, who signed out of high school, and Parker Messick, who went on to Florida State before being drafted by the Guardians in 2022. Carbaugh might be right-handed, but he has the chance to be the first player drafted from the school since Rogers in 1982 after initially showing off his size and stuff at summer showcase events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Perfect Game National, then continuing to miss bats during his senior season. Teams are likely to be intrigued by Carbaugh’s 6-foot-5 frame and potential three-pitch mix. He can crank his fastball up to 96 mph. It has two-seam characteristics, with more run than sink because he delivers it from a low slot. He has a slider, thrown around 80 mph, that has more sweep than tilt regularly. He hasn’t used his changeup much, but he has some feel for the low-80s offspeed offering. Considering his size, Carbaugh does a decent job of repeating his delivery and finding the strike zone, though it’s definitely control over command. The Mississippi State recruit reminds some scouts of 2024 prospect Dylan Jordan (who joined the Angels after receiving an over-slot deal in the fifth round that July), albeit without as much extension.

Thiel is one of the more projectable and most improved high school pitchers in the Midwest. The 6-foot-7 left-hander topped out at 88 mph during East Coast Pro tryout last summer and failed to make the team, but he has added about 5 mph to his fastball this spring. While many scouts believe he'd be best served by attending Ohio State and adding more strength and polish, there are enough interested teams that he may not get to Columbus. Thiel now reaches 94 mph early in games and operates at 89-91 mph throughout his starts, imparting carry and armside run on his heater. He gets good depth on a curveball that reaches the upper 70s and owns a slider with more power and horizontal action but less consistency. He also demonstrates feel for a changeup that parks around 80 mph and drops at the plate. After gaining significant strength during the last year, Thiel now carries 230 pounds on his tall frame and still has room to add more. He uses his size to create extension and angle that add deception. He throws more strikes than most teenage southpaws his size and projects to develop average control and command.

One of the biggest wild cards in the Draft, Jelkin got dismissed from Nebraska as a freshman in 2022 and teams are still wary of his makeup. He spent 2023 at South Mountain (Ariz.) CC before blowing out his elbow at Houston the following spring, requiring Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of last season at Kentucky. He turned down the Dodgers as a 14th-rounder in 2023 and the Mets as a ninth-rounder in '24. Though he'll be 23 years and seven months old on Draft Day, he also has top two rounds stuff and earned second-team All-Southeastern Conference honors as a redshirt senior. Jelkin operates with three solid pitches with high spin rates, the best of which is a low-80s curveball with quality depth. His fastball has sat at 93-96 mph and reached 98 with power sink this spring, and it touched 100 during fall practice. His upper-80s cutter features late break that keeps it off barrels. Jelkin also shows some aptitude for a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink. A lanky 6-foot-5, 195-pounder with room to add more strength, he slings his pitches from a low three-quarters slot that adds deception. While he provides consistent strikes, he does catch the heart of the plate too often and will need to upgrade his command.

American Heritage HS in Plantation, Fla., has produced a good amount of big league talent, from Eric Hosmer to Mark Vientos. But all have been hitters except for one: right-hander Shaun Anderson, who went on to the University of Florida before emerging as a third-round pick in 2016. Snow hopes to be the first pitcher from the program to be drafted since lefty Brandon Barriera was a first-rounder in '22 and just the fourth arm to be taken from the school since Anderson was a late-round pick who didn’t sign back in '13. Snow is a slightly undersized right-hander who gives off some Sonny Gray vibes in terms of his body type. After missing some time earlier this spring with an oblique issue, he came back throwing extremely well. He’s been up to 97-98 mph as his senior season wore on, showing he can maintain his velocity deep into starts. He backs it up with what he might call two different breaking balls, but is really an effective 78-80 mph power slurve, one with tight three-quarters shape with late finish when he’s landing it well. He has feel for a firm 85-87 mph changeup that can have depth and fade, but he doesn’t throw it much in games. Because of his size and his occasionally spotty command, there are some reliever risk concerns that might cap his Draft stock a bit. Some scouts put his ceiling at around the third round, and it might take him being selected there -- or paid at that level when taken a bit later -- to keep him from following in Anderson’s footsteps to pitch for the Gators in college.

American Heritage HS in Plantation, Fla., has produced a good amount of big league talent, from Eric Hosmer to Mark Vientos. But all have been hitters except for one: right-hander Shaun Anderson, who went on to the University of Florida before emerging as a third-round pick in 2016. Snow hopes to be the first pitcher from the program to be drafted since lefty Brandon Barriera was a first-rounder in '22 and just the fourth arm to be taken from the school since Anderson was a late-round pick who didn’t sign back in '13. Snow is a slightly undersized right-hander who gives off some Sonny Gray vibes in terms of his body type. After missing some time earlier this spring with an oblique issue, he came back throwing extremely well. He’s been up to 97-98 mph as his senior season wore on, showing he can maintain his velocity deep into starts. He backs it up with what he might call two different breaking balls, but is really an effective 78-80 mph power slurve, one with tight three-quarters shape with late finish when he’s landing it well. He has feel for a firm 85-87 mph changeup that can have depth and fade, but he doesn’t throw it much in games. Because of his size and his occasionally spotty command, there are some reliever risk concerns that might cap his Draft stock a bit. Some scouts put his ceiling at around the third round, and it might take him being selected there -- or paid at that level when taken a bit later -- to keep him from following in Anderson’s footsteps to pitch for the Gators in college.

As a Florida high school right-hander with pitchability and a quality changeup, Knaak could have gone in the top five rounds of the 2023 Draft, but he didn't command a high enough bonus to give up on attending Clemson. He became the first pitcher in Tigers history to earn all-Atlantic Coast Conference first-team recognition in each of his first two seasons, as well as the first to reach 100 strikeouts in each of his first two years. But his stuff and strike-throwing regressed this spring, when he got pounded for a 5.81 ERA. Knaak has advanced feel for his changeup, varying the velocity from the low 70s to the mid 80s while imparting plenty of fade and tumble, though it wasn't quite as dominant in 2026 as it had been in the past. His cambio helps him compensate for the lack of velocity and life on a 91-93 mph fastball that tops out at 96, and his heater plays up a bit because he commands it well. He doesn't show much aptitude for spin, however, and opponents raked at a .476/.500/.714 clip against his tight mid-80s slider and low-80s curveball this spring. Knaak does a good job of working around the edges of the strike zone with his fastball while setting hitters up for his changeup, but his lack of a breaking ball caught up to him as a junior. His delivery and control weren't as smooth as usual, which compounded his problems. While he lacks size and projection, he's strong and competitive and could become a back-of-the-rotation starter if he can regain his previous form.

Marsten overcame Tommy John surgery as a high school sophomore to reach 99 mph and generate top-three-rounds buzz at baseball power Harvard-Westlake (Studio City, Calif.) in 2024, though he went undrafted because of his commitment to Wake Forest. His career with the Demon Deacons hasn't played out as hoped, as he got hammered as a little-used reliever as a freshman and pitched his way out of the Atlantic Coast Conference rotation after just two starts this spring. He performed much better as a midweek starter but has the stuff to be much more than that. Marsten can miss bats with all four of his pitches, beginning with a 94-96 mph fastball that tops out at 99 with carry and armside run. He uses a tight mid-80s slider as his primary secondary pitch against right-handers and switches to a slightly harder cutter versus left-handers, with both grading as solid offerings. His fading changeup is tough to barrel but he shows little feel for locating it. This season, Marsten has dominated righties but gotten crushed by lefties, who tee off on his fastball because he can't land his cutter and changeup for strikes on a regular basis. He has a strong 6-foot-3, 220-pound build and offers the potential of a mid-rotation starter with three plus pitches but also little track record to suggest he can get there. It's unclear whether he'd be better off getting his pro career started now or returning to college and trying to rebuild his stock as a junior.

When most baseball fans think about Notre Dame High School talent in recent years, Hunter Greene (2017) comes to mind, with Giancarlo Stanton ten years earlier. The program hasn’t had a position player taken in the top 10 rounds since 2009, but Madrid hopes to buck that trend this July. The catcher wasn’t seen all that much on the summer showcase circuit but was impressing both area scouts and cross-checkers during his senior year, particularly with his work behind the dish. Madrid’s calling card is his defense. His abilities behind the plate give him a very high floor, with some evaluators claiming he has the best arm of any young catcher they’ve seen this year. It’s not just pure arm strength, as he also has a quick release and is very accurate controlling the running game. His overall defensive package, including receiving and blocking, is quite advanced. His ultimate ceiling will be determined by how much he hits. More than one scout gave a report that included a version of, “if he hits at all, he’s a big leaguer.” The Oregon recruit does have some raw power that he’s gotten to in games at times in front of evaluators, and a team that saw enough of that might look past the typically tough right-right high school catching profile to sign him away from his college commitment.

Morton damaged tendons in his throwing wrist while hitting fungoes as a Minnesota high school senior in 2023, so he made just two starts at the beginning of that season -- and reached 97 mph with his fastball and 91 with his cutter. He turned down a lucrative offer from the Brewers in the 19th around to attend Texas A&M, where he worked just 19 1/3 innings in two years while battling the strike zone and an oblique injury. After transferring back home, he became Minnesota's best pitching prospect since 2020 No. 3 overall pick Max Meyer before blowing out his elbow in his final regular-season start and requiring Tommy John surgery. Morton generates premium stuff from a sidearm slot and low release height, creating plenty of run and sink on a fastball that operates at 93-95 mph and touches 97. He produces premium spin rates on a mid-80s slider with excessive sweep and a cutter that parks in the low 90s. His firm upper-80s changeup features some fade but doesn't fool hitters. While Morton displayed much better control than he did with the Aggies, he caught the heart of the plate too often. None of his offerings elicit many chases because he throws so many strikes, and only his slider qualifies as a swing-and-miss pitch (while his sinker is valuable because it generates so much groundball contact). He doesn't have a weapon to get lefties out, though better command could help.

Because Jasa was so raw when he arrived at Nebraska as a Colorado high school recruit, Cornhuskers coaches not only redshirted him in 2024 but also wouldn't allow him to work against teammates in practice for fear he might injure them with an errant pitch. After posting an 8.68 ERA with 19 walks in 18 2/3 innings in his college debut last year, he has taken a huge step forward in 2026. He emerged as the ace of a team that earned Nebraska's first NCAA regional host bid in 18 years and displayed the best arm in the program since Joba Chamberlain two decades ago. Jasa averages 96 mph and reaches 98 with his fastball, but it lacks life and command and tends to get hit harder than would be expected, so he has used it just 28 percent of the time this spring. He leans much more on a tight upper-80s slider that tops out at 91 and plays well off his best pitch, a downer 78-82 mph curveball. Opponents went 6-for-111 (.054) with 81 strikeouts against his curve in 2026. Though he doesn't employ his low-80s changeup very often and has difficulty landing it for strikes, it shows promising tumble and fade at its best. Jasa has much better feel for his breaking balls than his dead-zone fastball, and while his control has improved, it's still below average. That means he comes with a good deal of reliever risk, though he also has huge upside as a starter if a team can help him improve his ability to shape and locate his heater. He's athletic and has improved tremendously in college, leading to hope he can continue to do so at the next level.

José Veras was a big right-handed pitcher who carved out a nine-year big league career as a reliever for eight different teams after signing out of the Dominican Republic. His equally large son Genson wants to go into the family business, albeit in a different division. Veras has gone to TNXL Academy in Florida for high school and offers some serious offensive upside, though swing-and-miss on the summer showcase circuit really hurt his Draft stock. The younger Veras stands at 6-foot-6, just like his dad, and is a lean and strong 225 pounds. A right-handed hitter and thrower, he possesses the tools of an everyday outfielder if he can get to them consistently. After posting a large strikeout rate over the summer, he made some adjustments during his senior year, both in his approach and in simplifying his swing, helping him get to his huge raw power a bit more consistently while facing a lot of junior college pitching. Veras runs well for his size, clocking solid 60-yard dash times and showing he can steal a base. He’s played center field for TNXL, and a team could send him out there, but he’s probably best suited for right, where his above-average arm would play well. The team deciding to try to sign him away from his Florida State commitment will be the one who felt they saw enough this spring to believe he can make enough contact to get to the impact necessary for an outfield corner at the next level.

Shelar is the latest prospect out of a Marist School (Atlanta) program that has produced seven big leaguers, most notably Kyle Farmer, and won 14 Georgia state championships. He's a physical player with an interesting combination of raw power and solid speed, and a team that believes in his bat could pay him a seven-figure bonus. If that doesn't happen, he'll head to Mississippi State. Already 6-foot-2 and 205 pounds, Shelar projects to have well-above-average raw power thanks to his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage. He led all high schoolers with 19 homers in 33 games this spring. There are mixed opinions about his bat, with some scouts worrying about his ability to make consistent contact against pro pitching. He takes aggressive hacks with an unorthodox right-handed stroke that can get uphill. If he does hit enough to tap into his pop, Shelar has the solid speed to become at least a 20-20 player. A center fielder in high school, he doesn’t have a quick first step but covers ground once he gets going. He likely will wind up on a corner in the long run and has the arm strength and offensive profile to fit in right field.

Gloucester Catholic High School is a powerhouse program in New Jersey, having won four straight state titles and a Garden State-leading 23 overall. But the school hasn’t had a player drafted since 2016, when Tyler Mondile was a sixth-round pick of the Reds. Danza, a strong and toolsy infielder who was named to NJ.com’s first-team All-State squad, is hoping to break that schneid and become the first position player taken from Gloucester since 2009. A 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter, Danza didn’t wow scouts last summer at the East Coast Pro Showcase but had all of his tools on display as the weather warmed in New Jersey during his senior year. He has outstanding bat speed with plenty of strength that generates a ton of raw power. With that comes a good amount of swing-and-miss, though he had stretches of being very locked in this spring. He records plus run times in 60 yard dashes, though that doesn’t always translate to acumen on the basepaths yet. Danza’s plus arm will play on the left side of the infield, but most think he’ll be best suited to shift over from his current shortstop to third, where he can be more of a reactionary defender. Questions about the hit tool at the next level might make some pause, but the overall toolset could be intriguing enough to try to sign him away from Mississippi State, a commitment he flipped from Virginia when coach Brian O’Connor left the Cavaliers for the Bulldogs.
