A product of the Jesuit High School program in Oregon that produced right-handed first-rounders in Mick Abel and Noble Meyer, Keljo is a left-hander who wasn’t as high profile as a prepster and went on to pitch at Oregon State. He missed bats and walked hitters out of the bullpen as a freshman, but improved strike-throwing as a sophomore reliever helped afford him a chance to start in 2025. He’s spent most of the year in the weekend rotation, with mixed results along the way. A big, strong 6-foot-4 southpaw, Keljo does have some ingredients that could give him the chance to start as a pro. He throws his fastball with deception and good life, averaging around 93 mph, but touching 97-98, especially in shorter stints. His changeup has taken a nice step forward this year and is now an above-average offering, especially against right-handed hitters, with the chance to be good enough in left-on-left matchups in the future. His 80 mph slider has inconsistent shape and some think adding a cutter to his repertoire is the way to go. There is effort in Keljo’s rigid delivery and his struggles in repeating it this year have led to a regression in his strike-throwing. A team taking him could very well send him out as a starter to see if they can iron things out, but the lack of command, repeatable delivery and inconsistent breaking ball could move him back to the 'pen.

A starter at Stetson right out of the gate when the New Jersey high school product arrived at the Florida school’s campus, Meola -- who is a cousin of famed USA soccer goalkeeper Tony Meola -- has done nothing but perform over three years for the Hatters. The infielder won ASUN Tournament MVP honors as a sophomore, then was named the conference’s Defensive Player of the Year and earned first-team All-Conference honors this spring. Meola keeps everything simple on both sides of the ball. While he tried to do a little too much early this spring, leading to more swing-and-miss than usual, he typically makes a lot of contact from the right side of the plate and really turned things up a notch in conference play this year. He’s never going to be a huge power guy, but he can impact the ball, showing some ability to backspin it out of the park to the middle of the field, with 12-15 homer potential at the next level. An above-average runner, Meola’s standout skills come on the dirt. He has outstanding footwork and hands and covers a ton of ground, giving him plus grades on his defense. Combine that with a strong and accurate arm, and he definitely has the goods to play shortstop for a long time. He might be a bottom-of-the-lineup glove-first type of big leaguer eventually, but he could be more than that if the bat develops and he’s the kind of player winning teams always seem to have on their roster.

Troy's best prospect since 2018 fifth-rounder and future big leaguer Brandon Lockridge, Bryan is one of the better catchers available in a down backstop crop. He played sparingly as a freshman before breaking out with 18 homers and a school-record 85 RBIs in 2024, then played with the U.S. collegiate national team during the summer. He has posted similar numbers this spring and could go as early as the fourth round. A left-handed hitter, Bryan has at least plus raw power and generates it with strength and an aggressive approach that includes a big leg kick and a pull-and-lift mindset. There's some question as to how much quality contact he'll make with wood bats against pro pitching because he chases too many fastballs and struggles against velocity and slow stuff. He probably won't hit for a high average but has 20-homer upside. Though he has a large frame for a catcher and lacks quickness, Bryan should be able to remain behind the plate. His receiving, framing and blocking still require more work, but he has worked hard to improve over the last year. He features solid-to-plus arm strength, but needs to upgrade his throwing accuracy.

Lefty-hitting catcher who swings with extremely aggressive intent. Above-average pull power. Kole Calhoun vibes/aesthetics from his stance and swing, but with less bat control. Lofty path with minimal adjustability, which results in big swing-and-miss, especially in the upper third of the zone. On defense, tends to stab at pitches rather than frame them; average arm, above-average mobility. Developmental catcher with power and hit tool risk.

Bravo spent his first season at Texas Tech as a little-used two-way player, getting 30 at-bats as an outfielder and 7 1/3 innings as a reliever. He blossomed as a full-time hitter in 2024, winning the Big 12 Conference batting championship at .378. He didn't defend that title this spring but continued to make consistent contact while improving his power and basestealing ability. A right-handed hitter, Bravo smokes hard-hit line drives to all fields. He's doing a better job of lifting balls in the air as a junior, showing more pull power and the potential for 15 homers per season. He'd be more effective at the plate if he made better swing decisions as his aggression undermines his bat-to-ball skills and cuts into his walk totals. Bravo has looked a bit quicker this year, flashing solid speed at times and making things happen on the bases more often. After splitting time between left and center field last season, he has moved to right and exhibited fine range and plus arm strength, no surprise considering his fastball reached 93 mph as a freshman. He also played some second base during fall practice and briefly this spring.

A two-way player as a Georgetown freshman in 2023, Bowker became a full-time pitcher last spring and earned Cape Cod League all-star honors during the summer. After transferring to Vanderbilt, he has become a solid No. 2 starter for the Commodores thanks to one of the more unhittable fastballs in the Draft. It's his lone better than average offering but could propel him into the top four or five rounds. Bowker usually operates at 90-95 mph with his fastball, but it's not velocity that makes it special. He uses a drop-and-drive delivery and a low arm slot, producing unusually high spin from an unusually low release height, which makes his heater appear to be rising more than most. He pounds the zone with his fastball and also gets chases with it, and it's almost impossible to deal with when he throws it at the letters. Bowker doesn't land his other pitches for strikes consistently, though he can entice batters to chase his sweeping low-80s slider. His cutter and sinking changeup both arrive in the mid-80s but can get pounded if he doesn't locate them well. Because he has just one weapon that can miss bats, he'll nibble around the strike zone with his other offerings.

Boser spent three years at South Florida and was on Draft radars last year, landing on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list after coming back from a broken hamate and continuing to show the kind of production he had the year prior as a sophomore. After playing well in the Cape Cod League, he moved from Tampa to Gainesville to play for the University of Florida and has put himself in position to be one of the higher-end senior signs of this Draft class. A strong, right-handed hitter, Boser has always shown a propensity for doing damage. There’s strength and bat speed with good balance at the plate. There’s also plenty of power for him to tap into, and he’s shown the ability to drive the ball for extra bases and out of the park to all fields. Whether he can get to that pop at the next level is the question as he does swing and miss quite a good amount, and his miss rate did go up as the Gators got into conference play. Boser gets very high marks for his makeup, and he worked hard to improve his athleticism, running speed and defensive ability to make him a more viable all-around prospect. He has the ability to play three infield positions capably, and some think he’s the best shortstop on the Gators, though he’s played more third than anywhere else this season. A team taking him could send him out at short, but he could develop into a regular at the hot corner or second, with a floor as a productive super-utility type.

Clemente headed from Florida high school power Marjory Stoneman Douglas to the University of Florida, only to miss all of his freshman season with a shoulder injury. He pitched almost entirely out of the bullpen in 2024, gradually getting chances in high-leverage situations, including during the Gators’ run in the College World Series. He began this year in the weekend rotation but was fairly quickly moved to the bullpen, where he has had more success as the team’s closer. A 6-foot-3 right-hander, Clemente checks off a lot of boxes in terms of size and power stuff. He has more than enough fastball, averaging close to 95 mph and touching 98-99 mph this year in shorter stints, missing a good amount of bats with his lively heater. He backs it up with a mid-80s slider that has more downer action and can be an effective secondary offering. In the past, he has shown some feel for a changeup, but it’s largely gathered dust on the shelf this spring. While Clemente has been very tough to square up, with a high strikeout rate and low batting average against, he’s also struggled at times in finding the strike zone consistently when his delivery gets out of whack. Because of that and the lack of a third pitch, most see his future as a reliever, but there have been some Gators relievers who find some success when sent out to start on the pro side, like Christian Scott or Dane Dunning.

A solid two-way player during his time at Reno High School, Grinsell put the bat down to focus on pitching when he headed to the University of Oregon. After spending his freshman season almost exclusively pitching out of the 'pen, he became a starter in 2024 and was the sole returnee from the Ducks’ weekend rotation. Serving as the Friday night starter, he was named to the first all-Big 10 team and became just the sixth Oregon pitcher in history to surpass 200 career strikeouts. Grinsell is the epitome of a college pitchability lefty whose feel is better than any individual offering in his repertoire. His fastball tops out at 92 mph, but it’s one of those “invisible” heaters hitters don’t square up. That appears to be for two reasons: the impressive extension he gets when throwing the pitch so it gets on hitters in a hurry and the feel he has for his outstanding changeup. He throws the cambio around 80 mph, selling it with tremendous arm speed and throwing it with good fade to hitters from both sides of the plate. He mixes in a breaking ball as well, but doesn’t lean on it as much as the other two. Allowing Grinsell’s stuff to play up is his excellent command of all of it and he projects as an above-average strike-thrower at the next level. His ability to stick in a rotation might come down to whether he can develop a breaking ball he uses more consistently, but that invisible fastball-changeup combination, along with him posting every weekend this year, should get him plenty of looks.

After missing his senior season of high school in California following Tommy John surgery, Reitz had two up-and-down years pitching mostly in relief at St. Mary’s before throwing relatively well in the Cape Cod League a summer ago and transferring to Oregon. He began the year once again as a reliever with mixed results, but he took an opportunity as the Ducks’ Sunday starter at the beginning of April and ran with it, posting a 2.50 ERA and a 0.98 WHIP over seven starts before regional play. A gangly presence on the mound at 6-foot-11, Reitz does have the chance to start with four potential pitches to work on as he moves forward in his fastball, cutter, slider and changeup. He and the Ducks have a tendency to pitch a little backwards and lean too heavily on his mid-80s cutter, though it has the chance to be a solid pitch. His fastball has been up to 97-98 mph, sitting more around 93, and he shows off the makings of a separate slider and a decent changeup. Reitz has struggled to be a consistent strike-thrower throughout his college career, though he found the zone more as a starter in the second half of this spring. He also doesn’t take full advantage of his size, with a short stride to the plate cutting off what could be impressive extension. Not everyone loves pitchers this big, but his improvement as Oregon moved into postseason play and the possibility of unlocking more with some delivery tweaks could be very intriguing.

After missing his senior season of high school in California following Tommy John surgery, Reitz had two up-and-down years pitching mostly in relief at St. Mary’s before throwing relatively well in the Cape Cod League a summer ago and transferring to Oregon. He began the year once again as a reliever with mixed results, but he took an opportunity as the Ducks’ Sunday starter at the beginning of April and ran with it, posting a 2.50 ERA and a 0.98 WHIP over seven starts before regional play. When teams decide to roll the dice on the risky high school right-handed pitching demographic, they typically want to see a few things: size, stuff and results. Grim is a little shy on the first two categories, but it’s hard to argue with how he’s taken the ball under the spotlight, throwing very well over the summer at the East Coast Professional Showcase and Area Code Games in front of a ton of scouts and continuing this spring to help pitch Governor Mifflin High School into the postseason in Pennsylvania. At 6 feet and 190 pounds, Grim isn’t quite “what they look like,” as a slightly under-sized right-hander. And while he doesn’t have electric stuff, he really knows how to use what he has. He typically sits in the 91-92 mph range with his fastball, touching 94 now and again, though it misses bats with some good riding life up in the zone. His breaking stuff has two distinct shapes -- a slider and a curve -- and depending on which day you see him, one is better than the other. There’s some feel for a changeup, and while it has some movement, it’s effective more because he sells it with arm speed than the action it has. Enabling all his stuff to play up is the fact that he fills up the strike zone with all four offerings and has an idea of how to set up hitters with his full arsenal. His ceiling might be that of a back-end starter or he might be a multi-inning reliever, an odd profile for a prepster, but his success on every mound he’s been on could convince teams to try to sign him away from his commitment to Virginia Tech.

The best player to ever come out of Northeastern University in Massachusetts is Carlos Peña, a first-rounder back in 1998, and outfielder Mike Sirota became the first Huskies hitter since then to be taken in the top five rounds when he was a third-round selection of the Reds last year. After a 2023 freshman year that saw him hit 13 homers and steal 32 bases, Maldonado seemed certain to join that select group. Even though he put a rough sophomore year behind him with excellent production this year, questions about his hit tool made him less of a top-round slam dunk. Maldonado does check off a lot of boxes in terms of strength, athleticism and raw tools. The 6-foot-3 right-handed hitter is a presence in the box, and there’s plenty of raw power for him to tap into. He’s gotten to it more this year than as a sophomore, allowing him to climb to among the career home run leaders at Northeastern. While he does draw a ton of walks, the strikeout rate is concerning to scouts, though that did improve a bit in conference play this season. A plus runner who routinely records elite-level times to first base, Maldonado is a definite basestealing threat. That speed also helps him cover a lot of ground in the outfield, where he has every chance to stick in center field and develop into a plus defender. He hasn’t improved his overall hit tool from his freshman year the way some scouts may have hoped, but the overall tool package is sure to be enticing to many teams.

Dominique Partridge was a late-round pick of the Braves back in 2001 and spent three seasons as a Minor League outfielder in their system. His son, Nic, has the chance to be much better and drafted a lot earlier than his dad. After spending two seasons at Lakeland Senior High School, Partridge moved over to Mulberry High to join forces with his old travel ball coach, and he was named Polk County Player of the Year as a junior and then helped lead his team to the Class 4A championship game as a senior. Partridge is a lean and wiry left-handed-hitting infielder with a current feel to hit along with some production projection. He has a really good feel in the box, with an advanced knowledge of the strike zone. It’s a hit-over-power look right now, with the ability to stay balanced and consistently find the barrel. He can get to some pull side loft at times, providing glimpses that there might be more thump to come, especially if he can add some strength to his 6-foot-2 frame. A decent athlete, Partridge is more of a fringy-to-average runner because he has a tendency to be a bit of a short strider. He’s played shortstop in high school, with decent hands, actions and a strong enough arm, but most feel a move will be in order at the next level because of that lack of quickness, with third base perhaps being the best fit. Whether that happens in pro ball or at the University of Florida will be determined by how the Draft goes.

Jean compiled a 3.51 ERA in three years as a part-time starter at Alabama, then completed his communications degree while missing 2023 after Tommy John surgery. He transferred to Houston and was the Cougars' most reliable starter last year before dominating out of the bullpen in 2025 and becoming perhaps the best college senior pitching prospect in the Draft. The Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year, he led NCAA Division I in opponent average (.168) and ranked second in strikeouts per nine innings (14.8). Working mostly three- and four-inning stints this spring, Jean has added 2-3 mph to each of his offerings this spring. His fastball sits at 90-94 mph and tops out at 96, creating a lot of chases and empty swings with its carry and armside run. He can miss bats with all three of his secondary pitches, and he has better command of his solid upper-70s curveball and mid-80s slider than he does of his fading low-80s changeup. Scouts aren't sure exactly what to make of Jean, who stands out more for his feel than his pure stuff, is in his sixth year of college and will turn 24 shortly after the Draft. He's athletic and repeats his delivery well enough to provide a steady stream of strikes. He'll probably move back to the rotation to begin his pro career and projects as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

A solid high school prospect in New Jersey, McCoy spent most of his freshman year at Maryland serving as a starter, but he hurt his elbow and required Tommy John surgery at the end of the 2023 season. He missed 2024 as a result but returned as the Terrapins' Friday night starter and earned third team All-Big Ten honors as a result, showing durability by going at least six innings in 10 of his 14 starts. A lean, 6-foot-6 left-hander, McCoy is more of a sum-of-his-parts kind of pitchability college southpaw, though it’s possible there could be more stuff to tease out given his frame. His best offerings are two different slider shapes, using a harder, bullet slider (up to 87 mph), as well as a gyro ball to miss bats at a 43 percent rate, per Synergy. His fastball is somewhat pedestrian, averaging just over 91 mph and touching 95, and it gets hit. He can fold in a decent mid-80s changeup as well. All of it comes from a funky three-quarters arm slot, coming across his body with his delivery to add deception. That does allow his stuff to play up at times, and he manages to repeat well and throw a ton of strikes. He might top out as a back-end starter who could be a good find on Day 2, but a team that can find more ceiling velocity-wise could get a steal.

Anker was a bit of a soft-tossing high school right-hander in northern California when he stayed in the region to pitch at Fresno State. After coming out of the Bulldogs' bullpen his freshman year, Anker has spent the bulk of the next two years in the rotation with mixed results. He's had some sparkling moments as the team's Friday night starter, including a 16-strikeout performance in April, but has also been hit more than hoped. The 6-foot-2 Anker still is more about his feel for pitching than any wow stuff, though he has added strength since high school, resulting in a few more ticks in velocity. Featuring some armside run, his fastball now sits around 91-92 mph and he's touched a lot of 94s and 95s, Anker relied heavily on his low-80s changeup, which has good depth, selling it with good arm speed, but then started pitching off his fastball more consistently. In high school, he had a big 12-to-6 curve and he'll occasionally flash that big breaker, though it's more of a three-quarter-type breaking ball now. He also has a mid-80s cutter, sometimes getting on the side of it, morphing it into more of a hard slider. Anker has always been a strike-thrower and he's taken a step forward in that realm this year with a minuscule walk rate, finding a more consistent delivery he repeats well. It's control over command, as he gets too much of the zone, leading to him getting squared up. But the sum of the parts could be a solid back-end starter in the future.

Missouri has a sneaky-deep group of high school pitching prospects this spring, though it's unclear how many of them will get drafted early enough to turn pro. Irlbeck is the least physically imposing of those arms but offers the best combination of ability and signability. If he attends college, he should contribute immediately at Iowa as a freshman. Irlbeck works at 90-92 mph and touches 94 with his fastball, which he can throw with carry and armside run, while boring it in on right-handers. He has advanced feel for a low-80s changeup with good depth that plays well in tandem with his heater. He can steal strikes with a slurvy mid-70s curveball and has begun to develop a tight slider in the low 80s. Irlbeck pounds the zone with his entire repertoire and does a nice job of mixing his pitches. He's just 6 feet tall but overcomes his lack of size with his twitchy athleticism. He repeats his athletic delivery consistently and creates deception with his low arm slot and flat approach angle. Scouts also love his competitiveness, which adds to his high-floor package.

When scouts flocked to Shawnee Mission East HS (Prairie Village, Kan.) in March for hard-throwing Nate Schlote's first outing, they didn't know anything about the right-hander who pitched the back end of the piggyback start. Winter didn't partake in the summer showcase circuit but quickly made a name for himself with his low-90s fastball and ability to throw three pitches for strikes. He performed well throughout his senior season and went from unknown to the best prep prospect in the Sunflower State. After operating with a mid-80s fastball as a junior, Winter now deals at 90-92 mph and touches 94 with armside run, and he'll work both up and down in the zone with his heater. His tight slider has benefited from a similar increase in power and now parks in the low 80s. His changeup has the same velocity as well as some fading action. Winter has an effortless delivery and provides consistent strikes with his whole arsenal. There's still a lot of projection remaining in his 6-foot-5 frame, so he should continue to add more velocity. He could factor into the top four rounds if he's signable away from Dartmouth, where he plans to study mechanical engineering.

Wisconsin's best prospect this year, Kussow flies under the radar more than he should. Like a lot of prep pitchers from cold-weather states, he lacks consistency, but he also looks like he belongs in the third round on his best days. He has the makings of a promising three-pitch repertoire and a projectable 6-foot-5 frame. Kussow works with a low-90s fastball that tops out at 97 mph with some carry and armside run. He can overpower hitters with a high-spin slider that climbs as high as 88 mph with two-plane break. He hasn't needed to use it much, but his mid-80s changeup has encouraging fade and depth. Kussow's size and ability to get down the mound well create a low release point and extension that make it difficult for hitters to pick up his pitches. He doesn't have the smoothest delivery, which further adds to his deception, though it also can compromise his ability to throw strikes. If he doesn't turn pro this summer, he could become one of the best college pitchers in the 2028 class after three years at Louisville.

Hailing from the same American Heritage High School program in Plantation, Florida, that produced big leaguers like Eric Hosmer, Mark Vientos and Tristan Casas, Dubovik provided the kind of toolset that had scouts hoping he’d be the latest from the school to jump up Draft boards. Those hopes were boosted after Dubovik showed glimpses of those skills at the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Games over the summer, and then for Brazil’s 18U national team at World Cup qualifying in Panama and the South American championship in Argentina. But a rough senior season had many scouts questioning what the immediate future might be for him. Dubovik might be on a short list of players in the Draft class with the best all-around raw tools. But the emphasis has been on raw this spring. The 6-foot-4 right-handed hitter always had a power-over-hit profile as a free swinger who looked to do damage early in counts. The raw power is legit, but his swing is way too long and his over-aggressiveness was getting the better of him in 2025. It’s been feast-or-famine, with way too much swing-and-miss both in and out of the zone, to project hitting success at the next level. A good runner, especially for his size, Dubovik has played both third and the outfield, and his athleticism might play best if he’s allowed to roam a corner in the grass. His easily plus arm that fires low-90s fastballs as a pitcher -- some area scouts have mused he might end up on the mound -- would profile in right field well. He’ll take his tools to Miami should the Draft not work out.

Righty-hitting corner defender. Incredible bat speed, might be truly elite at maturity. Doesn't track pitches especially well, chases and loses sight of the baseball often, sub-70% contact rate on the showcase circuit. Probably a right field fit on defense due to inconsistent hands on the infield. A prospect of extreme variance and risk due to the hit tool.

A mainstay on the summer showcase circuit, Graulau had his considerable raw tools on display at events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Area Code Games, albeit with mixed results. After a slow start to his senior season, he got hot as the season wore on and helped Jupiter High School reach the 7A state finals, losing to Stoneman Douglas. He’s hoping to become the first player from Jupiter High to get drafted since 2015. At 6-foot-3 and 200 pounds, Graulau is very much “what they look like,” if you’re looking for athletic high school hitters with a ton of projection. The tools are undeniable, with plus speed and plus raw power from the right side of the plate. There’s bat speed there, and when he finds the barrel, there’s impact and the ability to drive the ball. The issue has been his ability to hit enough to get to that power, with swing-and-miss concerns popping up against higher levels of competition. Graulau’s speed is an asset on the basepaths and in the outfield, and he has the chance to play center field for a long time. He also has a plus arm that fires 91-mph fastballs from the mound that’s an asset. Graulau should add more strength to his athletic frame as he matures, leading to more raw power, and a team that thinks they can help him catch up with the bat could try to sign him away from his commitment to South Florida.

The First Academy in Orlando has a storied history, including being the first team from Florida to win USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational, a team that included prospects Foster Griffin and Adam Hasely. The school hasn’t had a Draft pick since 2018, but thanks to players like Indomenico, who has a chance to become the program’s first player taken in the top 10 rounds since ‘17, it did take home a Class 2A state title this spring. While he’s not the biggest guy in the world at 6 feet, Indomenico does bring a ton of athleticism to the diamond as a multisport guy who has played both football and lacrosse in the past. A left-handed hitter and thrower, he can be a little crude and rigid in the box, but he has good bat speed and strike zone awareness to help him be a dangerous hitter. There’s pull-side pop, and he might a little too pull-oriented at times, but a prep left-handed bat with intelligence at the plate and some impact potential speaks to a lot of teams. Indomenico is an above-average runner with a fringy arm, and though he largely manned a corner for The First Academy, he has the skills to play center field. Any team wanting to take him and sign him away from his Oklahoma State commitment would likely send him out in center and see how that plays to maximize his value.

The First Academy in Orlando has a storied history, including being the first team from Florida to win USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational, a team that included prospects Foster Griffin and Adam Hasely. The school hasn’t had a Draft pick since 2018, but thanks to players like Indomenico, who has a chance to become the program’s first player taken in the top 10 rounds since ‘17, it did take home a Class 2A state title this spring. While he’s not the biggest guy in the world at 6 feet, Indomenico does bring a ton of athleticism to the diamond as a multisport guy who has played both football and lacrosse in the past. A left-handed hitter and thrower, he can be a little crude and rigid in the box, but he has good bat speed and strike zone awareness to help him be a dangerous hitter. There’s pull-side pop, and he might a little too pull-oriented at times, but a prep left-handed bat with intelligence at the plate and some impact potential speaks to a lot of teams. Indomenico is an above-average runner with a fringy arm, and though he largely manned a corner for The First Academy, he has the skills to play center field. Any team wanting to take him and sign him away from his Oklahoma State commitment would likely send him out in center and see how that plays to maximize his value.

Abeldt was one of college baseball's best relievers in his first two years at Texas Christian, recording a 2.81 ERA with 125 strikeouts in 99 1/3 innings and spending both summers with the U.S. collegiate national team. The Horned Frogs planned on turning him into a starter in 2025, but he blew out his elbow just before the beginning of the season and required Tommy John surgery in February. He still could draw interest in the first five rounds of the Draft. Abeldt relies heavily on a 91-94 mph fastball that peaks at 96 and is much more effective than its ordinary velocity would indicate. His heater has riding action and plenty of deception coming out of a crossfire delivery, and it's nearly impossible to lift when he works down in the zone. He can't overpower hitters with a slider that sits around 80 mph, but it can baffle them with its sweeping action when it's on. While he doesn't use it much, Abeldt has the makings of an effective low-80s changeup with sink. He looks like a shorter, stronger version of Chris Sale with his slingy delivery, and it generates a lot of empty swings and groundballs. It remains to be seen if he can succeed as a starter, but he comes with a high floor as a quality lefty reliever once he returns to full health.

Phillips set a Tennessee high school record by homering in eight straight games in 2023, then went deep 13 times as a Middle Tennessee State freshman last spring. He had less success as pitcher for the Blue Raiders, logging a 7.13 ERA with 27 strikeouts in 41 2/3 innings. But he performed so well on the mound during fall practice that he had a chance to go in the first three rounds as a sophomore before a hand injury and a stress fracture in his lower back limited him to six starts this spring. After sitting at 90-92 mph with his fastball as a freshman, Phillips parked at 92-94 and peaked at 97 last fall and this spring. Scouts would like to see him go with more four-seamers at the top of the zone because his heater gets pounded when he tries to work down with plane and sink. He has good feel for a solid low-80s slider, showing the ability to get in-zone misses and chases with it. Phillips' fading upper-70s changeup lacks consistency but has its moments with fade and sink. He's very much a work in progress but his upside may make him worth the wait. He's athletic, features plenty of arm speed and has a sound delivery, ingredients that should allow him provide consistent strikes and perhaps reach triple digits with a four-seamer.

Reid pitched just 19 1/3 innings in two seasons at Oklahoma State, prompting his decision to transfer to Abilene Christian. He became the Wildcats' Friday starter this spring and set the program's NCAA Division I record with 112 strikeouts in 88 1/3 innings. After allowing just one run in his final three starts, including seven shutout innings with 12 whiffs against Utah Valley in the Western Athletic Conference tournament, he should become Abilene Christian's highest Draft pick since 1969 third-rounder Bill Gilbreth -- the lone big leaguer in school history. Reid does a nice job of moving his running fastball around the strike zone, working at 91-94 mph and reaching 96 with the ability to get carry at the letters or sink at the knees. He throws his best pitch, an 82-84 mph changeup with fade and sink, nearly as much as his heater and will double and triple up on it, even against right-handers. He led all NCAA Division I pitchers with 66 strikeouts via the cambio. He doesn't have nearly as much trust in a slurvy low-80s breaking ball that rarely fools hitters. With a strong 6-foot-3 frame and an athletic delivery that he repeats well, Reid provides consistent strikes. His fastball can catch too much of the plate at times, so he needs to command his heater to set up his changeup and find success. He'll probably need to come up with a better breaker to remain in the rotation at the next level.

After starring in high school outside of Rochester, N.Y., Salina headed south to George Mason University for college ball. After a freshman year pitching sparingly out of the Patriots' bullpen, he moved closer to home, staying in the Atlantic 10 Conference to attend St. Bonaventure. He spent his sophomore year in the rotation and was off to a solid start as the Bonnies’ No. 1 starter this year when an elbow injury shelved him after four starts; he had Tommy John surgery in April. A 6-foot-1 right-hander, Salina has electric stuff when he’s healthy. He’s gained some ticks of velocity in his fastball from earlier in his college career and was averaging close to 95 mph with it, while touching 98 routinely and topping out at 102. The pitch misses bats thanks to excellent extension. So does his mid-80s slider, which is short and hard with two-plane break. He doesn’t go to his changeup often, but he has feel for the upper-80s cambio. While he’s strong and compact, Salina is a sneaky good athlete and does a decent job of repeating his simple, from-the-stretch delivery. He found the zone a lot in his first four starts and now teams will have to decide if they want to take him and let him rehab in their system.

Gonzaga has produced some solid arms over the years, including former first-rounders Marco Gonzales and, more recently, Gabriel Hughes. After two uneven seasons with the Zags, Graham’s strong fall had Pacific Northwest scouts excited that he could be the next early-round arm to come from the program, but he made just one start in the spring before hurting his elbow, eventually having Tommy John surgery in late April. At the start of his college career, Graham had a fringy fastball in the 88-91 mph range. He upped that to 93-94 mph in 2024, and last fall, he was easily cranking his heater in the 95-97 mph range. He was up to 96 mph in his one start before blowing his elbow out, throwing it with good life. He has two distinct breaking balls, with the curve flashing plus in the past with true downer shape. He has feel for a mid-80s changeup as well, and all four of his pitches have solid metrics. Graham is stronger and his stuff ticked up, but there’s no real track record of success. He’s struggled with command in the past, something he had hoped to remedy with a strong junior season. Now teams will have to decide when the right time is to take the right-hander and help him rehab post-surgery.

Soler had a lot of things going for him as the spring of his senior year in high school approached. He’s tall, projectable, left-handed and has MLB bloodlines, with his father Alay reaching the big leagues with the Mets in 2004 after defecting from Cuba. But the younger Soler was shut down early with an elbow injury and, after some time trying to rehab through it, had Tommy John surgery in early May. Before getting hurt, Soler was the type of prep arm who could have risen up boards with a strong spring. The 6-foot-3 southpaw has the chance to have a very solid three-pitch mix, with perhaps the only thing missing being present velocity on the fastball. He typically was around 90-91 mph, occasionally touching 93-94 mph, but it’s easy to dream on more velocity as he adds strength to his thin frame. He can really spin his upper-70s slider and it could be a true out pitch in time. He also has feel for his low-80s changeup. There were teams who were in early on Soler, seeing his ability to repeat his delivery and fill up the zone while projecting more electric stuff. Now they’ll have to decide if they want to try to sign him away from his commitment to Central Florida and rehab him in their system, perhaps as an overpay for a team with multiple picks.

As the spring approached, the hope was that Poly Prep in Brooklyn would be a frequent stop for scouts to see not one, but two high-end high school right-handers. Miguel Sime Jr. continued to prove that he’s one of the best pure power prep arms in the class and while de Jong, a legitimate two-way talent, had a more disappointing spring overall following a strong showing on the summer showcase circuit, there was still definitive interest in his stuff and projection. At 6-foot-3, de Jong has a ton of upside, especially when thinking about what might come when he focuses on pitching only. He’s shown a fastball up to 96 mph with life in the past, but after looking very good in winter workouts, he operated in the 89-91 mph range, though there should be more consistent velocity to come as he fills out that frame. He has two breaking balls in a hard downer curve that might be an out pitch in time and a quick, late slider. He’s shown the ability to throw his changeup in the zone with deception and isn’t afraid to use it. He’s capable of throwing all four of his offerings for strikes. While pitching is his future as a pro, de Jong could continue hitting, with plenty of power in his right-handed swing, at Duke. Even with the down spring, his makeup and stuff he’s shown in the past could entice teams to try to sign him away from his college commitment.

The younger brother of pitcher Andre Jackson, who last pitched in the big leagues in 2023 and is currently throwing in Japan, Isaiah Jackson was a solid, albeit raw, high school outfield prospect who landed on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 in 2022. The Astros took him late that July but he headed to Arizona State for college ball. He showed inconsistent glimpses of his potential over his first two seasons, but put it together in 2025 to earn all-Big 12 Conference first-team honors. A left-handed hitter, the 6-foot-3 Jackson has long had tremendous raw power and he started tapping into it consistently for the first time this spring. A lot of that had to do with making better swing decisions and being shorter to the ball compared to his first two years in school. After striking out 26.7 percent of the time as a freshman and sophomore combined, he cut that down to 17.1 percent this year while upping his walk rate from 8.8 percent (2023 and 2024) to 11.2 percent. While Jackson is an average runner, he’s very athletic, especially for his size. He knows how to steal a base and while at one point it was thought he’d have to move to a corner, he’s become an outstanding defender in center field, one who made the Pac-12 all-defensive team two years in a row. It likely will always be a power-over-hit profile at the plate, but his overall profile is helped by the fact he can stay up the middle at the next level.

Hailing from the Illinois high school ranks, Episcope needed Tommy John surgery at the end of his senior season, so he chose to defer a year so that he could focus on his rehab without the academic rigors of Princeton. He made 10 uneven starts as a freshman with the Tigers in 2024, but came out of the gate this year like gangbusters, with 26 strikeouts and just four walks in 20 innings, including a nine-strikeout, five-inning start at Wake Forest that opened a lot of eyes. But he came out of his fourth start with his biceps tingling, and it was eventually determined that he required another procedure, getting internal brace surgery in May. A six-foot right-hander, Episcope does have the pitch mix to potentially start when healthy. He was topping out at 97 mph with his fastball and averaging a touch over 94, while maintaining that velocity throughout his starts before he got shut down. He has two legitimate breaking balls, with a mid-80s gyro-like slider and more of a 12-to-6 power curve up to 82 mph that registered elite-level spin rates north of 3,000 rpm. Combined, the two breakers elicited a 60-percent miss rate over his four starts, according to Synergy. Episcope did an excellent job filling up the strike zone this spring, but given the lack of history on the mound and the multiple elbow procedures, it’s a little more difficult to pinpoint where he belongs in a Draft class. Some thought he could go as high as the second round as a future starter had his success continued, while others see his size and injuries and see a reliever profile.

Crespi Carmelite High School in California last produced a big league hitter when shortstop Trevor Plouffe, who would go on to spend parts of nine seasons in the big leagues, was a first-round pick of the Twins back in 2004. After performing at many summer showcase events, from Perfect Game National to the Area Code Games and PG's WWBA Wood Bat Championship in the fall, Velazquez could be Carmelite's next Draft prospect on the dirt to be selected, and he got more exposure by participating in this June's Draft Combine. Like Plouffe, Velazquez is a strong 6-foot-2 infielder, but unlike his Crespi Carmelite predecessor, he hits left-handed. Still 17 at Draft time, Velazquez is power-oriented, with a swing that is strength- and timing-based. He has considerable raw pop, especially to his pull side, though his swing can get long with too much sweep, causing some issues against elite velocity, while he also can have a little trouble with good spin. A shortstop in high school, Velazquez looks unlikely to stick at the premium position because of a lack of footspeed and range, though he could get the chance to play there should he go on to Southern Cal for college ball. The good news is he has the actions to stick on the dirt, with a plus arm that can fire fastballs up to 96 mph from the mound that should work well from third base, where he has quick enough actions to play the reaction-based position well. The team that thinks he can get to that raw power enough to profile at the hot corner could be the one to sign him away from playing for the Trojans.

Lohman sat in the upper 80s with his fastball as a junior and didn't attend many showcase events, so he wasn't a high-priority target entering 2025. That changed once his heater started touching 95 mph and he showed the makings of a pair of promising secondary pitches this spring. He could sneak into the top five rounds unless his commitment to Missouri scares teams off. Lohman works from 91-95 mph with his fastball and uses his 6-foot-4 build to create downhill plane. His over-the-top delivery enables him to stay on top of a low-80s slider that features two-plane depth at its best as well as a mid-70s curveball with similar shape. He has begun to use a low-80s splitter as a change of pace, and it along with his fastball and slider all could be solid offerings as he gains more strength and consistency. A short strider on the mound, Lohman has an upright delivery with a high release point. He doesn't have optimal shape on his fastball and slider, so he'll have to locate them well to succeed against more advanced hitters. He's an average athlete who provides a decent amount of strikes, and there's still plenty of projection remaining in his lanky frame.

Essenburg faced possible first-round left-hander Jack Bauer in April in one of the most highly anticipated high school matchups of the spring, and he didn't disappoint. Essenburg drilled an opposite-field homer off a 99-mph Bauer fastball and outpitched him as well, striking out 11 and permitting just an unearned run in five innings. He may have a brighter future on the mound, but he likes to hit, and it may be difficult to sign him away from an opportunity to play both ways at Kentucky. Essenburg mainly operates with two pitches, starting with a low-90s fastball that touches 95 mph with promising carry and armside run at its best. His mid-70s breaking ball features plenty of vertical and horizontal action and could become a weapon with more power. He'll occasionally flash a changeup that sits around 80 mph with fade. He's more physical than projectable at 6-foot-2 and 200 pounds and his delivery and control need more polish, but he also has the potential to improve significantly on the mound if he concentrates on pitching full time. Some scouts prefer Essenburg as a hitter, though his bats-right/throws-left profile isn't desirable. His aggressive swing, bat speed and strength give him 20-homer upside. He fits in right field with his fringy to average speed and obviously strong arm, though he could wind up at first base if he slows down.

Oklahoma high schools feature three shortstops with big league family ties. Ethan Holliday (Stillwater) is a potential No. 1 overall pick, Eli Willits (Fort Cobb-Broxton) won't go too far behind him and Brumbaugh had second-round aspirations before a so-so senior season. The son of former Rangers and Rockies outfielder Cliff Brumbaugh did help Edmond Santa Fe win the state 6-A title, providing three hits and earning the victory with 3 2/3 innings of relief in the championship game, but he looked less athletic and had more swing-and-miss issues than in the past. Though Brumbaugh can run his fastball up to 96 mph and flash a quality slider, teams prefer him as a position player. A right-handed hitter, he possesses solid raw power thanks to his bat speed and the strength in his 6-foot-2 frame. After previously showing a more measured approach and willingness to use the opposite field, he has aggressively looked to drive the ball this spring. Brumbaugh has bulked up and slowed down as a senior and now displays fringy speed. While his instincts help him play faster than that on the bases and in the field, he may lack the quickness to remain at shortstop at the next level. The Arkansas recruit does have the arm strength to make any throw necessary, and it will serve him well if he has to shift to third base in the future.

New Jersey's top prep position prospect in 2022, Martin turned down offers from pro clubs to stay home and play at Rutgers. He didn't see much action as a freshman with the Scarlet Knights, prompting a transfer to Georgia State in 2024, and he broke out this spring after another move to Kansas State. He slashed .320/.420/.612 with 14 homers while replacing 2024 Twins first-rounder Kaelen Culpepper at shortstop and also seeing action in center field. Martin's best tool is his plus raw power, which plays mostly to his pull side. His right-handed stroke features plenty of bat speed and leverage, producing high exit velocities. There are concerns about his frequency and quality of contact, however, because he has a swing-happy approach and struggles against non-fastballs. While Martin can display plus straight-line speed, he's more fringy to average out of the batter's box and isn't aggressive on the bases. He's an erratic defender with an average arm at shortstop, so he likely will move to second base or become a full-time outfielder in pro ball. He probably fits better on a corner than in center field at the next level.

Injuries limited Klein to 87 games in three years at Louisville, and a broken bone in his left forearm courtesy of a hit by pitch threatened to end his junior season in March. He returned in time for NCAA regional play, homered in his first two tournament games and helped the Cardinals finish third at the Men's College World Series. He has enough hitting ability and defensive acumen to project as a big league backup. A left-handed hitter, Klein makes consistent contact to all fields and proved himself with wood bats by hitting .375 in 25 games in the Cape Cod League last summer. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate and rarely misses fastballs, though changeups and sliders can give him trouble. He generates a lot of groundballs, so he may top out at 10-12 homers per season unless he learns to lift the ball more regularly. Klein runs well for a catcher but isn't much of a factor on the bases. He gets the job done behind the plate, had no issues handling the high-octane stuff of Louisville ace Patrick Forbes and makes accurate throws with average arm strength. Scouts also love his leadership ability and intelligence, and he needed just three years to graduate with a management degree.

Hawks pitched with Paul Skenes at Air Force in 2022 and spent another year with the Falcons before transferring to Vanderbilt in 2024. He missed the last three months of last season with a sprained elbow ligament but bounced back this spring to star as the Commodores' closer and become one of the better senior prospects available. He posted a 1.60 ERA, struck out 36 percent of the hitters he faced and earned eight saves, including the clincher in the Southeastern Conference tournament. Hawks' fastball operates at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96, playing better than its velocity because of its life (ride and run), metrics (low release height and extension) and his ability to command it. His go-to secondary pitch is a tight low-80s slider, though his fading mid-80s changeup is more effective. He also can catch hitters off balance with a mid-70s curveball that he lands for strikes. Because he has a legitimate four-pitch arsenal, Hawks likely will get a chance to start in pro ball. He helped his cause by improving his control as a senior, slashing his walk rate to 7 percent, down from 15 percent in his first three years in college. He only worked 120 1/3 innings in four years in college and missed two weeks in the middle of this season with mild shoulder inflammation, so he'll have to prove his durability.

Craig took a circuitous path to becoming one of the best sixth-year college prospects in the 2025 Draft. He began his college career at Tyler (Texas) JC in 2020, barely pitched at Texas A&M during a redshirt season in 2021, returned to Tyler in 2022 and then spent the last three years at Baylor. After sporadic success in the past, he posted a 0.56 ERA, .124 opponent average and 51/3 K/BB ratio in 32 innings this spring. The key to Craig's dominance, which included not surrendering an extra-base hit all season, is his wipeout slider. It sits in the mid-80s and touches 88 mph with huge sweep and some depth as well, and opponents went 8-for-72 (.111) with 43 strikeouts against his slide piece. He sets it up with a 93-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with armside run in the opposite direction of his out pitch. Craig works exclusively out of the stretch with a high release point and pounds the zone with both of his offerings. He's a two-pitch reliever who turns 24 ten days before the Draft, but he also could move quickly to the Majors. He could factor into the first five rounds as a deep-discount candidate.

Recruited by Auburn as a left-handed pitcher, Snell redshirted while dealing with injuries in 2021 before transferring to Wallace-Dothan (Ala.) CC and starring as a two-way player. The national junior college player of the year in 2023, he played both ways at Alabama in 2024 before becoming a full-time left fielder this spring. He’s one of the more attractive discount hitters available as a Southeastern Conference performer with intriguing data and also no college eligibility remaining. Snell offers one of the better combinations of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities in the college ranks. He has a quality left-handed stroke, rarely misses a fastball while handling all types of pitches and drives the ball to all fields. While he’s a hit-over-power guy, he has enough strength to provide 15 homers per year and perhaps more if he learns to lift balls in the air more regularly. While Snell will flash close to average speed at his best, he’s more of a below-average runner with limited range in left field. He has an average arm and topped out at 93 mph with his fastball as a redshirt junior. Scouts love his competitiveness and leadership, and his all-star summer with wood bats in the Cape Cod League in 2023 is another point in his favor.

McCutcheon homered just twice in his first two seasons at Missouri State, the second of which was cut short when he broke his right arm running into an outfield fence last March. He concentrated on adding strength during his recovery, and that has paid off with off with 15 homers and a .358/.444/.647 junior year. Data-driven teams will be attracted to his combination of swing decisions, contact and exit velocities, all of which are better than average. McCutcheon employs a leg kick yet usually is on time with his quick left-handed swing. His bat speed and ability to square up balls produces solid raw power, with most of his homers traveling to his pull side. He does damage against all types of pitches and lefties as well as righties, though his tendency to hit the ball on the ground may limit him to 15 homers per year with wood bats. While he can be slow out of the batter's box, McCutcheon has fringy to average speed once he gets going and shows some savvy on the bases. Counting summer leagues, he has played everywhere on the diamond but catcher, and he spent most of the last two seasons in left field after playing mostly second and third base as a freshman. More of a gritty than a smooth defender, he'll probably get another shot at second base in pro ball, with left field as his fallback position because he has fringy arm strength and range.

One of the more projectable prep left-handers in the 2023 class, Adams went undrafted because he was strongly committed to Alabama. His stuff plateaued during his freshman season and in a summer stint in the Cape Cod League before making a jump last fall, when he looked like a possible first-rounder. But he regressed this spring while posting a 5.54 ERA, which along with his sophomore eligibility makes it tough to figure where he might land. During fall practice, Adams operated with a 92-95 mph fastball with improved life and backed it up with his trademark plus curveball in the upper 70s. Neither pitch was as sharp during his sophomore season, when he worked with an 89-92 mph heater that topped out at 94 and his curve didn't miss as many bats. His best offering this spring was a 78-81 mph changeup that dies at the plate, and he also toyed with a mid-80s cutter. Adams has a loose, athletic frame with the potential for average control as he gains more strength and repeats his delivery more efficiently. He ran into trouble with walks as a freshman, pounded the strike zone on the Cape and in the fall, then was inconsistent with his strike throwing this spring. He has shown mid-rotation potential but needs to reclaim it.

Arvidson battled the strike zone in 2023 at Texas A&M, where he redshirted, and last year at San Jacinto (Texas) JC, where he finished second among national junior college pitchers with 15.9 strikeouts per nine innings. He settled down some this spring at Tennessee, where he couldn't crack a talented rotation but came up big in the postseason. He struck out nine in 5 1/3 innings against Texas in the Southeastern Conference tournament and 12 in 5 1/3 frames against Vanderbilt in the NCAA regionals. Arvidson averaged 16.3 strikeouts per nine innings for the Volunteers, thanks primarily to a wicked 81-84 mph curveball that he can throw with two-plane depth for chases or tighten up for in-zone swings and misses. It plays well off his fastball, which sits at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with carry when he locates it at the letters. His heater can get straight, so it can get rocked it he doesn't work it up in the zone. Coming out of the bullpen, Arvidson worked mostly with his curveball and fastball while occasionally mixing in a mid-80s changeup that he can't land in the strike zone. Though his upright, high three-quarters delivery isn't pretty and he doesn't repeat it consistently, he did reduce his walk rate from 16 percent in 2024 to 13 percent as a redshirt sophomore. He should get a chance to start once he turns pro, and he could with Tennessee if he returns for 2026.

Colorado’s top prep pitching prospect in 2022, Foutch declined overtures from pro teams to attend Arkansas. While he has shown some of the best pure stuff on loaded Razorbacks pitching staffs, he never has been able to crack the rotation or hold down a high-leverage role. He began this spring as a closer but was relegated to mop-up duty by the end of March. Foutch’s fastball averaged 98 mph and topped out at 100 this year, though it features lackluster life and he had trouble landing it in the strike zone, often leaving it over the heart of the plate when he did. His upper-80s splitter is a more reliable offering and tumbles when it’s on. He totally lost the feel for his mid-80s slider and all but abandoned it. Foutch comes with at least setup man ceiling but has a lot of work to do to get there. Though he works exclusively out of the stretch, he has well below-average fastball command and his splitter can get whacked when he doesn’t bury it. He also must prove his durability after missing time in his first two seasons and getting shut down in the Cape Cod League last summer.

In 2025, Penn State’s baseball program was the beneficiary of a pair of players coming from St. Joseph’s. Ryan Weingartner was the Nittany Lions’ shortstop and DeSanto was a mainstay in the rotation after two years of starting for the Hawks and a strong turn in the Cape Cod League, when he was named Harwich’s Pitcher of the Year. The big left-hander wasn’t quite as effective with Penn State, but he did take over as the Friday night guy in March. From a pure stuff standpoint, the 6-foot-4 DeSanto isn’t anything to write home about. It’s a below-average fastball from a velocity standpoint, averaging only around 88 mph in 2025 and topping out at 93 mph. But the data on the pitch is off the charts, with huge spin rates that lead to a ton of carry to make it very effective above the hands, a reason why it produced a 24-percent miss rate and opponents only hit .182 against the pitch. His upper-70s slider also features good spin, and he kills it with a changeup thrown a tick or two harder than the breaking ball. In addition to the metrics, DeSanto’s funky delivery adds a ton of deception, allowing all of his stuff to play up. There’s not a ton of margin for error here based on the velocity profile -- perhaps a team will think a few more ticks out of that big frame are possible -- and he’ll have to find better command, especially of his breaking stuff, for him to be a back-end starter at the highest level.

It’s not always so easy for scouts to get to the Florida panhandle to see players, but Willcox forced evaluators to check him out. The big right-hander got off to a little bit of a slow start, but he picked things up as the spring went on, helping his South Walton HS team rise up national rankings and reaching the 3A State Championship game before going on to pitch at the Florida High School All-Star Game in late May. Willcox is a strong and athletic 6-foot-4 right-hander with some solid \"now\" stuff and some possible projection. More often than not this spring, Willcox has been 91-94 mph with a fastball that features occasional tailing and sinking action to it, but he’s shown he can reach back for 96-97 at times early in games, so there might be more consistent velocity in the tank. He complements the heater with a good overhand curveball, and he’s shown glimpses of a decent splitter as an offspeed offering that could be an average pitch in time if he commits to throwing it more. Willcox’s athleticism does help him repeat his delivery, and while his command needs refinement, there’s some belief he could reach average control in time. He’s part of a strong Georgia Tech recruiting class, but might not set foot on campus if he gets taken early enough in the Draft.

Parents always hope their kids will surpass their achievements and there’s no question that Benny Agbayani, a 30th-round pick in 1993 who spent parts of five seasons in the big leagues, wants that for his son Bruin, the top player coming out of Hawaii in this Draft class. The high school shortstop proved his mettle at events like the Area Code Games and Perfect Game’s WWBA world championship last fall, then made a strong impression with a hard-hit triple and some impressive on-base skills during the MLB Draft Combine High School Game in June. The Hawaii Gatorade Player of the Year, the younger Agbayani is a couple of inches taller than his dad and unlike Benny, he hits left-handed. Bruin’s feel to hit is his carrying tool, with at least above-average bat speed and a feel for finding the barrel and controlling the zone. There’s some loft to his pull side, as evidenced when he turned around a 93 mph fastball at the Combine for his 106 mph triple to right-center field. It’s a hit-over-power profile right now, with more gap pop than anything, though it’s not too hard to dream on more damage in the future. An above-average runner who is aggressive on the basepaths, Agbayani’s bat comes with some questions about where he can play defensively at the next level. He probably doesn’t have the actions or hands to stay on the dirt, with the best option likely to be left field. He’s committed to Michigan if the Draft doesn’t go his way.

The best position prospect among south Texas high schoolers in 2022, Flores went undrafted because he wanted to attend Texas and learn from five-time All-Star Troy Tulowitzki. He struggled offensively and defensively after Tulowitzki left the coaching staff before his freshman year but has thrived the last two seasons after Tulowitzki returned. After his commitment to the Longhorns once again left him unpicked as one of the top sophomore-eligibles in 2024, he led the team in extra-base hits for the second straight season but slumped horribly in the final two months. An aggressive right-handed hitter, Flores looks to launch balls in the air to his pull side and has the bat speed, strength and leverage to generate 20 homers per season. He's equally effective against lefties and righties, though his free-swinging ways make him unlikely to hit for a high average or draw many walks. He has some of the highest chase rates in college baseball against curveballs and sliders but makes consistent contact when he swings at strikes. He struggled offensively and defensively after Tulowitzki left the coaching staff before his freshman year but has thrived the last two seasons after Tulowitzki returned. After appearing in 16 games, all but one in relief, as a Virginia Tech freshman, Stieg moved into the Hokies’ rotation as a sophomore in 2024. He showed enough glimpses of now stuff and upside serving as the team’s Sunday starter to generate buzz for an exciting Draft year in 2025. That never came to pass as he needed Tommy John surgery at the end of his sophomore season and didn’t throw a pitch this year. There are many attributes the 6-foot-4 Stieg can bring to a professional organization once he’s healthy. It all starts with a two-seam sinking fastball that has extreme run to it. In 2024, it averaged 93.5 mph and topped out at 97 mph, and while it didn’t miss many bats, it did get groundball contact. He complements it with a solid low-80s slider that can miss bats and an effective changeup thrown around the same velocity that serves as a swing-and-miss pitch as well and gets weak contact on the ground. Stieg delivers all of his offerings from a three-quarter slot and did a fine job of throwing his arsenal for strikes in 2024. He has the makings of a back-end starter if he can build off his sophomore campaign, though the lack of track record -- he’s thrown just 70 1/3 college innings in his career -- could make some teams pause. A team could send him out as a starter, but he could eventually find his way to the bullpen, where his sinker-slider combination could tick up.

Moore had some success pitching almost exclusively out of the bullpen in his first two years at Old Dominion. He had scouts excited about what his junior year might look like when he was up to 97 mph with his fastball last fall and given a chance to start full-time. The results were mixed as his stuff and command regressed when asked to stretch out as part of the Monarchs rotation, though he still provides some intriguing traits from a left-hander. At 6-foot-4, Moore has size and some projection on his side. While he’s shown more premium velocity in shorter stints and topped out at 97 mph this spring, his heater fluctuated throughout the year and he averaged around 92 mph with the pitch. During his mound session at the Draft Combine, he averaged 93.7 mph with his fastball, throwing it with good sink. He has good feel to spin his low-80s slider and can miss bats with it, though he’s landed it for strikes and got more swing-and-miss with it as a reliever in the past. He’s worked on a low-80s changeup, but it’s clearly behind the other two offerings. Teams that believe Moore can develop a true three-pitch mix might give him the chance to start out of the gate to see if he can find more consistency. But given the issues he had with maintaining his stuff and the regression in his command when he was in Old Dominion’s rotation, it might be better for him to head back to the bullpen, where his sinker-slider combination could tick back up.

After needing Tommy John surgery in high school that wiped out his senior year in Reno, Nev., Scolari also missed his true freshman year at San Diego in 2024 as he rehabbed. He returned as a Draft-eligible redshirt freshman in 2025, serving as the Toreros’ Friday night starter and winning West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year honors. But he went undrafted and transferred to Oregon for 2026, where his improved stuff out of the gate had scouts bullish about him being a college performer who could go in the top few rounds. Missed time with arm issues made teams pause, but he did return and had a dominant five-inning, 10-strikeout shutout performance against Washington in Big 10 Conference Tournament play. Scolari is a big, strong right-hander standing at 6-foot-4 and 220 pounds, and when he’s been healthy this year, his stuff has taken a big step forward from his year at San Diego. After sitting in the low-90s in 2025, he’s averaged a touch over 94 mph this year, topping out at 98. His mid-80s slider is still his best secondary offering, missing bats at a 42-percent rate heading into Regional play thanks to good depth and tilt. He now also has a slower 80-mph curve that can elicit some swing-and-miss, and there’s some feel for a firm changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much. All of that, along with an overall solid delivery, gives Scolari a chance to start. His command is tracking in the right direction, with some thinking he’ll be an average strike-thrower in time, but his lack of track record in consistently finding the zone along with the injury history does add some reliever risk to his profile.

The Las Vegas high school scene has produced its fair share of big league talent, with five players taken and signed in the top five rounds over the past four Drafts alone. Go back a bit more and you’ll find talent that went on to college and became first rounders, like Austin Wells and Kris Bryant, and of course there’s 2010 No. 1 pick Bryce Harper. Dallimore fits in somewhat with some of his predecessors as a big, strong hitter with some pop, though teams will have to wait to Draft him since he withdrew his name from the Draft and plans to honor his commitment to Texas Christian University. A right-handed hitter who creates an imposing presence in the box at 6-foot-4, Dallimore combines bat speed and strength to create impact at the plate. He has plus raw power, especially to his pull side, but with long levers and a long swing, there are questions about whether he’ll hit enough to get to that power at the next level. There are also swing-and-miss and chase concerns, especially against breaking stuff. Dallimore’s best defensive tool is his easily plus arm that has plenty of carry. He has good tempo to his exchange and release, though there’s work to be done on his accuracy and his overall receiving. There are some skills behind the dish, but his size and lack of mobility make it all work better from a one-knee setup. He is athletic enough to potentially handle first base or a corner outfield spot, where his power could profile well. Teams will get the chance to consider his skillset again in two years when he’ll be a Draft-eligible sophomore at TCU.

Millikan High School in Long Beach, Calif., has produced more than 30 draftees over the years, with Spencer Steer the most recent success story, though he went on to the University of Oregon first before signing. Pack has the chance to be the first Millikan player to be drafted since Steer in 2016 after cutting his teeth at MLB Develops events like the Dream Series and Hank Aaron Invitational and showing off his skills at this June's Draft Combine. A compact left-handed hitter at 5-foot-10, Pack is a hit-over-power type who can make a ton of contact. His game is to mostly spray the ball all over the field with some gap power, using the middle of the field well. He knows the strike zone and is willing to take his walks. While he might clock in as just a tick above-average as a runner, he is better underway, both on the bases and in the outfield. Pack has the chance to play center field for a long time. He likes to play deep, enabling his run tool to play better. His reads and routes are already solid and will keep improving with more reps. From a strength standpoint, his arm is below-average, but his accuracy helps it play up. The Texas recruit gets high marks for his makeup and work ethic as well.

Wake Forest produced seven pitchers selected in the first four rounds of the last two Drafts, leaving little opportunity for hurlers who didn't throw strikes. Ariola totaled just 26 1/3 relief innings in those two seasons and battled his control in summer ball as well, though he did pitch in the Cape Cod League All-Star game last summer. He made some promising progress during fall practice but worked his way out of the Demon Deacons' rotation after just two starts this spring, when he walked 23 percent of the batters he faced. Ariola's fastball sits at 92-94 mph and reaches 96, exploding past bats with carry up at the letters, but he can't consistently land it in the strike zone. His upper-70s curveball features high spin rates and can be devastating as well, though he has similar issues throwing it for strikes. He has a harder breaking ball in the mid-80s that's caught between a cutter and a slider, and he hasn't shown much feel for a changeup with similar velocity. Both Ariola's fastball and curveball can be plus pitches when he throws them over the plate, but his control was worse than ever this spring and he clearly lost his confidence on the mound. He's athletic but struggles to repeat a delivery that includes a long arm action. While he has the pure stuff of a No. 3 starter, he's almost certainly going to max out as a reliever and will need time and patience to develop.

Early in his high school career, Peeples emerged as one of the top outfielders in the 2025 prep class. He looks the part with a pretty left-handed swing and a frame that resembles that of a young Christian Yelich, though his struggles on the showcase circuit last summer have clubs wondering if they can draft him early enough to lure him away from a Georgia commitment. With Peeples' combination of bat speed and projectable strength, as well as a stroke designed to drive balls in the air to his pull side, he could grow into 25-homer power or more. To get there, he'll have to improve his timing at the plate after having swing-and-miss issues against all types of pitching last summer. He has a big leg kick and gets overly aggressive rather than allowing his pop to come naturally. Peeples' instincts allow him to play a little quicker than his fringy speed on the bases and in the outfield. Nevertheless, he won't be a basestealing threat and almost certainly will have to move from center field to a corner in pro ball. His arm stands out more for its accuracy than its average arm strength.
Projectable lefty power bat with pull-oriented swing.

Indiana's high school pitching crop runs deeper than usual this year, and Flores has the loudest stuff of the group. He features one of the best curveballs in the national prep class, though he also averaged a walk per inning as a senior. He comes with a high ceiling but also a good deal of reliever risk. Flores' hammer curveball ranges from 82-85 mph with downer break, grading as a well above-average pitch at times but also moving so much he has difficulty landing it in the zone. He has better command of a tighter slider with similar velocity. Hitters can't really guard against his breaking balls because his fastball sits at 92-95 mph and touches 97 with some armside run and carry. Flores barely utilizes his mid-80s changeup, which flashes some interesting tumble. The Kentucky recruit has a long arm action and effort in his delivery, which hampers his ability to throw strikes, let alone locate his offerings with much precision. He'll be an intriguing project for a team that believes in its ability to develop pitchers.

Magana was an up-and-coming high school infielder at G. Holmes Braddock High School in Miami when he made the decision to switch over to Christopher Columbus High, another powerful prep program in the area. After making the rounds on the showcase circuit at events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Area Code Games, Magana and Columbus went 3-1 at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational, though his play during his senior year was a bit uneven. From a raw tools and athleticism standpoint, there’s a lot to like about Magana. A 6-foot-3 switch-hitter, he projects as an interesting power-speed combination type at his best. There has been considerable raw power in the past, more from the right side of the plate, though it has come with considerable swing-and-miss from both sides of the dish. Some scouts were concerned with a lack of thump this spring, as Magana appeared more inclined to focus on contact first, without as much impact. Perhaps some of that was the young hitter trying to address his hit tool deficiencies, but some feared a loss of strength and physicality. Magana is at least a plus runner, especially if he can regain that strength, it should serves him well on the basepaths and defensively. While he had played shortstop in the past, he’s largely been a third baseman of late, and evaluators think he should move off the dirt and let his athleticism play in center field. Whether a team will be able to sign him away from his commitment to the University of Miami remains to be seen.

A high school standout in southern New Jersey, Weingartner spent two years playing middle infield at St. Joseph’s in Philadelphia, earning first team all-Atlantic 10 honors as a sophomore in 2024. He transferred to Penn State for his junior season, and while he struggled offensively, particularly in Big 10 play, he also was one of just seven players in all of Division I baseball to finish the season with 11 or more homers and 30 or more stolen bases. While Weingartner’s surface stats in 2025 don’t jump off the page, he does show a propensity for professional at-bats from the right side of the plate. He walked more than he struck out with the Nittany Lions and rarely chases out of the zone. There’s some power to his pull side, though it’s with an uphill swing, and there was some concern about whether a wood bat would impact him. Weingartner tried to answer some of those questions by taking BP at the Draft Combine and registering an average exit velocity over 98 mph during his swings. Weingartner is a plus runner who clearly knows how to steal a base, and that quickness is also an asset defensively. Most don’t think he’ll play shortstop long-term, with second base the most likely destination, and he’s seen time at the keystone in the past. If he can’t stay on the dirt, then his future profile gets a little cloudy.

The state of Delaware hasn’t had a player drafted in the top 10 rounds since 2013 and hasn’t seen a high schooler go that high since the year before that. Mitchell started creating some buzz this spring after performing on the showcase circuit at events like the Area Code Games and Perfect Game’s WWBA World Championship, earning Gatorade Player of the Year honors for the First State. Hailing from the same high school that produced current A’s infielder Zack Gelof, Mitchell has the chance to break Delaware’s top 10-round drought. Mitchell is a strong and physical catcher, standing at 6-foot-3. He’s a left-handed hitter, something teams love from their backstops, and he has the chance to do damage at the plate. He has plus raw power and can get to it at times, though he sometimes sells out for it, working too hard to add loft to his swing, ending up out in front as a result. A quintessential power-bat, power-arm type, Mitchell has plenty of arm strength behind the plate, though there’s work to be done on consistency and on his overall receiving. That’s something that often gets called into question with catchers this size, though most feel he should be adequate defensively long-term. Any team trying to sign him away from his commitment to head to the SEC and play for Kentucky, though, will be buying the bat and the power potential.
