Brannigan has the best college arm in the Midwest and can look like a first-rounder at times -- but it's hard to scout him on the mound. He worked just 14 2/3 innings this season, giving him 23 1/3 in three years at Notre Dame, and he prefers to play third base and wants to sign as a position player. A pro team may have to give him the opportunity to hit before trying to persuade him to become a full-time pitcher. Brannigan's fastball sits at 95-97 mph and reaches 100 with armside run, and he generates premium velocity with little effort. His mid-80s slider can be a wipeout pitch at times with quality depth as well as some horizontal action. He even shows some feel for a fading changeup with similar velocity, though he doesn't use it very often. Primarily a reliever for the Fighting Irish, Brannigan has the three-pitch mix, resilience and athleticism to make it as a starter. He'd need to improve his control and his consistency, which should happen if he focuses on pitching. A solid defender at third base with obvious arm strength, he makes contact from the right side of the plate and has the potential for average power but didn't drive the ball with wood bats in the Cape Cod League last summer.

A two-way player and the best prospect on a veteran Notre Dame team, Brannigan has some pull power but he's more likely a prospect as a relief pitcher, where he's been up to 100, sits 96, and has solid glove-side command of a mid-80s slider.

Adam Faurot was a late-round pick of the Brewers in 1996 out of Florida State who played four seasons of Minor League ball in Milwaukee's and Boston's systems. His son, Drew, grew up in Tallahassee and was a standout football and baseball player in high school, but he actually started his college career at Central Florida. He \"came home\" to the Seminoles after one season and has been a starter for the past two years, helping his Draft stock early with a better approach in 2025. A switch-hitting infielder who has cooled off a bit after a really hot start, Faurot made some mechanical adjustments at the plate that have led to more consistent results. He eliminated a big leg kick and flattened out his stroke a bit, with the limited movement allowing him to see the ball better. While his power production has been modest, he's been routinely registering solid exit velocities, and there's some hope he'll tap into his raw pop more as he progresses. He absolutely punishes fastballs but hasn't done as strong a job at adjusting to spin and softer stuff. Faurot has gotten a bit more physical, which could help him in the power department, but his run tool has backed up a little bit. He's still a very good athlete who can play a couple of different positions. He's best suited for second base, where he could develop into a solid defender in the future.

The defensive glue on the U.S. national team that won a gold medal at the 2017 18-and-under World Cup and featured 11 future first-rounders, Young struggled offensively on the showcase circuit the following summer and went undrafted as a Washington high schooler in 2019. He hit 16 homers in his first full season at Vanderbilt but also led NCAA Division I with 84 strikeouts in 61 games, with some scouts wondering if a left shoulder injury that required offseason surgery contributed to his whiffs. That doesn't appear to be the case because he has continued to swing for the fences and pile up strikeouts while batting .207/.327/.383 this spring. Young has transformed himself since high school, adding 20 pounds and getting much more uphill with his stroke from both sides of the plate. After showing little power as a prepster, he now has average pop that plays to his pull side as a right-handed hitter and to all fields as lefty. To realize his 20-homer potential in pro ball, he'll need to tone down his stroke and stop chasing pitches out of the strike zone. Young plays quicker than his average speed thanks to his advanced instincts on the bases and in the field. He covers ground at shortstop, where his hands, strong arm and internal clock make him a solid and reliable defender. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, he has the versatility and skills to fill a utility role.

Young was a known, toolsy high school prospect who looked incredible taking infield and BP, then struggled to hit in games. Concern about his hit tool and a strong commitment to Vanderbilt brought Young all the way from mountainous Selah, WA to Nashville, where Young has showed as an underclassman that he's capable of tapping into the power even while swinging and missing a lot. He had 33 extra-base hits in 61 games as a sophomore in the SEC, while also playing excellent shortstop defense. Things came unglued in his draft year, when he K'd 30% of the time and hit .207 with just 16 XBHs. He can still pick it at shortstop, and is an interesting bounce back candidate, but now projects as a glove-first utility infielder.

Scouts who like college pitching have had the ability to head to watch Gonzaga play and stay all weekend. Friday night starter Gabe Hughes looks like a solid first-rounder and Trystan Vrieling has stepped into the Saturday role and opened some eyes. Kempner, who transitioned from a relief role to a starting one in 2021, began the year as the Saturday guy, missed nearly two months with a finger ligament issue, and has come back effectively as the Sunday starter. There’s a lot to like stuff-wise about the 6-foot Kempner. He throws a very heavy fastball that has flirted with triple-digits, has been up to 97 mph consistently and has averaged close to 95 mph this spring as a starter. He misses bats and gets ground ball outs with it and he backs it up with a solid low-80s slider that features good lateral break and has been a strikeout pitch for him. His upper-80s changeup flashes average at times, too, though throwing that pitch might have been the cause of his finger injury. Kempner uses a cross-fire delivery with a sidearm slot, which makes for an uncomfortable at-bat. It’s also not an easy delivery to repeat, and Kempner’s command has been inconsistent. He likely profiles as a reliever at the next level, but one who could be a really tough arm coming in late in games.

Kempner has huge arm strength with a rise/run fastball that doesn't really play in the zone. He needs more pitch manicuring than the typical college prospect but a good dev group might help his fastball be more effective. For now he's a fastball/slider relief prospect.

A 33rd-round pick by the Cubs out of an Illinois high school in 2019, Ritter attracted more scouting attention the following year at John A. Logan (Ill.) CC but went unpicked in the shortened five-round Draft. He transferred to Kentucky and became one of the top defensive shortstops in the Southeastern Conference last spring. His glove alone might land him in the top three rounds in 2022, though persistent questions about his bat could knock him down a bit. Capable of playing anywhere on the diamond, Ritter is a smooth defender with nice actions at shortstop. His quickness gives him plenty of range and he has soft hands and a good internal clock. He features plus arm strength and makes consistently accurate throws from a variety of angles. The question is how much Ritter will hit because he has down little damage with the Wildcats and initially struggled with wood bats in the Cape Cod League. Scouts don't love his right-handed swing and he doesn't make consistent contact against non-fastballs, though he did make adjustments and rallied at the end of his stint on the Cape. Built along the lines of Marcus Semien, he has some strength that could produce at least 15-homer power if he figures things out at the plate, and he's also a solid runner out of the batter's box and plus underway.
Ritter has a huge arm and is a capable defensive shortstop. His lacking hit tool prevents him from getting to power.

McElvain committed to Vanderbilt before throwing his first pitch as a Tennessee high schooler and served as a reliever in his first two college seasons. He became the Commodores' Friday-night starter this spring and worked the first seven innings of a no-hitter against Kentucky on April 22. He mostly struggled afterward before striking out 11 in seven frames against New Mexico State in his final start in the NCAA regionals. McElvain's most effective pitch is his solid 81-85 mph slider with depth, and he also can turn it into a harder 85-88 mph cutter. His fastball sits at 91-93 mph and touches 95 with enough riding action to keep it off barrels. He'll flash an average changeup with some tumble, though it's too firm in the mid-80s and he doesn't trust it very much. While scouts praise McElvain's competitiveness and ability to pitch above his pure stuff, he'll need to throw more strikes to remain in the rotation. His delivery should be conducive to better control, and he gets into trouble when he falls behind in the count because he lacks the arsenal to overpower hitters. He'll get the chance to start in pro ball but could wind up as a slider-heavy reliever.

McElvain spent his first couple of years at Vanderbilt in the bullpen, then moved to the rotation in his draft year. He has a plus two-plane breaking ball and his fastball plays up due to its riding life, but it isn't hard enough to miss bats within the zone; instead, McElvain needs to live above the zone to avoid getting hurt. For this reason, he was walk-prone in 2022, but his command actually isn't bad, it's just what he has to do to get by. Because he's so new to a rotation, he may just be scratching the surface in some areas and could develop and hold velocity once he's used to working a starter's inning load.

Freeland was a solid infield prospect coming out of Mariner High School in Cape Coral, Fla., after his pandemic-shortened senior season. He wasn’t taken in the abbreviated five-round Draft that June, but scouts knew he would be eligible again as a sophomore at Central Florida two years later. He stepped right into the Knights’ lineup as a freshman and has been a mainstay offensively and at shortstop since. Freeland is a switch-hitter who has the chance to have some impact with the bat. He’s had excellent plate discipline while at Central Florida, drawing a ton of walks in both seasons, and he’s cut his strikeout rate considerably as a sophomore. He has legitimate extra-base pop, especially to his pull side, from both sides of the plate, showing more power right-handed this season. While he’s played shortstop exclusively at UCF, scouts don’t see him sticking there at the next level, with a lack of quickness limiting his range, though he does have good hands and actions to stay on the dirt. He played second and third during his time in the Cape Cod League last summer, and some evaluators think his best shot at being a regular will be as an offensive-minded second baseman at the professional level.
A switch-hitting left-side infielder (shortstop in college, probably 3B in pro ball) who doesn't chase, Freeland's doubles pop likely plays in a part-time infield role.

The Puerto Rico Baseball Academy has produced a fair share of shortstop prospects in the Draft, the most notable one being former No. 1 overall pick Carlos Correa, and most recently Mariners 2021 second-rounder Edwin Arroyo. Another shortstop, Rodriguez will represent the Academy as this year’s best Draft prospect from Puerto Rico, though he is not quite as highly regarded as his aforementioned predecessors. Rodriguez is definitely a glove-over-hit middle infielder right now. His soft and quick hands work very well at short and he has more than enough arm, with good carry on his throws, to stick at the premium position long-term. He’s an above-average runner and should have plenty of range for the spot as well. There are more questions about his offensive profile. The right-handed hitter does have some feel for the barrel and contact, though some scouts don’t love his setup at the plate and he’ll need to refine his approach. He also will need to add strength so he can impact the ball more. Teams will surely be interested in the Alabama-Birmingham recruit’s glove and it will be interesting to see how the hot start of Arroyo, who had a similar “needs to add strength” evaluation, might impact decision-making when it comes to Rodriguez.

A standout in high school who starred at SoCal powerhouse Orange Lutheran and for USA Baseball’s 18U national team, Rajcic went undrafted in the shortened 2020 Draft, partially because of his strong commitment to UCLA. He served as an effective closer for the Bruins as a freshman before making a successful move to their weekend rotation this season. While not the biggest guy in the world at six feet tall and fairly physically mature, Rajcic does have an intriguing four-pitch mix he can use for a solid north-south kind of attack. The right-hander can run his fastball up to 95 mph, averaging around 91 mph. He has two distinct breaking pitches, with his true upper 70s curveball with downer action better than his low-80s slider, though both are usable pitches. He throws his low-80s changeup with conviction and fade. While none of Rajcic’s pitches grade out as plus, they play up because he can throw strikes at the top and the bottom of the zone very consistently. He’s super-competitive on the mound and has never shied away from the spotlight, something that will appeal to many teams, even if his size and delivery carry some reliever risk.

A three-star tight end prospect in high school, Cumbest played two sports in his first three years at Mississippi State, catching five passes for the football team before missing last fall after surgery to repair a dislocated shoulder. Also a part-timer in his first three seasons on the diamond, he helped the Bulldogs win the College World Series last June. He has made progress while finally getting regular playing time in 2022 and has the upside to factor in the first five rounds. At 6-foot-6 and 235 pounds, Cumbest is built along the lines of Giancarlo Stanton and his strength and bat speed give him well above-average raw pop. He won't fully tap into his power potential until he gets more upright in his stance to gain more leverage with his right-handed stroke. He also needs more at-bats to continue to refine his approach at the plate and learn how to cope with breaking balls and changeups. Extremely athletic for his size, Cumbest has solid speed and good instincts on the bases. He has seen time in center field this spring but spent most of the season in left field. He has average arm strength and could become a solid defender on the corners with more experience.

He also needs more at-bats to continue to refine his approach at the plate and learn how to cope with breaking balls and changeups. Extremely athletic for his size, Cumbest has solid speed and good instincts on the bases. He has seen time in center field this spring but spent most of the season in left field. He has average arm strength and could become a solid defender on the corners with more experience.

Jenkins has an unusual profile as an extremely aggressive hitter who strikes out in nearly a quarter of his plate appearances yet also makes a lot of loud contact. Though he has played only first base at Georgia Tech, he may have some untapped defensive value as well. He batted third in a Yellow Jackets lineup that could have as many as seven players drafted in July. Built along the lines of Andrew Vaughn, Jenkins has a compact right-handed swing with plenty of bat speed and strength. He gets to most of his plus raw power, generating high exit velocities and driving the ball with authority to all fields. He rarely walks and is vulnerable to sliders, so there is some concern as to how his approach will play at the next level. More athletic than he looks, Jenkins can show average run times out of the batter's box and moves well for his size. An average to solid defender at first base, he has a stronger arm than most at the position. A third baseman and catcher in high school, he might merit a look at the hot corner or in left or right field.

Adler comes from a football family, as his grandfather Marlon Smith was a running back at Missouri and his father Marlon was a quarterback for the Tigers. He earned Cape Cod League reliever of the year honors in 2021 after topping the prestigious summer circuit with seven saves while posting a 1.15 ERA with 29 strikeouts in 15 2/3 innings. He remains one of the more intriguing bullpen prospects in the 2022 Draft despite losing his closer's job because of an inability to throw strikes. There's nothing wrong with Adler's pure stuff, starting with a fastball that parks at 94-96 mph and touches 98 with high spin rates that create difficult carry up in the zone. His hard breaking ball gives him a second plus pitch with curveball depth and slider velocity at 80-85 mph. He also can break out an upper-80s cutter that reaches 92 mph, though he mainly operates with his heater and curve. Though Adler is athletic, he never has been able to provide consistent strikes because he struggles to repeat his three-quarters delivery and stay online to the plate. His control has gotten worse than ever this spring, deteriorating to the point where he was getting few chases because he was missing so badly. He has the upside of a high-leverage relief option but is going to have to significantly upgrade his ability to locate his pitches to get there.
Adler sits 92-95, he'll touch 98, and he has a nasty low-80s power curveball with two-plane break. His delivery puts him in a relief-only prospect bucket.

Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 60 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 One of the best prep athletes in the 2022 Draft, Jordan went unselected because he planned on playing baseball and football at Mississippi State. The three-star wide receiver recruit wound up giving up the gridiron and handled the rugged Southeastern Conference well, batting .336 and bashing 30 homers in two seasons. He has improved faster than scouts expected and could factor into the first round this July as a sophomore-eligible. Jordan may have more bat speed than anyone in the 2024 Draft, and his lightning-fast right-handed swing and strength produce huge exit velocities and at least plus power to all fields. He made strides with his pitch recognition and plate discipline as a freshman, inspiring confidence that his pop will translate at higher levels. He still needs to prove he can make consistent contact, because he swings through fastballs and chases breaking balls, weaknesses that contributed to a 29 percent strikeout rate this spring. While Jordan has at least plus speed and may have plus-plus straight-line quickness, he's still learning how to make the most of it. He's not aggressive on the bases and is shaky in the outfield, where he spent most of his freshman year in left. His arm has gotten a little stronger since high school and now grades as average.

Overshadowed in a Georgia high school class that could produce the No. 1 overall and three first-rounders, Snow has a broad base of tools yet may factor in the top five rounds for only a few clubs because he didn't stand out on the showcase circuit last summer. He set a national high school record with 18 triples in 2021, then batted .628 with 17 homers and 15 steals in 28 games this spring. Snow has a simple right-handed swing and a mature approach that makes use of the whole field. While he's just 5-foot-10, his bat speed and deceptive strength should allow him to hit 15 or more homers per season. He's at least a plus runner and aggressively uses his speed on the bases. With his quickness and solid arm strength, Snow has the tools to remain at shortstop. He has smooth actions and reliable hands as well. If he winds up attending South Florida, he could become the Bulls' best position prospect since 2017 supplemental first-rounder Kevin Merrell.

Gatorade's Ohio player of the year and the state's best prep prospect in 2019, Anglin went undrafted because of his strong commitment to Clemson. He might have gone around the fourth or fifth round as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2021 but returned to college after his price tag dropped him to the Nationals in the 13th round. His scouting report is unchanged from a year ago, as he continues to generate elite spin rates and battle the strike zone. Anglin once again features two of the more intriguing breaking pitches in the Draft, favoring his mid-80s slider with two-plane break over his low-80s downer curveball. Both can be plus-plus weapons at their best. He sits at 92-95 mph and reaches 98 with run on his fastball, though it gets hit because his long arm action enables batters to see his heater well and he doesn't command it. Though he has served as Clemson's No. 1 starter for most of the last two seasons, Anglin profiles strictly as a reliever as a pro. He has below-average control and command, even when he tries to dial back his stuff to find the zone, and he shows little feel or trust for his low-80s changeup with fade. If he can learn to harness his breaking balls and to dodge more bats with his fastball, he could be a high-leverage bullpen weapon.

Anglin has one of the best breaking balls in the draft, a two-plane demon with big depth and sweep. It typically ranges anywhere from 83-87 mph, though he seemed to be backing off it and throwing it more softly, with curveball shape, early in 2021. Two well-demarcated breaking balls will likely be a developmental focus for Anglin, who has a chance to have two great ones because his feel for spin is elite. But fastball viability will be a hurdle even though Anglin throws quite hard. His upright delivery and vertical arm slot create a lot of downhill angle, which mirrors bat paths. He doesn't miss many bats in the strike zone with it, instead relying on hitters to be late on heaters away from them. This is what stands between him and comfortable starter projection, even though Anglin made real strides as a strike-thrower in 2021.

Part of a Chicago-area pipeline that has served Louisville well, Prosecky was the second-best Illinois prep prospect in 2019 behind Pirates first-rounder Quinn Priester. A top-five-rounds talent who turned down the Phillies after signability dropped him to the 35th round, he was a midweek starter in his first college season but missed most of 2021 with a shoulder strain. He has served as Louisville's closer this spring but may get an opportunity to start in pro ball. Prosecky has more velocity than most left-handers, operating with a 92-95 mph fastball that tops out at 97 with some riding action. He works heavily off his heater, backing it up with a mid-70s curveball that can get swings and misses but also eludes the strike zone too frequently. He also has a firm mid-80s changeup with modest life but doesn't use it much as a reliever. With the potential for three average or better offerings, a strong 6-foot-3 frame and a delivery with no glaring flaws, Prosecky may tempt a pro team to try him as a starter. To succeed in the rotation, he'll have to use his secondary pitches and significantly improve his control. It's more likely that he'll wind up in the bullpen, where his role will depend on his ability to locate his fastball and curve.

Lewis was a solid two-way player at Marina High School in Huntington Beach, Calif., before heading to join a Santa Barbara program that has produced first-round arms like Michael McGreevy last year and Dillon Tate in 2015, not to mention Shane Bieber in 2016. After redshirting in 2020, Lewis spent most of 2021 pitching capably as a starter before helping the Gauchos win the Big West title again as their all-conference Friday night starter. The 6-foot-5 Lewis brings a unique array of pitches to the mound, all coming from an athletic frame. While his fastball typically sits in the 90-92 mph range, topping out at 95, he uses excellent extension and high spin rates to get swings and misses on the pitch up in the zone. He throws a solid 11-to-5 downer of a curveball in the upper 70s that misses bats consistently. He’s fiddled with a work-in-progress changeup and mixes in an occasional cutter, though that might be his worst pitch. Lewis also throws a legitimate knuckleball that he would float up around 80 mph that confounded hitters and catchers alike. Though he didn’t throw it much, it’s the kind of pitch he could turn to if being a “regular” pitcher doesn’t work out. Generally a strike-thrower, Lewis got tired at the end of the season and his command suffered, but his combination of size, interesting stuff and strong analytics, not to mention the track record of his school, should have teams interested in seeing how it works at the next level.

Knuckleballer alert! Lewis doesn't throw many of them but he does incorporate a knuckler into his mix, though he is mostly a prospect for other reasons. He gets an unusual amount of in-zone whiffs on his 90 mph fastball because he tilts out like Michael Wacha, creating a vertical arm slot that imparts riding life on the baseball. He can also turn over a pretty good changeup from that slot, which is rare, but also Wacha-ish (though not as nasty). Ideally he'll find more velo in pro ball but he could conceivably work in bulk relief even if he doesn't.

Only one player has been drafted in the history of Lawton Chiles High School in Tallahassee -- right-hander Harrison Francis, a fourth-round pick of the D-backs in 2017. Stanfield, a speedy center fielder, could be the second after a strong spring season that came on the heels of a summer in which he showed off his tools at events like MLB’s PDP League, USA Baseball’s 18U Team Trials and the East Coast Professional Showcase. Stanfield has the chance to be an exciting player who can stay up the middle. He has some definite bat speed from the right side of the plate, and while he should be able to answer questions about impact by continuing to add strength to his 6-foot-2 frame, some scouts have concerns about some swing-and-miss in his game. His best tool is his speed, which allows him to be aggressive on the basepaths. His wheels also enable him to cover a lot of ground in center field, where he should be able to stay long-term, with a strong arm to go along with his defensive instincts. Stanfield is part of a strong Auburn recruiting class, but there might be some teams willing to draft his overall set of tools early enough to keep him from playing for the Tigers.

As a Hawaiian prep standout, Arquette's athleticism -- he also played basketball in high school -- stood out on the summer showcase circuit, and he landed in MLB Pipeline’s Top 250. The D-backs took him in Round 18 of the 2022 Draft, but he headed to the University of Washington. After playing sparingly with the Huskies as a freshman, he earned all-Pac 12 honors after finishing with a .959 OPS as a sophomore. Over the summer, the infielder entered the transfer portal, played well in the Cape Cod League and transferred to Oregon State for his junior season, where he has been one of the most consistent college performers. Scouts see the 6-foot-5, 220-pound Arquette as the best college player in the Pacific Northwest this year -- and one of the best college hitters in the country. While minor wrist surgery cut into his fall with his new school, the right-handed hitter showed he has easy raw power to tap into, with more to come, and he's used it in games consistently this spring. He routinely barrels the ball with good bat speed and a fluid swing, giving him the chance to be an above-average hitter with above-average power, and he could hit 20-25 homers annually as a big leaguer. While Arquette is an average runner and played second base at Washington, he showed on the Cape that he should have the chops to play shortstop long-term, with easy actions, soft hands and more than enough arm with carry at every angle across the diamond. College bats with pop at a premium position are always a hot commodity, so Arquette should get plenty of attention in the first round.

Jerzembeck hails from Providence HS (Charlotte, N.C.), which has produced a trio of big leaguers (Ty Buttrey, Kevin Shackelford, Richie Shaffer) and a pair of first-rounders (Shaffer and Logan Davidson, after they went to Clemson) in the last decade. He has big league bloodlines, with his father Mike pitching three games for the 1998 Yankees. Eli led the Panthers to a 34-0 season and the state 4-A championship this spring, riding one of the better breaking balls in this year's prep class to a 13-0, 0.42 record and a national-best 195 strikeouts in 87 1/3 innings. Jerzembeck's money pitch is an upper-70s curveball that features downer break and spin rates that can exceed 3,000 rpm, though he can fall in love with it too much at times. His fastball has increased from the upper 80s last summer to the low 90s this spring, with a peak of 95 mph, but it lacks notable life or carry. He also has a low-80s changeup with sink that he has yet to use very often. Scouts don't love the upright finish to Jerzembeck's delivery and wonder how much projection remains in his 6-foot-2 frame. He attacks hitters and throws strikes, though his control is more notable than his command. He turns 19 a month before the Draft and will be eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2024 if he attends South Carolina.

Kentucky's top 2022 prep prospect as a power-hitting third baseman, Forbes went undrafted because of his strong commitment to Louisville. The Cardinals used him more as a DH/outfielder as a freshman before shifting gears in 2024, when an errant pitch broke his left hand in his lone plate appearance, sidelining him for a month. After working just 38 1/3 innings on the mound in his first two college seasons, he took off as a full-time pitcher in 2025 and ranked third in NCAA Division I with 14.8 strikeouts per nine innings. Forbes has explosive carry on his high-spin fastball, which averaged 94 mph last spring, ticked up with Team USA and in the Cape Cod League last summer and now sits at 94-96 with a peak of 100. He also has added more power to his slider, which now runs from 81-85 mph and can be a plus pitch at its best, and he'll occasionally turn it into an upper-80s cutter. He hasn't had much time to refine an upper-80s changeup that features plenty of fade when it's on but also can get too firm. As Forbes concentrates all of his energy on pitching, the hope is that he'll be able to improve his changeup and strike-throwing. His delivery features some effort and he missed two starts in April with a flexor strain, though he recaptured his stuff when he returned and helped Louisville reach the College World Series. If everything comes together, he could fit in the front half of a big league rotation.

Few high schoolers in the 2022 class could match LaViolette's combination of physicality and athleticism, but swing-and-miss concerns left teams hesitant to buy him out of his Texas A&M commitment. A down junior season ended his chances to become the first four-year college outfielder to go No. 1 overall since Darin Erstad in 1995, but he's still one of the best college position players available. He set school career records with 68 homers and 169 walks and led the Aggies to the College World Series Finals last year. Possessing as much raw power as anyone in the Draft, LaViolette is built to crush balls with a quick left-handed stroke, the strength and leverage in his impressive 6-foot-6 frame and a focus on launching pitches to his pull side. He also makes quality swing decisions but the lone flaw in his offensive game does scare some teams. He frequently swings and misses within the strike zone, even on fastballs, leading to a .258 average with a 25 percent strikeout rate as a junior. Remarkably athletic for his size, LaViolette posts solid run times out of the batter's box and is even quicker once he gets going. He played the outfield corners as a freshman before moving to center field last spring, with most evaluators projecting him to spend the bulk of his big league career in right. His power and solid arm strength fit the right-field profile to a tee.

He also makes quality swing decisions but the lone flaw in his offensive game does scare some teams. He frequently swings and misses within the strike zone, even on fastballs, leading to a .258 average with a 25 percent strikeout rate as a junior. Remarkably athletic for his size, LaViolette posts solid run times out of the batter's box and is even quicker once he gets going. He played the outfield corners as a freshman before moving to center field last spring, with most evaluators projecting him to spend the bulk of his big league career in right. His power and solid arm strength fit the right-field profile to a tee.

After spending the shortened 2020 season and full 2021 campaign largely pitching out of Stanford’s rotation, Mathews threw well in a four-start stint in the Cape Cod League in 2021. He followed that up by pitching well as a swingman/multi-inning reliever last year, landing on MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 250 list. The Rays took him close to the end of the Draft, and Matthews returned to campus for his senior year, where he’s been effective as the Cardinals' Friday night starter. The 6-foot-5 left-hander brings four pitches and plenty of funk and deception to the mound. He can dial his fastball up to 94 mph, and it averages just over 91 mph, but his best pitch is his low 80s changeup, which features a ton of fade to both miss bats and get ground-ball outs. He throws his tight slider around the same velocity, and he also has a slower low-70s curve with three-quarter shape to it. The long and lanky southpaw has done a better job of finding the strike zone compared to last year while continuing to post high strikeout rates and certainly raised his profile with a string of strong postseason starts. His ceiling might be somewhat limited to a back-end starter, with teams considering him knowing that he knows how to get outs coming out of the bullpen.

White first became a pitcher of interest in 2021 when he mostly relieved for the Cal Bears. He moved on to many scouts’ follow lists when he struck out 12 in eight innings of work for USA Baseball’s College National Team and got evaluators excited when he registered double-digit strikeouts in each of his first three starts with a move to the rotation as Cal’s Friday night starter. He wasn’t able to maintain that, however, losing his spot in the rotation and struggling in conference play, though he was finding his footing a bit and closing some games late in the year. At 6-foot-1, 205 pounds, White does not fit the “projectable right-hander” label, but he does have a four-pitch mix. He can run his fastball up to 97 mph, especially in shorter stints, though he sits more in the low 90s as a starter. He is capable of throwing a tight slider in the low to mid-80s and a distinct slower curve, and misses a lot of bats with both, but they can run into each other and commanding his breaking stuff has been an issue. He has a changeup that can be effective at times as well. White’s biggest issue has been his command, especially of his secondary stuff, both in and out of the zone, leading to inflated hit and walk rates. That, plus the effort in his delivery, likely points to a future as a reliever.

White pitched in a myriad of roles as an underclassman, then became Cal's Friday starter in 2022. He sits 92-95 mph, touching 96, with some arm-side run, and makes heavy use of a mid-80s slider with late break, and a 79-81 mph curveball with occasional depth. He has trouble locating any of them consistently and has relief risk, but he may come into yet more arm strength with a move to more consistent relief, where fringe athletes like this tend to fit.

A product of SoCal’s San Dimas High School, perhaps best known for producing the pitching brothers duo of Jimmy and Peter Lambert, Smith went undrafted in the pandemic-shortened 2020 Draft and headed to Southern Cal. He played somewhat sparingly but hit well as a freshman in 2021, then looked solid offensively in the new Appy League that summer. He’s been the Trojans’ everyday shortstop as a Draft-eligible sophomore. When Smith was in high school, the 5-foot-9 infielder got some attention for his knack for making contact. While that largely has continued at USC, the right-handed hitter has been selling out for power a bit more, leading to a slightly higher strikeout rate and not as positive results as some hoped for when this season began, though he was drawing a fair amount of walks. An average runner, Smith plays with very high energy at short, but most scouts think he’s overachieving there. His arm likely isn’t reliable enough to stick there, but he could find a home at second base at the next level. Scouts who like him were hoping he could put up numbers like 2021 second-rounder Connor Norby did, but his struggles in conference play have hurt his stock a bit.

In 2019, Newell was a talented high school outfielder from Pennsylvania who landed on MLB Pipeline’s Top 100 based on his raw tools, though they didn’t consistently show up in games. He didn’t get selected until close to the end of the Draft and honored his commitment to the University of Virginia. After opening some eyes with a strong showing in the shortened 2020 season, he’s looked more like the raw player he was in high school in 2021 and 2022. A left-handed hitter, Newell does show glimpses of being able to drive the ball to all fields. He needs to refine his approach, as there has been way too much swing-and-miss in his game. He has cut his strikeout rate and drawn more walks this season, which has helped him get to his power more. He punishes fastballs but struggles against breaking stuff. Newell runs well and can steal a base, and he’s reached double digits in home runs and stolen bases this spring. Newell’s speed should allow him to stick in center field, which certainly doesn’t hurt his profile. It all comes down to if he can keep improving his approach and make more contact. There are a lot of tools to unlock here, and while Newell isn’t the Top 100 prospect he was as a prepster, there are bound to be teams who will be willing to roll the dice on his skillset.

The best player to come out of Lake Brantley High School in Florida was catcher Jason Varitek, who turned himself into a first-round pick after heading to Georgia Tech for college and went on to have a very successful 15-year big league career. This year's Draft class features another Lake Brantley backstop in Heyman, who most recently showed off his abilities at the plate at the Draft Combine. The two tools that stand out for Heyman currently are his raw power at the plate and his raw arm strength behind it. Some scouts put a 60 grade on his raw pop from the right side of the plate, and he registered some high-end exit velocities at the Combine, though there is concern about his ability to make adjustments and hit enough to get to that power in games at this point. Heyman's pure arm strength also gets a 60 from evaluators, but he needs to work on his footwork and transfer to get the most out of that tool. He will also need to improve his overall receiving, especially as the game speeds up at higher levels. While he definitely has the raw skills to eventually be a successful big league catcher, there are those who think he's likely to head to the University of Florida, where he could develop into an early-round prospect, just like Varitek did.

Rincones’ father, Gabriel Sr., pitched briefly in the Mariners organization. His son is a pure hitter who played for H.B. Plant, the Tampa school that produced Wade Boggs and Kyle Tucker, among others. Rincones went from high school to starring at St. Petersburg Junior College in 2020, then posted a 36-game hitting streak in 2021 and was a first-team All-American. He was drafted in the 19th round by the Padres, then moved on to Florida Atlantic in 2022, earning Conference USA Newcomer of the Year honors by hitting 19 homers with a 1.110 OPS. It’s Rincones’ left-handed bat that has scouts interested. He’s always been able to hit with an advanced approach at the plate, something that continued with high walk and low strikeout rates after the move to Division I baseball. The power started really showing up this season, especially to his pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields. He punishes fastballs with pitchers only finding success in getting him out with offspeed stuff. Rincones is going to have to hit to become a big leaguer because he is limited defensively. He has a below-average arm and doesn’t run well, meaning he’s likely either a left fielder or a first baseman. He likely has shown enough on the offensive side for teams that like college performers to consider him on Day 2 of the Draft.
A physical outfielder with above-average power, Rincones is adept at hitting pitches at the top of the zone and struggles with breaking balls in the lower third of the zone and below.

Teams are always on the lookout for toolsy up-the-middle talent in every Draft, so there has been particular interest in Brennan since he was an underclassman. A shoulder injury kept him from really putting himself on the map during last summer’s showcase circuit, and while he did show off some of his skill set early this spring, he once again missed time, leaving him a bit difficult to put on Draft boards. Brennan is definitely the kind of exciting player who is “what they look like,” with a strong and athletic 6-foot-2 frame. In early glimpses, he looked like one of the better high school players in California, with plenty of bat speed and potential impact from the left side of the plate, and there’s more power to grow into for sure. An above-average athlete, Brennan is capable of posting plus run times, but hasn’t always shown it. He has the chance to be at least an average defender in center field with enough arm strength to move to a corner if need be. Teams that saw Brennan early might be in on the tools and could be willing to try to sign him away from his commitment to UCLA.

Ryan Clifford earned a seven-figure bonus out of Pro5 Academy (Apex, N.C.) in 2022 and has since played his way onto MLB Pipeline's Top 100 Prospects list as a member of the Mets' organization. But at the time he was drafted, there were some evaluators who thought another outfielder on the same club was a superior talent. Serrano opted to attend North Carolina State, where he has impressed with his bat-to-ball skills, yet disappointed with his power. He helped the Wolfpack reach the College World Series as a Draft-eligible sophomore this year but hit just .289 with 14 homers in two seasons. Serrano has a smooth, easy left-handed swing and a lanky 6-foot-5 frame that provides leverage. He makes consistent contact with ease despite his long limbs and can crush some balls in batting practice, but he doesn't drive the ball in games and is feeble against southpaws. He projected as a 25-30 home run threat in high school but hasn't grown into the bat speed or strength that scouts expected. Though he's a fringy runner out of the batter's box, Serrano moves well once he gets going. After playing first base as a freshman, he played a credible center field with average-to-solid arm strength this spring. He has good instincts in center, but he's probably destined for an outfield corner as a pro.

Despite attracting interest as one of the best shortstop defenders in the 2022 high school class, Silva withdrew from the Draft with a week to go because he wanted to attend Texas Christian. He helped lead the Horned Frogs to the 2023 College World Series while earning consensus Freshman All-American honors in his first season in Fort Worth. He has slumped significantly as a sophomore-eligible and his skills stand out more than his pure tools, so it's unclear where he may fall in the Draft. Silva isn't flashy at shortstop but has good actions and a finely tuned internal clock. He makes plays with quick hands and solid arm strength, showing the ability to execute throws from a variety of angles. He's not the most athletic shortstop and has puzzled scouts by looking less rangy and dynamic in the field this spring. Silva has a simple approach at the plate and puts the ball in play to all fields with a relatively flat right-handed stroke. He has shown some sneaky raw power in the past but isn't driving the ball with any authority as a sophomore, generating a lot of harmless contact. Though he has below-average speed, he has fine instincts and has a knack for knowing when to steal bases.

Austin's athleticism and versatility might have landed him in the top five rounds as a Georgia high schooler, but he withdrew from the 2022 Draft to fulfill his Vanderbilt commitment. He started at second base as a freshman and at first base as a sophomore, when he saw action at all four infield positions as well as left and center field. He hasn't put up huge offensive numbers in three college seasons but had a strong 2024 summer with the U.S. collegiate national team and in the Cape Cod League. Austin has a lot going on with his right-handed swing and employs a big leg kick, but his hand-eye coordination and sense of timing allow him to make repeated contact to all fields. He almost puts the bat on the ball too easily, producing too much ground-ball contact and cutting into his walk totals. He lacks power and rarely drives the ball in the air to his pull side, so he may not offer more than 10-12 homers per season. With plus speed and a high baseball IQ, Austin is a proficient basestealer. He covers ground and has good defensive instincts, though his fringy if accurate arm limits his effectiveness on the left side of the infield. He fits best at second base or center field, and he manned the latter position capably this spring. Scouts love his makeup.

Madison (Miss.) Central claimed a share of the national high school baseball championship in 2021, when scouts flocked to see Jaguars two-way star Braden Montgomery, who’s now at Stanford. They’ve returned this spring to evaluate Highfill, one of the more athletic catching prospects in the 2022 prep class. He flipped his college commitment from Southern Mississippi to Mississippi State last summer, and it’s unclear whether he’ll go high enough in the Draft to lure him away from the Bulldogs. Highfill’s defense is ahead of his offense at this point. He consistently recorded plus 60-yard dash times on the showcase circuit, is more of an average runner out of the batter’s box and moves well behind the plate. His quick footwork enhances his solid arm strength, and he could have the receiving skills to match once he adds more polish. A right-handed hitter, Highfill has some offensive potential as well. He doesn’t try to do too much at the plate but needs to develop better timing to produce more quality contact. He has the strength and bat speed to provide 15-20 homers per season if he can become more consistent at the plate.

The best prospect to come out of Holly Springs HS (N.C.) since Carlos Rodon 11 years ago, Wills has some parallels to fellow Tar Heel State product Greg Jones. Jones impressed scouts with his speed and athleticism at Cary HS (N.C.) in 2017, but there were questions about his physical readiness for pro ball and his ability to stick in the infield. Jones blossomed into a first-round pick after two years at UNC Wilmington, and Wills has a similar profile as well as a commitment to the Seahawks. Wills is a better hitter than Jones was at the same stage, showing advanced bat-to-ball skills despite a less-than-smooth left-handed stroke and an approach that gets overly aggressive at times. He doesn't provide much impact at the plate because he carries just 165 pounds on his 5-foot-11 frame. While power never will be his game, he'll need to get stronger and clean up his swing before he's ready to handle pro pitching. A quality athlete who also starred as a quarterback, Wills has plus speed and can flash well above-average run times on occasion, so his focus should be getting on base to take advantage of his wheels. His hands and actions aren't conducive to staying at shortstop, and his average arm is a bit stretched on the left side of the infield. Draft-eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2024 if he attends college, he could wind up at second base but may eventually land in center field.

Maxwell attracted scouting interest as a Georgia high schooler with a big 6-foot-6 frame, a fastball that reached 98 mph and flashes of a hammer curveball, albeit with scattered control. After turning down the Yankees in the 30th round of the 2019 Draft to attend Georgia Tech, he presents the same scouting report three years later. He pitched his way out of the rotation a month into the 2022 season and continued to battle the strike zone as a reliever, though he boosted his stock by striking out 11 in six innings against No. 1-ranked Tennessee in the NCAA regionals. Maxwell operates at 95-97 mph and has reached 101 in short stints, though his fastball has modest armside run and gets hit when he works in the bottom half of the strike zone. His breaking ball combines curveball depth with slider velocity in the mid-80s and touches 90 mph, but he has trouble landing it in the zone and tends to miss badly, so he doesn't generate a lot of chases. He fiddled with a changeup as a starter but has scrapped it as a reliever, which will be his role at the next level. Though he's throwing more strikes than he did in his first two years at Georgia Tech, Maxwell still has well below-average control and command. He has lost some weight but still has a soft body and needs to improve his conditioning, which might help him maintain his release point more reliably. He has the ability to dominate with his fastball and curveball but has yet to prove he can do so on a consistent basis.

His breaking ball combines curveball depth with slider velocity in the mid-80s and touches 90 mph, but he has trouble landing it in the zone and tends to miss badly, so he doesn't generate a lot of chases. He fiddled with a changeup as a starter but has scrapped it as a reliever, which will be his role at the next level. Though he's throwing more strikes than he did in his first two years at Georgia Tech, Maxwell still has well below-average control and command. He has lost some weight but still has a soft body and needs to improve his conditioning, which might help him maintain his release point more reliably. He has the ability to dominate with his fastball and curveball but has yet to prove he can do so on a consistent basis.

Georgia not only boasts the top high school pitcher available in Dylan Lesko but also another intriguing right-hander in Murphy. While he's not as spectacular as Lesko, Murphy has a similar build with plenty of athleticism and projection as well as the potential for a three-pitch mix. He performed well on the showcase circuit and finished with a dominant outing at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October, though he has been up and down this spring. Murphy's 88-92 mph fastball currently tops out at 94 but should pick up more power as he adds more muscle to his lean 6-foot-3 frame. His heater plays up with armside run and carry up in the zone and he also can work it down with some sink to get ground balls. His low-80s changeup features fade and sink that generate a lot of swings and misses, and it's more reliable than his slider with similar velocity but inconsistent bite. Murphy's arm action is a bit long in the back but he repeats his delivery well and throws strikes. He has good feel for pitching and shows the ability to move his fastball around the zone. Committed to Auburn, he's a potential mid-rotation starter.

Mederos had enough stuff to fit in the top three rounds of the shortened 2020 Draft as a Florida high schooler, but he went unpicked because of his commitment to Miami, where he was the jewel of a top-rated recruiting class. He began last spring in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation but control difficulties relegated him to the bullpen for the final two months. He displayed one of the better arms yet continued to battle the strike zone in the Cape Cod League during the summer, then transferred to Oklahoma State and has continued to light up radar guns while getting hit hard. Mederos can sit at 94-97 mph and reach 99 with arm-side run on his fastball, but his heater doesn't miss many bats because he doesn't command it well and often has to dial it back to find the zone. His mid-80s slider with two-plane depth is his best pitch and he also can get swings and misses with his downer low-80s curveball, but he can't land the latter for strikes. He has flashed a plus mid-80s changeup with quality fade in the past but has barely used his cambio this spring. Strong and physical, Mederos has the ingredients for an intriguing four-pitch arsenal but has yet to prove he can harness it. Given his struggles, the effort in his delivery and his arm action, many evaluators believe he's destined to wind up as a reliever. If he can learn to throw enough strikes, he has the stuff to close games.

Mederos had a lot of profile as a high schooler because he had big stuff, but a violent delivery and poor command plagued him. At the start of his freshman year, he had slimmed and toned his delivery down, and he has kept trending that way. Still a bit wild, Mederos' strike-throwing has improved to the point where he belongs among the other 2022 college starters near the top of the class because nobody has three pitches as good as his, but he's yet to have sustained on-field success.

In his first two years at Santa Barbara, Bremner has slid back and forth between starting and relieving, finding success in both roles in 2024 to put up gaudy numbers. He began the year in the rotation but moved to the bullpen when Hudson Barrett got hurt. He was back in the rotation when Matt Ager struggled, helping the Gauchos reach (and host) a Regional. He hasn't taken the step forward this year many anticipated, knocking him from the top of the Draft conversations. Entering the spring, the hope was that Bremner would continue to show the makings of three plus pitches, but it hasn’t worked out that way. His fastball is still averaging around 95 mph and touching 98 with good ride, lighting up the radar gun with little effort and with some feeling there's room for growth and more velocity to come in pro ball. His best secondary offering is his easily plus changeup that some scouts hang a 70 grade on. He'll throw it to any hitter in any count, and it stays on the fastball plane for a long time with late, hard fade, missing bats at a 46 percent clip in 2024. One of his bigger issues this spring has been that his 86-88 mph slider with gyro-type shape has backed up -- he's struggled to throw it for strikes -- and he’s been more of a two-pitch pitcher. Bremner is still answering questions about durability, as this is his first full season of starting. But he's generally around the strike zone and is capable of missing bats with all three offerings. Even with some of the question marks this spring, he’s still firmly in the first-round picture.

A bit of a late bloomer, Kerkering didn’t make his Venice High School varsity team until his junior year but then helped the Florida power win back-to-back state championships as a starter. He began his career at South Florida as a reliever, scuffling a bit initially in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, then thriving as the Bulls’ closer in 2021. He moved into the Friday night starter role and opened a lot of eyes early, but after struggling, he has largely been back in a reliver role since late April. Always pitching from the stretch, Kerkering does have three pitches in his arsenal. The 6-foot-2 right-hander tops out at 97 mph with his fastball, especially in shorter stints, and has averaged around 93 mph. He hasn’t always commanded it well and it’s been squared up more than it should. His best pitch is his slider, a sharp 83-85 mph breaker that flashes plus and can be a nasty strikeout pitch at times. His mid-80s changeup isn’t as good, but it does offer some fade away from left-handed hitters. Kerkering does a nice job of hiding the ball and creating some deception with his delivery. And while his overall command needs to improve, he’s done a better job of finding the strike zone than he did in 2021. A team taking him at some point on Day 2 of the Draft might want to give him a chance to start, but there’s a pretty good chance he lands in a bullpen, where that slider could really play.

Left-handed hitters who can play shortstop are always a hot commodity, and California has produced some good ones, from Brandon Crawford to Corey Seager to last year’s No. 4 overall pick, Marcelo Mayer. Garate has a long way to go to belong in a conversation with that group, but as a bit of a pop-up prospect at Murrieta Mesa High School in Southern California, he was getting more attention as the spring wore on. Right now, Garate is definitely field over hit. He has a solid swing from the left side, with good balance and while he can get overly aggressive at the plate and needs to work on pitch recognition and plate discipline, he makes a lot of contact. The real question about his offensive profile is his potential impact. He’ll need to add a lot of strength to his 6-foot-1 frame to be more than a bottom-of-the-order type of hitter. There are no concerns about his ability to play shortstop for a long time. He has excellent hands and actions, and his above-average speed contributes to his excellent range. His arm should be at least above-average. There’s a commitment to the University of Oregon to contend with, but teams who believe that offensive impact will come with physical maturity might be interested in buying the glove.

Sandlin was part of an all-prospect rotation in 2021 at Eastern Oklahoma State JC, joining Christian McGowan (who signed with the Phillies as a seventh-rounder) and Andrew Walling (who pitched three innings this year at Mississippi State after transferring). Sandlin moved on to Oklahoma, where he had an up-and-down regular season before coming up big repeatedly in the postseason. He struck out 10 in a win over Kansas State in the Big 12 Conference tournament, beat Florida in the NCAA regionals and fanned 12 in a College World Series victory over Texas A&M. Sandlin's best pitch is a 78-80 mph curveball with depth and horizontal action that flashes plus, though he doesn't use it as often as his solid 82-85 mph slider with more lateral movement. The key for him at the next level will be missing more bats with his fastball, which sits at 91-93 mph and tops out at 96 with a bit of armside run. He'll also have to refine a mid-80s changeup that needs more velocity separation from his heater and more fade to be effective. Though Sandlin throws strikes, his control isn't as advanced as his command. He'll need to add more power or life to his fastball, which gets pounded when he leaves it in the middle of the zone. If he can't make the necessary adjustments, he could become a breaking ball-heavy reliever.

Burkhalter was effective as a reliever but had trouble locating his pitches in his first two seasons at Auburn before pounding the strike zone and taking off in his third. He finished second in NCAA Division I with 16 saves this spring, including both of the Tigers' super-regional wins and their lone College World Series victory. His 10.1 K/BB ratio would have ranked fourth if he had logged enough innings to qualify. Burkhalter scrapped a slider he couldn't land for strikes and replaced it with an upper-80s cutter that shows signs of becoming a plus offering and works against both left-handers and right-handers. He sets it up with a 92-95 mph fastball that touches 98 and features carry and armside run. He also has upgraded his control of his 82-85 mph changeup, a solid pitch with fade and sink. Though he has three pitches and cut his walk rate from 6.8 per nine innings in 2020-21 to 1.4 this season, Burkhalter is strictly a reliever. He never started a game in college and is a 6-footer with some effort in his delivery. If he can improve his command in similar fashion to the gains he made with his control, he could serve as a set-up man at the next level.

Burkhalter's stock exploded during the college World Series, where he was bumping 97, tilting in a hellacious cutter as hard as 92 mph, and also missing bats with the occasional changeup. He has three distinct pitches, which give him a shot to start, but his violent delivery pushes him toward multi-inning relief projection.

Scouts have had a difficult time figuring out Martin, whose fastball velocity and secondary pitches fluctuated during a season in which he made five starts but spent the bulk of his time in the bullpen. He saved his best outing for last, striking out an Oklahoma State-record 16 in 6 2/3 innings of relief as the Cowboys overcame an early 12-0 deficit to outslug Missouri State 29-15 in an NCAA regional playoff. Martin averages 94 mph with high spin rates and carry on his four-seam fastball, but he'll mix in outings in which he deals at 94-98 with others in which he operates at 90-94. He relies heavily on his heater, because while his slider sits at 82-85 mph and reaches 89, he doesn't land it for strikes and its modest break means it often gets pounded when he does. He can morph his slider into a harder cutter and also messes around with a curveball and a sinking changeup, but none of them are particularly effective. Draft-eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore, Martin is more about potential than present stuff. A team that believes it can teach him a better breaking ball could turn him into at least a quality two-pitch reliever and perhaps more. His 6-foot-3, 238-pound frame is built for durability and a potential starting role if he can develop his secondary offerings, though he'll also need to become more efficient with his strike-throwing.
Trevor Martin has a riding fastball up to 98, though sitting quite a bit below that. He has a maxed frame and need to develop a more reliabel secondary pitch.

Auburn features three pitchers who could get drafted in the first six or seven rounds, and Barnett has better pure stuff than Trace Bright and Blake Burkhalter. He also never nailed down a regular turn in the Tigers' Southeastern Conference rotation in three college seasons, making him an enigma to scouts. Some believe he could succeed as a starter in pro ball, while others think he's destined for the bullpen. Barnett's best pitch is an 82-85 mph slider that touches 87 with plenty of depth. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and reaches 98, though it lacks life and gets whacked when he doesn't locate it well. He also employs a mid-70s downer curveball and a mid-80s changeup but can struggle to land them in the zone. When his pitches are at their best, Barnett can display a plus fastball and slider and a solid curveball and changeup. While he made some progress in 2022, he never has displayed consistency with his stuff and strikes, and his long arm action costs him deception and command. He'll probably get the chance to start at the next level but most likely will wind up as a fastball/slider reliever.

Ball State produced a pitcher who went in the top four rounds of each of the last three Drafts: Diamondbacks first-rounder Drey Jameson (2019), Marlins second-rounder Kyle Nicolas (2020) and Astros fourth-rounder Chayce McDermott (2021). Schweitzer doesn’t light up the radar gun like they can but could approach the same territory this July. A reliever in his first two seasons with the Cardinals, he won Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a starter this spring and finished second in NCAA Division I with 11 victories. Schweitzer’s fastball parks around 90 mph and only occasionally reaches the mid-90s, but it gets swings and misses up in the strike zone with its induced vertical break and high spin rates. He backs it up with three average secondary pitches, the most effective of which is his upper-70s slider with two-plane depth. Both his slider and slower, more downward-breaking curveball can be plus offerings at their best. Schweitzer also utilizes a low-80s changeup with depth against right-handers. He has significantly improved his control and command this year while holding up well in his first season as a college starter. His feel for mixing his pitches and locations adds to his package as a high-floor, back-of-the-rotation type.

JSerra Catholic High School in San Juan Capistrano, Calif., has produced a good amount of Draft talent, most notably former No. 1 overall pick Royce Lewis. After three pitchers from the program got drafted a year ago, including current Giants’ Top 30 prospect Eric Silva, this year could be Gough’s turn, especially after he went to the MLB Draft Combine and struck out all five batters he faced in game action. Gough is an aggressive right-hander with arm strength who has the chance to have at least three average or better offerings in the future. His fastball can touch 95 mph, but typically sits in the 91- to 94-mph range, thrown with good spin rates up in the zone. While he typically features a slurvy breaking ball in the upper 70s, he showed a distinct slider and curve, the latter of which led to three of his strikeouts at the Combine. He has some feel for his changeup, but it’s a work in progress. The 6-foot-2 righty is more control over command right now, but he does a solid job of finding the strike zone. He attacks and goes right after hitters, leading some to wonder what he would look like in a relief role where he could just blow it out for an inning at a time. He’s committed to Oregon State, where he’d likely get a chance to start.

A lack of physicality was a concern in terms of impacting the ball, but he had added some strength between the summer and early spring, even though his offensive performance tapered off as this season wore on. If the bat doesn’t come around, Ortiz has plenty of upside on the mound, with some scouts wondering if he’d be better off there to begin with. Without much instruction, or perceived desire to excel, he’s been up to 95 mph with his fastball, sitting 92-93 mph with ease while flashing an average slider and a little feel for a changeup. A team that signs him away from his Florida International commitment could send him out as a shortstop knowing the mound is a very viable Plan B.

Most believe Ortiz’s future is on the dirt, and all signs point to him preferring to be a position player at the next level. There’s no doubt he can play shortstop for a very long time, with a plus arm, good range and loose, easy actions. The bat is behind the glove, but he does have a loose and easy swing from the right side and he makes a lot of contact. A lack of physicality was a concern in terms of impacting the ball, but he had added some strength between the summer and early spring, even though his offensive performance tapered off as this season wore on. If the bat doesn’t come around, Ortiz has plenty of upside on the mound, with some scouts wondering if he’d be better off there to begin with. Without much instruction, or perceived desire to excel, he’s been up to 95 mph with his fastball, sitting 92-93 mph with ease while flashing an average slider and a little feel for a changeup. A team that signs him away from his Florida International commitment could send him out as a shortstop knowing the mound is a very viable Plan B.

Penn State hasn’t had a position player taken in the first two days of the Draft since catcher Ben Heath was a fifth-rounder back in 2010. Thanks to a big 2022 season in which Wood finished among the Big 10 leaders in several offensive categories, the fellow backstop has the chance to break that schneid. Wood finished the season with a 1.147 OPS thanks to a strong approach from the left side of the plate -- he walked more than he struck out -- and an ability to tap into his raw power more consistently. He’s more strength than bat speed but tapped into his pop this spring to reach double digits in home runs, more to the pull side. The backstop has decent defensive tools, with solid arm strength and the ability to stay behind the plate long-term. Those who believe in him see a lefty-hitting catcher, always a commodity, with tremendous on-base skills and some pop. Doubters see a guy who had a good year in a bad conference. Either way, he should join Heath on that list of Nittany Lions hitters taken on Day 2, giving him the chance to be the first Penn State player to reach the big leagues since 1998 first-rounder Nate Bump spent parts of three seasons in the Marlins bullpen.

Wood is a sweet-swinging lefty-hitting catcher who had a whopping four-to-one ball-in-play to swinging strike ratio in 2022. He's an okay receiever who sometimes struggles to control the running game.

The son of longtime scout and former professional player Tim Huff, Kody was a solid prep catcher at Arizona powerhouse Horizon High School, garnering enough attention to get taken in Round 32 of the 2019 Draft before heading to Stanford for college. He became the starter for the Cardinal in 2021 but didn’t really put himself on the map as a Draft prospect until his bat woke up in 2022, with a .315/.411/.567 line making him a much more intriguing option. It’s Huff’s makeup and baseball IQ that stand out more than any one tool. He’s always been a solid defender, with decent receiving and blocking skills to go along with a solid average arm that did a nice job helping to control the running game. The right-handed hitter makes a lot of contact, limiting strikeouts and upping his walk rate this year. That helped Huff get to his power, with 13 homers this spring, mostly to the pull side. Huff’s blue collar approach and leadership behind the plate help his tools play up. Add in the fact that he grew up around the game, has gotten better since his high school days and performed well at a top program in the Pac-12, and teams will be giving this over-achiever some serious looks on Day 2 of the Draft.

Video scouting repor t » Two years ago, Notre Dame featured Joe Boyle, a tall fireballer who struggled to throw strikes and went in the fifth round. Simon could follow the same path after helping the Fighting Irish reach the College World Series for the first time since 2002. He wowed scouts with 16 strikeouts over eight scoreless innings at the Atlantic Coast Conference tournament and NCAA regionals, though his control deserted him again in the super-regionals and at the CWS. While Simon can't quite match Boyle's height or velocity, he's still an imposing figure on the mound at 6-foot-4 and can reach 101 mph with his four-seam fastball. He usually operates at 94-97 mph with armside run and downhill plane on his heater, which can get hammered if he doesn't locate it well. His slider misses more bats with its combination of 82-85 mph velocity, sweep and depth, though he has even more trouble landing it in the zone than he does with his fastball. As a two-pitch guy who averaged 8.2 walks per nine innings during his college career, Simon is definitely a reliever. The key to his success going forward will be his ability to repeat his mechanics and stay online toward the plate. He yanks a lot of pitches into the lefty batter's box and can't be trusted with a high-leverage role until he proves he can provide more strikes.

Wisconsin is one of the more underrated states in terms of producing talent and Louisville routinely has landed several of its best prep hitters. That's true again this year with the Cardinals getting commits from the Badger State's top two position prospects, Milton shortstop Gavin Kilen and Vierling. A cousin of Phillies outfielder Matt Vierling, Will is a catcher who stands out most for his advanced bat. Vierling makes consistent contact to all fields with a quick left-handed stroke. With his hitting ability, bat speed and projectable strength, he should produce 15-20 homers per season. He also has an advanced understanding of the strike zone and should draw a healthy amount of walks. Scouts haven't had an easy time appraising Vierling's defense because he played through a broken hamate on his mitt hand on the showcase circuit last summer. Quicker than a typical catcher, he moves well behind the plate and has an average, accurate arm with a quick release. His biggest backers think he has the hands and athleticism to become at least an average receiver, while some evaluators think he'll end up at first base.

Major League players who are 6-foot-7 don’t come around very often, even if Aaron Judge and Oneil Cruz are very impressive current exceptions to the rule. Tejeda is hoping to join their ranks, though it’s still a bit to be determined whether he does so on the mound or at the plate. He entered the spring as one of the most intriguing two-way talents in the class, and while some saw some regression, there are teams very intrigued by his upside. Many teams think Tejeda wants to hit, and he does have considerable raw power from both sides of the plate. Because of his long levers, however, there is length to his swing and a lot of zone to cover because of his size, leading to concern about his hit tool. While he’s not unathletic, he’d likely be limited to first base as he fills out. There is a lot of projection with him on the mound. Some have seen him up to 97 mph, but he’s typically in the 91-93 mph range, using his size to throw it with good plane. His changeup is his go-to secondary offering now, which he can sell decently out of his hand with some sink. His breaking ball is a slower slurve right now, but he could become a hard sinker-slider type in the future. He could have the chance to both pitch and hit at Florida, though most see his future as a pitcher.

Thomas exhibited some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the Texas high school ranks in 2022, but he missed time with a wrist injury and was unsignable from a Texas commitment, so he went undrafted. Two years later, he's one of the best pure hitters and top sophomore-eligible prospects in the 2024 Draft. He's adding to his value by showing he can play center field in addition to first base for the Longhorns. Thomas has good feel for the barrel and doesn't try to do too much at the plate, letting his pretty left-handed swing work for him. He has traded some contact for power this spring, hitting the ball harder and showing that he should be able to provide 15-20 homers per season. He offers one of the higher floors among college bats and his ceiling continues to rise as he displays more pop. To complement his hitting ability, Thomas offers several other promising tools. He's a solid runner and quicker once he gets going, though he's not much of a basestealer. He provides a plus glove at first base and also is a solid defender with arm strength to match in center field.

A swingman on a North Carolina State club that finished third at the 2021 College World Series, Villaman provided three innings of clutch relief in the super-regional finale against Arkansas to help send the Wolfpack to Omaha. He pitched for the U.S. collegiate national team last summer and has operated exclusively out of the bullpen this spring. He increased his Draft stock with a strong performance at the Atlantic Coast Conference tournament, including five shutout innings with eight strikeouts against North Carolina in a championship-game loss. Villaman relies heavily on a 90-93 mph fastball that tops out at 95, using it more than 80 percent of the time overall and more than 90 percent against left-handers, and it plays better than its velocity. He can command it all over the strike zone, with good carry at the top and nice downhill angle at the knees. He keeps right-handers off his heater by mixing in an improved low-80s changeup with fade and sink. Villaman has a strong 6-foot-2 frame and pounds the strike zone, and some scouts wonder whether he could succeed as a starter in pro ball. The biggest question is his lack of feel for spinning the ball and he doesn’t show much faith in a flat, slow slider in the upper 70s. It’s more likely that he’ll remain in a multi-inning relief role at the next level.

Crighton won three Michigan state championships and 114 of his last 115 games in three years at St. Mary's Prep (Orchard Lake), including Division 2 titles in 2019 and 2021 and a Division 1 crown as part of a 44-0 team this spring. Scouts consider him the best hitter on a deep Eaglets squad that also features Brock Porter, the favorite to be the first pitcher drafted in July. Crighton missed three weeks in May with a shoulder injury but returned for the playoff run. Advanced at the plate for his age, Crighton has a quick right-handed stroke and a gap-to-gap approach. He focuses on making line-drive contact rather than swinging for the fences, but he has the hitting ability and bat speed to grow into average or better power once he fills out his lanky 6-foot-3 frame. He has clocked some plus 60-yard dash times but will be more of a solid runner after he matures physically. Crighton also played basketball at OLSM and his athleticism translates to the hot corner. He has a quick first step and moves well laterally at third base, where he should be at least a solid defender with arm strength to match. Because he has more projectable than present tools, he may not get taken high enough to lure him away from his Michigan commitment, but he could blossom into a top-two-round pick in 2025.

Prep Baseball Report’s Player of the Year for the state of Florida, Hodges had success on both sides of the ball for St. John’s Country Day School in Jacksonville. And while he showed off skills as a hitter and pitcher when his team made it to the championship game at this spring’s National High School Invitational, his future most certainly will be on the mound. Hodges presents himself as an advanced college lefty in many ways, with a legitimate four-pitch mix at his disposal. His velocity is slowly climbing, though it’s still fringy from a miles per hour standpoint, the typically in the 88-90 mph range, touching 92. He holds his velocity deep into starts and it plays up because he can command it so well. He does have a distinct curve and slider, the latter slightly harder with more bite, though they can run into each other at times. He also has good feel for his changeup, with the off-speed pitch a touch behind the breaking stuff. The lefty has shown the ability to throw all four of his pitches for strikes, with a willingness to throw any of them in any count. The biggest issue with Hodges might be his signability, with a very strong commitment to the University of Virginia, with the potential for him to emerge as an even better and stronger version of himself in a few years.
