Lonsway was a prime Draft prospect in both 2017, when he was Ohio's top high schooler and fell to the 19th round, and in 2020, when he led NCAA Division I in strikeout rate (21.0 per nine innings) as a redshirt sophomore at Ohio State but went unpicked. Academically ineligible because of a transcript snafu in 2018, he's now 22 and in his fourth year of college, so his negotiating leverage is diminishing. He has one of the best curveballs in this year's Draft and can look like a first-rounder on his best days -- such as when he struck out 17 with just one walk against Indiana in early April -- but his inability to throw strikes makes him almost certainly destined for the bullpen in pro ball. Lonsway's curve has quality power (low 80s) and depth that earn it comparisons to Barry Zito's bender when at its best. Both his 91-96 mph four-seam fastball and his mid-80s slider/cutter can flash as plus pitches as well. He shows some feel for a changeup though he doesn't incorporate it very often. While Lonsway can land his curveball for strikes, his control and command are serious concerns that figure to make him a reliever in the long run. He doesn't locate his fastball well and has averaged more than six walks per nine innings between Ohio State and two summers in the Cape Cod League. He has an odd delivery that features an extremely high arm slot and severe head tilt, and he struggles to keep his mechanics in sync.

Lehigh University in Pennsylvania has had two players in the last 15 years taken in the top three rounds: right-hander Levi Stoudt, a Mariners' third-round pick in 2019, and catcher Matt McBride, an Indians supplemental second-round pick in 2006, who touched the big leagues. Black, who jumped on the map with a very strong Cape Cod League showing after his freshman year in 2019, has the combination of size and arm strength that should help him join that duo in July, though his stuff had backed up some as Lehigh’s Friday night starter in 2021. The 6-foot-3 Black has shown one of the better fastballs, at least in terms of velocity, in the Draft class. He's thrown it in the 97-100 mph range and will hit 99 mph consistently in a one-inning look, with average life, but sat around 94 mph as a starter this spring. He can back it up with a hard 87-88 mph slider that flashes above-average but is inconsistent. It can be more cutter-like with some tumble to it but often doesn’t have late snap, and he had trouble commanding it in 2021. He will also mix in a fringy changeup. In addition to the up-and-down secondary stuff, Black has had trouble finding the strike zone at times. His delivery will need some work, with too much effort even though he has a good, durable starting pitcher frame. A team taking him early could very well send him out as a starter and see if his secondary stuff and command can develop, but it’s possible he ends up in a bullpen when all is said and done.

Black looked good during summer ball, both on the 2019 Cape (he pitched well enough there to start the All-Star Game) and in the 2020 South Florida Collegiate Baseball League, where he won Pitcher of the Year. He missed a huge chunk of his freshman year due to an appendectomy, then only made a handful of collegiate 2020 starts due to the pandemic, then his stuff fell off toward the end of the 2021 collegiate season with Lehigh. He shortened his arm swing over the summer but his arm action is still pretty long, and Black has an intense, demonstrative mound presence that I think fits in a bullpen. He'll sit in the mid-90s with tail on his two-seamer, movement that pairs well with a changeup, though the rest of his repertoire is a work in progress.

Black, who jumped on the map with a very strong Cape Cod League showing after his freshman year in 2019, has the combination of size and arm strength that should help him join that duo in July, though his stuff had backed up some as Lehigh’s Friday night starter in 2021. The 6-foot-3 Black has shown one of the better fastballs, at least in terms of velocity, in the Draft class. He's thrown it in the 97-100 mph range and will hit 99 mph consistently in a one-inning look, with average life, but sat around 94 mph as a starter this spring. He can back it up with a hard 87-88 mph slider that flashes above-average but is inconsistent. It can be more cutter-like with some tumble to it but often doesn’t have late snap, and he had trouble commanding it in 2021. He will also mix in a fringy changeup. In addition to the up-and-down secondary stuff, Black has had trouble finding the strike zone at times. His delivery will need some work, with too much effort even though he has a good, durable starting pitcher frame. A team taking him early could very well send him out as a starter and see if his secondary stuff and command can develop, but it’s possible he ends up in a bullpen when all is said and done.

Black looked good during summer ball, both on the 2019 Cape (he pitched well enough there to start the All-Star Game) and in the 2020 South Florida Collegiate Baseball League, where he won Pitcher of the Year. He missed a huge chunk of his freshman year due to an appendectomy, then only made a handful of collegiate 2020 starts due to the pandemic, then his stuff fell off toward the end of the 2021 collegiate season with Lehigh. He shortened his arm swing over the summer but his arm action is still pretty long, and Black has an intense, demonstrative mound presence that I think fits in a bullpen. He'll sit in the mid-90s with tail on his two-seamer, movement that pairs well with a changeup, though the rest of his repertoire is a work in progress.

Webb flashed second-round upside in his fourth college season at Georgia in 2021, highlighted by 13 strikeouts in a duel with Vanderbilt and No. 2 overall pick Jack Leiter in April, but he blew out his elbow a month later and required Tommy John surgery. The Guardians drafted him in the fourth round and handled him with care in his first full pro season before turning him loose in 2023. He led the Arizona Fall League with 36 strikeouts in 22 2/3 innings last offseason and is challenging for the lead in whiffs in the Double-A Eastern League this summer. Webb's best offering is a plus upper-70s curveball with depth, though he uses it mainly against right-handers and less often than the other three average pitches in his arsenal. His fastball usually ranges form 91-94 mph and tops out at 96, lacking notable action but showing some carry when he locates it up in the zone. His low-80s slider has good depth and his low-80s changeup tumbles when it's on. When he was in college, Webb's upright delivery and lack of durability led many scouts to project him as a reliever. He's doing a better job of getting down the mound and piling up innings as a pro, and his control and command continue to improve. He has a ceiling of a No. 4 or 5 starter with a fallback as a multi-inning lefty reliever who can get righties out.

Leftwich has intrigued with his arm strength since his high school days in Florida and was a late-round pick by the Tigers out of TNXL Academy in 2017, though it was common knowledge he was headed to pitch for the University of Florida. He’s both started and relieved since joining the Gators' staff in 2018, showing glimpses of power stuff in both roles. He began the 2021 season throwing well as part of the weekend rotation, then showed how dominant he could be during some multi-inning relief outings in April. The 6-foot-2 right-hander has largely been a two-pitch guy, though those two pitches have been very good. He’ll crank his fastball up to 96 mph regularly, sitting around 94 mph, though it can be a bit true at times. He’ll miss bats with his slider, which flashes plus, but he does struggle landing it within the strike zone. He does have a changeup, but it’s not nearly as good as his other offerings. Because of the two-pitch mix, the spotty command and the bulldog mentality on the mound, many scouts feel Leftwich is better suited to a relief role at the next level. A team taking him in the top five rounds could send him out as a starter to see how his stuff develops, knowing that shortening him up and letting him rely on that fastball-slider combination could get him to the big leagues quickly.

After a strong prep career at Piedra Vista High School that saw him earn 2018 New Mexico Gatorade Player of the Year honors, Silseth began his college career at the University of Tennessee. After amassing just 20 2/3 innings, almost all in relief, he transferred to the College of Southern Nevada in 2019 to get the chance to start, and he made five of those before the shutdown in 2020. He impressed enough to get the chance to head to Arizona in 2021, where he’s served as the Friday night starter. Performance-wise, Silseth has been a bit up and down with the Wildcats, but overall has an intriguing mix of pitches that could give him the chance to start. He’ll throw his fastball up to 96 mph regularly and complements it with what he describes as two distinct breaking pitches, though they often run into each other. The slider is better when they are separated, a low-80s offering with good three-quarters shape and late, firm bite. While he hasn’t used his changeup a ton in games, there are those who think the offspeed pitch, with good sink and fade, is actually his best pitch. Silseth is only six-feet tall, which automatically leads some to question his durability as a starter long-term. He’s done a good job with his conditioning and he stays around the strike zone, giving him a chance to stick in a rotation and putting him in the top five round landscape, with a team taking him knowing the stuff might tick up in shorter stints out of the pen.

Silseth was among the hardest-throwing college pitchers in the country but his fastball lacks action so it still gets hit around. His arm talent and two good secondaries -- a slider and, maybe, a splitter -- make him a nice developmentla piece despite the lack of fastball movement. Silseth threw a splitter in junior college but he's de-emphasized it in favor of the more average slider, and he looks to be using a more straight change grip. Whether an org's dev group helps impart better movementon the fastball or finds a way to re-introduce the splitter, there are obvious avenues for development here that make Silseth a good bet to be a relief piece eventually.

Charlotte hasn't had a pitcher selected in the top five rounds since the Giants made Brion Treadway a third-rounder in 2000, but McGowan should change that in July. The 49ers' No. 1 starter since the start of his sophomore year in 2020, he displayed improved stuff last fall and began this season by permitting just three runs in his first five starts. He gave up 16 runs in just 11 innings over his last four starts, clouding his Draft status a bit. After working at 90-92 mph as a sophomore, McGowan hit 97 during fall practice and has operated at 92-94 with repeated forays into the mid-90s and some riding action this spring. His best secondary offering is an 82-85 mph slider that shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch, and he also has an upper-70s curveball he'll use to give hitters a different look. He has feel for a sinking changeup as well, though it can get a bit firm at times. Though McGowan has a four-pitch repertoire, many scouts see him as a reliever in the long term. He lacks size and projection and features some effort in his delivery, which hampers his ability to throw strikes. He'll need to upgrade his control and command significantly at the next level, even if he winds up in the bullpen.

Having a good bat to consider from the University of Arizona is nothing new. Austin Wells was a first-rounder in last year’s Draft, one of nine Wildcat hitters taken in the top five rounds since the 2016 Draft. Boissiere has hit since he set foot on campus in 2019 and that continued this year and he landed on the Golden Spikes Award Midseason Watch List. A left-handed hitter and fielder, Boissiere has shown off an advanced approach at the plate for three years. He can drive the ball to all fields, work counts and draws walks while limiting his strikeouts. While he hasn’t put up huge power numbers, he’s shown more extra-base authority this spring and there’s average power in there. While Boissiere is limited to first base, he has very good actions there, with good hands and agility to be an above-average defender at the position. Some see a little Mark Grace in him and a team that likes college performers could take Boissiere off the board at some point on Day 2.

Branden Boissiere (third) entered the spring with less of a profile than other Wildcats and then had the best statistical season on the team and led Division-I in hits. He has a good shot to be the larger half of an outfield platoon, at least.

After hitting 22 homers and stealing 19 bases in his first two seasons at Coastal Carolina and performing well in the Cape Cod League, Chavers positioned himself as a potential top-two-rounds pick for 2020. But he never made his way back to the diamond after surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right (throwing) shoulder in December 2019 and went undrafted last June. He's again displaying some of the best all-around tools in the college crop and a more mature approach at the plate, but worries about his shoulder and his age (he turns 23 two weeks after the Draft) will affect his status. Chavers generates at least solid raw power with a quick left-handed swing and the strength in his compact frame, and he's not swinging for the fences as much as he did in the past. He used to let his stroke get too uphill and pull-oriented, but now he's making more consistent hard contact. While he has made strides handling left-handers, questions still persist as to whether he can do so well enough to be more than a platoon player. Chavers is doing a better job of using his plus speed to steal and take extra bases. He's still honing his instincts in center field but should be able to remain there as a pro. Though his arm earns average to solid grades, it remains a concern because he had labrum surgery in high school.

Miller logged a 7.10 ERA in his first two seasons as a reliever at NCAA Division III Waynesburg (Pa.) before he was diagnosed with Type I diabetes. After changing his diet, he put nearly 50 pounds on his 6-foot-5 frame and added velocity to his pitches, setting a school record with 97 strikeouts in 67 2/3 innings in 2019 and continuing to dominate in the shortened 2020 season. He completed his degree in finance last spring and received interest from Arkansas and Coastal Carolina as a graduate transfer before opting to pursue an MBA and a professional baseball career at Gardner-Webb, where he has established himself as one of the hardest-throwing starters in college baseball this spring. Miller averages 95 mph with his fastball, tops out at 99 and works in the mid-90s deep into games. While his heater doesn't feature a lot of life, he displays the ability to locate it to either side of the plate. His low-80s slider and mid-80s changeup show flashes of becoming solid offerings but need more consistency, with his slide piece sharper last fall than it has been this spring. For a big guy, Miller has good body control and repeats his delivery well enough to reliably provide strikes. He'll need to learn to finish off more advanced hitters, but he has a legitimate chance to start and a nice fallback as a flamethrowing reliever. He belongs in the first five rounds on talent alone and could match Gardner-Webb's record for highest pick ever (third round) because he'll turn 24 a month after the Draft and thus will come with a discount.
Miller was an early senior sign of Oakland likely to accomodate an overslot first rounder. Up to 98 with his fastball, he has rare arm strength for a senior sign.

Cal State Fullerton has a well-deserved reputation for developing starting pitchers with extreme strike-throwing ability, with arms like Thomas Eshelman (0.4 BB/9 in college) and Connor Seabold (1.4 BB/9) the standard bearers, both of whom went in the top three rounds of their respective Drafts. Bibee is trying to follow in their footsteps after becoming a full-time starter as a sophomore in 2019, and while he pitched very well in four outings as the Friday night starter in 2020, he went unselected in the shortened Draft and returned as the Titans’ ace in 2021. Bibee has continued to be stingy with the bases on balls, filling the zone with a solid -- albeit unspectacular -- three-pitch mix. His fastball has added a tick more velocity and now sits in the 90-92 mph range while touching 94, and he’ll mix in both a two- and a four-seam fastball. He’ll show two breaking balls and has favored his curve more this year than his slider compared to 2020. He also factors in a usable changeup. All of his stuff plays up because he commands three pitches extremely well and has a good understanding of how to game plan and keep hitters guessing. Like with the Fullerton starters who preceded him, Bibee’s ceiling is somewhat limited, but he has a similar chance to be a back-end starter in the big leagues if it all clicks.

Merritt Island, just off the East Coast of Florida, has produced a fair amount of Draft talent, including 2018 first-rounder Mason Denaburg of the Nationals, eventual Royals second-rounder Brady McConnell (who didn’t sign until after his college career) and dating all the way back to Clint Hurdle, a first-round pick in 1975. Hartman, who hails from Merritt Island and attends Rockledge High School just across the Indian River, could be the next in line. Hartman currently stands out for his 6-foot-4 frame and his fastball-slider combination. He can touch as high as 95 mph now, usually sitting in the 90-92 mph range and thrown with some riding life to it. He complements it with an upper-70s slider with good bite to it that will flash above-average at times. He fiddles with a changeup but doesn’t use it in games. Especially given his size, Hartman does a nice job repeating his delivery and finding the strike zone. And there’s reason for excitement given his projectable frame and the chance he’ll throw harder in the future. If the Draft doesn’t work out, he’ll head to the University of Florida and we could be talking about him a lot more in a few years.

Varnado began his high school career playing locally for Port Neches-Groves High School in Texas. He moved to Kelly Catholic High School, also in Texas, as a sophomore in 2019, before making the move to Florida to attend IMG Academy. He’s steadily raised his profile since and performed well over the summer at events like the Perfect Game National Showcase and East Coast Pro Showcase, with his stock rising as the spring progressed in 2021. Varnado began at IMG playing second base, but he has since moved to shortstop to provide more of a showcase. He’s taken advantage of the opportunity, showing off solid all-around defensive skills. He makes the routine plays and has solid instincts, with plenty of arm to stay there long-term, giving him the chance to be an above-average defender in the future. He’s routinely recorded plus 60-yard times and that speed should be an asset on both sides of the ball. The middle infielder has a good feel to hit with solid bat speed and there is some power to tap into, though he will need to continue to add strength to his frame. A lack of shortstops who can stay at the position after the top tier may help his stock even more and it will be interesting to see if he gets taken high enough to keep him from attending the University of Arkansas in the fall.

Calvary Christian Academy in Fort Lauderdale is quite the high school powerhouse in 2021, with potential first-rounder Andrew Painter leading the way, followed closely by fellow right-hander Irving Carter. Ulloa, who plays up the middle behind those two pitchers, has undoubtedly been taking advantage of all that attention from scouts, though he’d done plenty to put his own name on the map with strong performances at events like the Baseball Factory All-Star Classic and Major League Baseball’s Regional Scouting Series showcase last fall. Ulloa is the kind of high energy player who grows on you the more you see him play. Scouts like his right-handed bat more than anything else. He’s shown he can really hit against premium competition, with a good idea of what he’s doing at the plate and the ability to drive the ball with excellent bat speed. He’s recorded above-average run times and can maximize his speed with an aggressive approach that carries over to his baserunning. That helps him as well on the defensive end, where he’s shown he has good instincts and hands to go along with an average arm. The question remains whether he can play shortstop long-term, with many seeing a move to second base at the pro level, though he’d likely continue to play short should he head to Oklahoma State.

Ulloa's skillset compares closely to Michael Chavis' at the same age. He's a compact-framed power hitter who takes a very athletic, high-effort swing, and though he plays shortstop right now he's likely to funnel down the defensive spectrum, maybe as a fringe 2B or as a 3B/1B type. He showed a roughly even BIP/whiff split during summer showcase play, in which Ulloa participated  heavily.

He's a compact-framed power hitter who takes a very athletic, high-effort swing, and though he plays shortstop right now he's likely to funnel down the defensive spectrum, maybe as a fringe 2B or as a 3B/1B type. He showed a roughly even BIP/whiff split during summer showcase play, in which Ulloa participated  heavily.

If it seems like Abel has been on the amateur prospect radar for a very long time, you aren’t wrong. The right-hander snuck on to the back end of MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 200 as a right-hander with a good feel for pitching from the Southern California prep ranks back in 2017, though the industry knew he was keen on honoring his commitment to Oregon State. He starred in the College World Series as a freshman in 2018, then made only three starts in 2019 and didn’t return before the shutdown in 2020. He was Oregon State’s Friday starter in 2021. In many ways, Abel is the same pitcher he was entering college in terms of his all-around feel with a solid three-pitch mix. He generally throws his fastball up to 91 mph, occasionally touching 92, but sitting more often than not in the 88- to 90-mph range while showing the ability to command it to both sides of the plate. His changeup, a plus offspeed offering, is his best secondary pitch and he’ll throw his above-average curve at any point in the count. For someone who has the reputation for having such an advanced feel for pitching, Abel has at times struggled with throwing consistent strikes, with a career walk rate over 5.0 per nine innings -- perhaps a result of him nibbling too much. He does mix his pitches well and keeps hitters off balance with his consistent performance, pointing to a future in the back end of a rotation.

Abel dominated as a freshman in the College World Series clinching game for the Beavers with an ordinary average fastball/breaker but a plus changeup and plus feel. He was doing well in his sophomore year before blowing out and needing Tommy John surgery. He started 2021 strong, then fell off a cliff.

A year ago, Case Williams became the first Colorado high school pitcher to get drafted and signed in the top five rounds when the Rockies took him in the fourth round. Lansville, who jumped on teams’ radars with a strong showing at the Perfect Game National Showcase, the Area Code Games and a perfect inning at the PG All-American Classic last summer, has the chance to give the Centennial State two prep pitchers in a row to go in the early rounds. While Lansville is a bit undersized at six-foot, he’s strong, compact and athletic on the mound. His fastball sits in the 93-94 range, but it has some ride to it and a shorter arm stroke leads to some deception, making the pitch tough to square up when he’s commanding it well. He throws a short, three-quarter power breaking ball in the 81-83 mph range that he calls a curve, but has more slider action to it at times. Whatever you call it, it’s firm and late, with some bit and shape to it, and it could be a true swing-and-miss pitch for him in the future. His mid-80s changeup isn’t quite as good, but it does have some cutter-like qualities to it. Lansville generally throws strikes, and while there isn’t a ton of projection here, his combination of stuff, deception and feel for pitching is generating interest in the top few rounds. He’s committed to Louisiana State.

A year ago, Mick Abel was not only the top high school arm from the Pacific Northwest, he was the top prep pitcher in the entire 2020 Draft class. Debiec isn’t quite in that stratosphere, but after jumping out of the gate on the summer circuit and lighting up radar guns at the Perfect Game National Showcase, he had the chance to represent the region well in the 2021 Draft. A rough start to his spring hurt his stock some, then he required Tommy John surgery in June to further cloud his Draft status. At 6-foot-7 and 202 pounds, there is a ton of projection in Debiec’s lanky frame when healthy. He touched 97 mph with his fastball at the PG event, though he’s typically more in the 90-94 mph range. There will be more consistent velocity as he adds strength. He throws both a two- and four-seam fastball, the former showing good heavy life to it, and he complements it with a good feel to spin a breaking ball. He can throw both a 12-to-6 type of curve in the upper 70s and a low-80s slider, though they do run into each other. He’ll need to continue to work on his feel for his changeup. As tall as he is, Debiec has more of a three-quarter arm slot in his delivery. His arm action gets long in the back at times and added strength should help him repeat his delivery more consistently and improve his overall command, which was a big issue in his early 2021 outings. Also a basketball standout in high school who was playing both sports simultaneously because of the pandemic, Debiec is committed to head to Washington for college should the Draft not work out.

The University of Connecticut has produced a good amount of big league arms over the years, with former first-round pick Matt Barnes leading the more recent crop and Jacob Wallace and Tim Cate having gone in the top three rounds over the last few Drafts. Casparius, a Connecticut native who spent two years hitting and pitching at North Carolina before transferring to UConn, might not go quite that highly, but his combination of stuff and relatively fresh arm intrigued scouts in 2021. While not the biggest guy in the world at 6 feet, Casparius is strong and athletic and has the chance to have a legitimate three-pitch mix. His fastball sits around 91 mph in most starts, but he’ll touch 94-95 on occasion. He can miss bats with his upper-80s cutter, a breaking ball with good hard, short action to it, but it’s his changeup that’s his best pitch, an offspeed offering also in the low 80s that features good fade, can serve as a strikeout pitch and gets weak contact on the ground. He’s generally a strike-thrower, with a couple of bad outings upping his walk rate this year, and his simple and repeatable delivery point to good command in the future. Prior to starting for UConn, Casparius had thrown just 27 innings, so there isn’t a lot of mileage on his arm. That also means there’s not a ton of history on him, though the Huskies helped offset that with a very scout-accessible fall program. He’s been a consistent member of their weekend rotation this spring.

Originally committed to Miami, Conley spent a semester there before transferring to Texas Tech. After sitting out 2019 per NCAA transfer rules, he has started at shortstop for the Red Raiders the past two years. He doesn't have a standout tool but can do a little bit of everything and has a chance to stick at short at the next level. A switch-hitter, Conley is more polished as a lefty yet is productive as a righty as well. His feel for hitting stands out more than his raw power, but he has added some strength and can drive the ball on occasion. He hit an upper-deck home run at Minute Maid Park in March and homered from both sides of the plate against West Virginia in April, though some scouts question how much pop he'll have with wood bats. Conley has solid speed and plays with constant energy. His average arm is a bit light for shortstop, though he makes plays thanks to his instincts and internal clock. He'll get the opportunity to play short in pro ball, though most evaluators project him as a second baseman or utilityman.

Fourth round shortstop Cal Conley out of Texas Tech originally attended Miami (but never played there) and transferred to Texas Tech, where he only played the 2020 and ’21 seasons. He slugged .600 during his career there. Conley is a switch-hitter with pull power from both sides of the plate. He looked rough on defense during the college postseason and may not have the hands for the infield. But because we're talking about a switch-hitter with power, Conley has some exciting potential outcomes, even if he has to move to the outfield. He has a chance to be a valuable, bat-first utility type.

A product of the same high school (Stevens in Rapid City, S.D.) that produced Mark Ellis, Bowman could have a similar future as a multidimensional second baseman. He starred for two years as a shortstop at Iowa Western CC, batting .418 with 44 steals in 84 games and helping the Reivers finish runner-up at the 2019 Junior College World Series, before transferring to Louisville for 2021. He has settled in at second and the leadoff spot and become the Cardinals' most dependable hitter outside of potential No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. Bowman has a smooth right-handed swing, good feel for hitting and a patient approach, allowing him to make regular contact and get on base. He has a quick bat with solid raw power and can drive the ball out of the park from gap to gap, giving him 15-20 homer potential. He's surprisingly fast for a 6-foot, 205-pounder, recording plus to plus-plus run times and showing a knack for stealing bases. Though he has slightly improved his arm strength since junior college, Bowman still is average at best in that regard and throws with a funky stroke, so he's better suited for second base than shortstop on an everyday basis. His quickness gives him good range at the keystone, though he needs to improve his consistency. He runs well enough to play center field if needed.

Part of a deep crop of eastern Pennsylvania high schoolers in 2021, Holman was a top-five-rounds talent who lasted until the Blue Jays took him in the 20th round because of his commitment to Alabama. After spending two seasons with the Crimson Tide, he transferred to Louisiana State and should factor in the first two rounds of the 2024 Draft. He was the best pitcher on the U.S. collegiate national team last summer, striking out 15 in eight scoreless innings. Holman's fastball has dipped a bit in 2024, sitting at 92 mph and topping out at 94, but it plays better than its velocity because he commands it well and rides it at the top of the zone with quality induced vertical break. His best pitch is a low-80s slider that he also locates well and features two-plane depth. He also has an upper-70s breaking ball with similar shape and curveball velocity but doesn't have the same feel for it or a sparsely-used mid-80s changeup with some fade and sink. Holman has a high floor as at least a No. 4 starter because he throws consistent strikes with his two main offerings. He already shows aptitude for sequencing his pitches and mixing locations. He has a lean 6-foot-4 frame and more projection remaining than a typical college junior, so his stuff could get better.

Three years ago, Troy had a twitchy 6-foot-1, 185-pound center fielder who went in the fifth round of the Draft, and Brandon Lockridge since has become one of the Yankees' better position prospects. Now the Trojans have another center fielder with the same build and profile who figures to go in the same range this July. Part of two national championship teams at Parkview High (Lilburn, Ga.), Cerny offers one of the best combinations of raw power and speed in the 2021 crop. The question with Cerny is how much he'll hit, because he has a busy right-handed swing and a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. He chases a lot of pitches out of the strike zone and struggles with breaking balls and changeups. But his bat speed and strength produce legitimate pop from gap to gap when he connects, and he could have 25-homer power if he can make more consistent contact. Cerny's plus-plus speed and aggressive nature on the basepaths make him a dynamic basestealing threat. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground and combines with his defensive instincts to make him a quality center fielder. He has solid arm strength and provides some added intrigue with his catching experience in high school.

Hayslip displayed some of the best raw power on the high school showcase circuit last summer but also hurt his cause by having trouble catching up to good velocity. He has dominated lesser Tennessee high school competition this spring, though he struck out twice in two at-bats against potential top-two-rounds pick Chase Burns in late March. He could go as early as the third round to a club that believes he can tap into most of his pop. Hayslip offers plenty of bat speed from the left side of the plate and plenty of strength in his 6-foot-2, 205-pound build, giving him at least plus raw power that plays to all fields. He has cleaned up his left-handed swing some and has displayed better timing at the plate this spring, though his stroke still gets long. There's not much projection remaining in his frame, but if he can make some further adjustments at the plate he might produce 25-30 homers per season. While Hayslip moves very well for his size and can clock some solid-to-plus run times, he should be more of an average runner once he's physically mature. He shows good instincts in center field but projects more as a solid right fielder with arm strength to match. He'll be 19 years old on Draft Day, which hurts him with teams that emphasize age, and will be sophomore-eligible in 2023 if he attends college at Alabama.

A backup catcher on Vanderbilt's 2019 College World Series championship team, Keegan was set to take over behind the plate for the Commodores in 2020 before offseason surgery to remove a rib and a complicated recovery left him at less than full strength during the pandemic-shortened season. He didn't become a full-time player for Vanderbilt until 2021 but has been the team's most productive hitter each of the past two years. He spent last season at first base, turned down the Yankees as a 19th-round pick after sliding in the Draft because of signability and finally saw significant action at catcher this spring. Keegan is exceedingly strong and the ball jumps off his bat to all fields despite what looks like an effortless right-handed swing. His ease of operation allows him to provide consistent hard contact and he has made adjustments to do much more damage against breaking balls this year than he has in the past. Though he's a fourth-year college player, he won't turn 22 until August and his track record in the Southeastern Conference is hard to ignore. Keegan has helped his cause by improving his defense and showing he can be an adequate catcher. He has the work ethic to continue to get better and has quickened his transfer and release to get more out of his throws, though his solid arm strength plays more as average. He's an average defender at first base and moves well enough to perhaps play left field.

In 2016, Southeast Missouri State featured a left-hander who was a priority senior sign and went in the fourth round before rocketing to the big leagues. That scenario is repeating itself five years later with Dodd following in Joey Lucchesi's footsteps. He started his college career as a two-way player at Kankakee (Ill.) CC, winning the Division II Junior College World Series in 2017, but has focused on pitching with the Redhawks. The Ohio Valley Conference pitcher of the year, Dodd has a money pitch in his low-80s changeup with good depth, and he'll double up on the plus offering and use it any count. His four-seam fastball has improved from 88-90 mph at Kankakee to 90-93 with a peak of 95 at SEMO, missing bats with high spin rates and riding life. After having well-below-average breaking stuff in junior college, he has developed an average low-80s slider and a fringy-to-average upper-70s curveball. A good athlete who repeats his high three-quarters delivery with ease, Dodd has natural feel for throwing strikes and uses his arm slot and 6-foot-3 frame to create downhill plane. Though he'll turn 23 a month before the Draft, his age is less of a factor because he's a left-handed pitcher equipped to move quickly as a pro ball. A tough competitor, he held Arkansas (college baseball's No. 1-ranked team for much of the year) to two runs in six innings while striking out 10 in front of a crowd of scouts in February.

Dodd began his career at a junior college, then transferred to Southeast Missouri State. His fastball generates a ton of whiffs in the zone. He locates his secondary stuff pretty consistently but they are of mixed quality.

McGowan drew scouting interest in 2020, when he ranked fourth among national junior college pitchers with 58 strikeouts in 35 1/3 innings, but ultimately went unpicked. He initially planned on transferring to Kansas State for 2021 but opted to return to Eastern Oklahoma State JC, where he's part of a rotation that could have three members selected in single-digit rounds this July. While Mountaineers left-hander Andrew Walling is ahead of McGowan in MLB Pipeline's Draft rankings, the latter has more athleticism and room to add polish. McGowan operates at 92-94 mph and reaches 99 with his fastball, which features more downhill plane than true life. He gets depth on an 82-84 mph slider that peaks at 88 with bite when it's on but gets slurvy when it's not. His mid-80s changeup has nice fade and shows flashes of becoming at least a solid pitch at its best, though it gets too firm and he struggles to throw it for strikes. While he's naturally athletic, McGowan throws with effort and recoil in his three-quarters delivery, which compromises his ability to control and command his arsenal and also casts doubt on his long-term future as a starter. One scout likened him to Trevor Rosenthal when the future All-Star was at Cowley County (Kan.) CC. Clubs could get a better read on McGowan if he attends Texas Tech in 2022, but his arm talent may be too enticing to pass up this summer.

His mid-80s changeup has nice fade and shows flashes of becoming at least a solid pitch at its best, though it gets too firm and he struggles to throw it for strikes. While he's naturally athletic, McGowan throws with effort and recoil in his three-quarters delivery, which compromises his ability to control and command his arsenal and also casts doubt on his long-term future as a starter. One scout likened him to Trevor Rosenthal when the future All-Star was at Cowley County (Kan.) CC. Clubs could get a better read on McGowan if he attends Texas Tech in 2022, but his arm talent may be too enticing to pass up this summer.

Before last summer’s showcase circuit started, Gray was a talented two-way high schooler from Illinois. He transferred to IMG Academy for better exposure and competition in his senior year, then performed much better on the mound than as an outfielder, raising his profile as a projectable left-handed pitcher considerably. Trouble with command and what some scouts believed to be a minor arm issue kept Gray from pitching much in the second half of the spring and left his Draft stock a bit up in the air. A left-handed hitter when he’s in the lineup, Gray runs well and can make a lot of contact with power potential to grow into. He’s done less pitching by comparison, though the step forward some were hoping for over the summer never really came to fruition this spring and he ended up pitching on IMG’s B team before shutting it down on the mound. There are still some very intriguing pieces, including a fastball that was largely 88-92 mph but touched 94 at times. Over the summer, he showed a distinct low-80s slider and a mid-70s curve, though they ran into each other, and he showed mostly the latter breaking pitch this spring. While he didn’t throw many, there’s been some feel for a changeup. While Gray was certainly going to be projection over ability, his difficulty in throwing strikes with below-average command overall was concerning to some scouts and his reduced time on the mound didn’t help in that regard. A team could roll the dice on his tremendous upside, but he could head to Arkansas to play with older brother Evan if the Draft doesn’t work out.

Gray is an athletic, projectable two-way player. He gets way down the mound and is very balanced over his lead leg as he delivers home with big extension and flat angle. He also has feel for a loopy breaking ball that lefty hitters struggle with because of Gray's length. He has some young Josh Hader traits.

Stewart underwhelmed on the showcase circuit last summer before breaking out at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October, when his fastball reached 95 mph with impressive spin rates. He started strong as a senior this year before his stuff fluctuated later in the spring, and how much teams like him depends on when they viewed him. A cousin of Kohl Stewart, the No. 4 overall pick in the 2013 Draft, he could fit as high as the third round for a club that saw him at his best. Stewart's four-seam fastball velocity has ranged from 88-95 mph in 2021, featuring some cutting action up in the strike zone. Like his heater, his slider can be a plus pitch at times, with his best ones operating at 82-84 mph with some two-plane break. His third offering is a sinking changeup that he rarely has needed in high school. With the athleticism to repeat his clean delivery, Stewart has no problems throwing strikes. If he adds strength and gets more consistent with his stuff, he could fit into the middle of a big league rotation. He'll play collegiately at Texas if he doesn't turn pro this summer.

Those who have followed the Santa Barbara baseball program were not surprised that another strike-thrower appeared to be on his way to an early-round selection. Following in the footsteps of 2016 fourth-rounder Shane Bieber and 2021 first-round selection Michael McGreevy, Ager seemed to be the latest Gauchos starter ready to take his place in that group. After relieving as a freshman, he made a successful move into the rotation. Following a turn on Team USA's staff over the summer, he had a chance to be one of the best college arms on the West Coast, but his stuff and results regressed this spring, and he lost his rotation spot as a result. At his best, Ager can flash a four-pitch arsenal. He has shown the ability to pound the strike zone with a fastball that averaged a little over 92 mph and touched 96 in 2023. His best secondary offering is a low-80s slider that flashes plus and misses a lot of bats. His slower curve is a fringy get-me-over kind of pitch, but it works with his mix. And while he hasn't used it much, he'll show at least an average changeup. Ager's ability to repeat his delivery and throw strikes with all of his pitches -- he walked just 2.5 per nine in 2023 -- were big selling points to a future as a starting pitcher at the next level, but his walk rate has soared this year. He had an oblique issue in November that slowed him, and it's possible that's impacted him this spring. There's still some projection, with perhaps more in the tank, with teams still considering him in the top three rounds.

An unheralded transfer who went undrafted out of high school and during two years at Palomar (Calif.) JC, Olthoff recorded a 0.32 ERA in four starts at Tulane during the shortened 2020 season, ranking third in NCAA Division I in strikeouts (47, including 16 in one game against Cal State Fullerton) and sixth in WHIP (0.54). He hasn't been as spectacular this spring and missed an April start with a sore forearm, but he still has been one of the best strike-throwers in college baseball and finished fifth in D-I in K/BB ratio (91/11). The Green Wave's best pitching prospect since 2008 supplemental first-rounder Shooter Hunt, he should get picked around the fifth round. Olthoff's low-80s changeup is his lone plus offering, one he sells with fastball arm speed before it dives and disappears at the plate. His heater has pedestrian velocity at 88-91 mph and a peak of 93, but it plays up thanks to his sink and command. His upper-70s slider can be a solid pitch at times and he can manipulate it into a curveball with similar velocity but more depth. Olthoff has tremendous feel for pitching, and his ability to tunnel and mix his pitches gives him a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter. He has an effortless, upright delivery with a short stride that adds deception, and he can both pound the strike zone or get hitters to chase his secondary pitches off the plate. He doesn't have much margin for error but rarely makes mistakes, and he was 180 innings and three-plus seasons into his college career before he surrendered his first homer in late April.

Early in the spring, UCLA’s weekend rotation had three interesting prospects with Zach Pettway, a potential intriguing senior sign on Fridays, Bergin on Saturdays and Nick Nastrini on Sundays. Pettway has had a big dip in velocity while Nastrini has lost feel for the strike zone. Bergin has maintained his stuff overall, but has been hit harder than expected. There are things to like about Bergin, starting with his 6-foot-4 frame. He kept velocity on his fastball all spring, throwing it mostly in the 90-92 mph range and topping out at 94-95 mph on occasion. His solid slider is his best pitch, a hard short breaker with bite thrown in the low-80s. He has a fringy changeup that he uses inconsistently early in counts to get hitters off balance. Bergin’s delivery has some effort to it, with two-piece arm action in the back that often keeps him out of sync timing-wise on the mound. A team taking him might try to help iron out that delivery and give him a chance to start, but scouts were more frequently seeing a reliever at the next level, with the fastball-slider combination perhaps playing up in shorter stints.

Swift went from Arizona high school powerhouse Hamilton straight into Arizona State’s lineup as a freshman in 2018, seeing time at both middle infield positions, more at shortstop than second, but not hitting much. His offensive profile didn’t improve much as a sophomore as he played second regularly in deference to Alika Williams, a 2020 comp-round pick. Swift hit well in that shortened ’20 season and has kept it up this year while manning short every day, greatly improving his Draft stock. There are no questions about Swift’s glove. Most scouts see him as a plus defender with outstanding instincts, hands, footwork and enough arm to stay at short for a very long time, and he’s already shown he’s a plus defender at second should he have to move around the infield at the next level. Whether he’ll have to do that or can play shortstop every day at the Major League level will depend on what he can do at the plate. He’s definitely improved and was finding a bit more extra-base authority this year, but the question will be just how much he can impact the ball on a consistent basis. He gets high marks for his athleticism and his makeup, giving confidence he’ll maximize the tools he does have.

Calvary Christian Academy in Florida has one of the best 1-2 punches in terms of starting pitching prospects in Andrew Painter and Irving Carter. So it only stands to reason they would need a quality backstop to catch them. They have exactly that in Lastres, a glove-first catcher whose defense stood out on the summer showcase circuit in a class that has some prep catching depth. He played through a small hand fracture as a senior and showed much of the same skillset. At 6-foot-3 and 205 pounds, Lastres has a strong and durable frame. He caught and threw well all summer and records pop times under two seconds consistently, with a plus arm. He’s a good receiver and blocker as well, and clearly handles premium stuff well. His bat is a bit behind his defense, though he has a good right-handed swing and should have solid power in the future, even if he ends up with a power-over-hit profile. Also working in Lastres’ favor is the fact he’ll still be 17 years old at the time of the Draft. Potentially working against him, in terms of when he’ll get drafted, is a strong commitment to the University of Florida, where he’d continue to be Painter’s batterymate should both head to campus.

Priester presents something of a conundrum as a catcher with intriguing but raw tools who hasn't been scouted extensively by a lot of clubs. He didn't do a lot on the showcase circuit last summer, though he did play well at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October. He also has to buck the history of Louisiana high school backstops -- only one who signed out of the Draft has made it to the big leagues, and that was Braves fourth-rounder Bob Didier back in 1967. Priester's most enticing tool is his plus raw power, the product of strength, bat speed and an aggressive approach. He runs into trouble when he sells out for home runs, as he gets too long with his right-handed swing and too pull-happy. When he doesn't try to do too much, he shows some feel for the barrel. More athletic than most catchers, Priester can flash some solid run times but projects to have fringy speed once he's physically mature and accumulates some wear and tear behind the plate. His plus arm has produced some sub-1.9-second pop times, and he has worked hard to refine his receiving. The Meridian (Miss.) CC commit should be able to remain a catcher, but he moves well enough to play an outfield corner if a team wants to maximize his offensive potential.

A rare third-year freshman, Bosnic redshirted at South Carolina in 2019 while recovering from Tommy John surgery and worked just 6 2/3 innings last year during the shortened season. He opened this spring as the Gamecocks' Sunday starter but control issues landed him in their bullpen a month later. He has looked better in shorter stints with a pair of quality pitches that score well in analytic measures and could land him in the top five rounds. Hitters don't seem to see Bosnic's fastball, which usually sits at 91-93 mph and tops out at 97 but sneaks by bats up in the strike zone with elite vertical action. He generates even more swings and misses with an upper-70s curveball that features high spin rates and spin efficiency. He also has a low-80s changeup with some tumble but rarely uses it as a reliever. Bosnic's high-three-quarters slot creates deception, but the effort in his delivery and his lack of athleticism make it hard for him to keep his mechanics in sync. Though he doesn't have any history of providing strikes, he'll probably get a chance to start at the outset of his pro career. He'll likely be a reliever in the long run and could fill a high-leverage role if he can develop some control and command.

When Cardenas was a high school catcher committed to UCLA, he was known as a glove-first backstop and he went undrafted in 2018, cementing his desire to play for the Bruins. His defense landed him in the starting lineup right out of the gate as a freshman and he hit better than expected, finishing with a .375/.476/.500 line. Cardenas hasn’t replicated those offensive gains, either during the shortened 2020 season or in 2021, somewhat limiting his Draft stock. Teams interested in Cardenas will be buying his work behind the plate. He has plus instincts to go along with plus blocking and receiving skills, with outstanding agility. He handles UCLA’s pitchers very well and his plus arm has enabled him to throw out more than 50 percent of those who have made the mistake of trying to steal against him. At the plate, Cardenas does have excellent contact skills from the right side of the plate. He’s strong, but hasn’t shown much power to date and some worry about what kind of offensive impact he’ll have at the next level. College backstops who can really catch always garner attention, though Cardenas’ limited offensive ceiling will limit how early he goes.

A useful swingman during his first three seasons at Texas A&M, Saenz finally got the chance to be a full-time starter in 2021. He recorded double-digit strikeouts against Samford, Georgia and Missouri during the first seven weeks of the season but has struggled for the most part during Southeastern Conference play. He still holds appeal as a lefty with a solid slider and could sneak into the first five rounds. Saenz relies heavily on his low-80s slider, which has quality horizontal and vertical break and works against both left-handers and right-handers. He sets it up with a 90-93 mph fastball that tops out at 95 with some sink and is most effective when he keeps it down in the zone. He also has a low-80s changeup that he'll mix in against righties but he doesn't trust it very much. Because the 5-foot-11 Saenz lacks physicality, many scouts believe his best long-term role is as a multi-inning reliever. When he's fresh, he locates his pitches well, his slider plays more consistently as a plus offering and his fastball has more life. His competitive nature also would serve him well in high-leverage situations later in games.

Baker made an immediate contribution as a freshman at Texas Tech in 2019, starting at shortstop and third base and helping the Red Raiders to their best-ever finish (tied for third) at the College World Series. He moved into the leadoff spot and shifted to the outfield corners last year and has remained there this spring, catalyzing Texas Tech's offense. He batted .440 in the first six weeks of the season before sustaining a quad injury that sidelined him for six games. Baker's best tool is his speed, which earns plus-plus grades from some evaluators and makes him a basestealing threat. He has quick hands and a compact right-handed swing built for consistent line-drive contact. While he has average raw power, he focuses more on getting on base than driving the ball and projects to max out around 10-12 homers per season with wood bats. Though his best positions for becoming a big league regular would be second base or center field, Baker hasn't played them in college. He doesn't have the cleanest infield actions and his fringy to average arm isn't suited for an everyday role at shortstop or third base. He has the quickness to cover the gaps in center, a more viable spot than the outfield corners because his lack of pop doesn't fit the profile there.

Hurter looked like he was headed for the top three rounds of the 2020 Draft as a Georgia Tech sophomore the previous spring, then blew out his elbow that April and required Tommy John surgery. He missed all of last season before returning in 2021, showing similar stuff to what he had previously but not missing as many bats. He still comes with a high floor as a potential No. 5 starter. While Hurter's fastball usually ranges from 88-92 mph and tops out at 94, it plays better than its velocity and elicits a lot of weak ground-ball contact because he sinks it and locates it well. His best pitch is a sharp 78-82 mph slider that shuts down left-handers and is effective against right-handers. He throws his changeup at the same velocity and it shows flashes of becoming a solid offering with some tumble. Hurter has cleaned up his delivery a bit since having his elbow reconstructed and continues to pound the strike zone, though he gets in trouble when his command wavers because he has little margin for error. He has good feel for mixing his pitches and uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and plane. If he doesn't make it as a starter, he could be a reliever who relies on his slider.

He has good feel for mixing his pitches and uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and plane. If he doesn't make it as a starter, he could be a reliever who relies on his slider.

The University of Santa Barbara was a great place for scouts to spend a weekend, and not just because of the location. The Gauchos’ weekend rotation featured potential first-round pick Michael McGreevy as well as Boone, a pitchability lefty who doesn’t have the same kind of high profile as his rotation-mate, but was still impressing scouts with his ability to dominate opponents. It was Boone, not McGreevy, who was named Big West Co-Pitcher of the Year with Long Beach State’s Johnathan Lavallee. Boone has been a starter at Santa Barbara since his freshman year in 2019, showing an ability to miss bats without premium stuff. From a velocity standpoint, his fastball is below-average, topping out at 90 mph and typically sitting in the upper-80s. He commands the pitch well and isn’t afraid to come up in the zone with it to get hitters to chase and deception in his delivery allows it to play up. He mixes in a big looping overhand curve that’s only thrown in the low-70s, a pitch he’s been inconsistent with in terms of landing it for strikes. He sells his 77-79 mph changeup, his best pitch, really well with good arm speed. While Boone’s walk rates at Santa Barbara aren’t as low as you’d think, scouts have little questions about his strike-throwing ability. His ceiling is limited because of the lack of wow stuff, but a back-end left-handed starter who knows how to keep hitters off-balance will get some looks during Day 2.

Allen's ability to do a little bit of everything combined with his instincts and hustle made him an immediate starter at South Carolina and have endeared him to scouts during his three years with the Gamecocks. He reached double figures in homers and steals by mid-May and could have average tools across the board if he makes adjustments at the plate. He's a gut-feel guy for enough clubs that he could fit in the first five rounds. A rare bats-right, throws-left player, Allen should be able to hit for average with his swing, feel for hitting and ability to handle both velocity and breaking balls. He hasn't done so consistently in college, however, because he makes too much groundball contact and struggles against changeups. His plus raw power translates into average home run production, and it's playing better to all fields in 2021. Allen has average speed but plays faster than that on the bases and in center field because of his quick first step and his instincts. He's an average defender in center field and solid in right field, where he has just enough arm strength. He might be more of a platoon player or a fourth outfielder, though he has the makeup to exceed expectations.

A Rockies 37th-round pick out of a California high school in 2017, Hardman starred in the Cape Cod League two summers later, winning all-star recognition and the home run derby while ranking third with eight homers in 44 games. But he didn't get a chance to build on that momentum during the shortened college season in 2020, when he went unselected in the five-round Draft. He used his pandemic downtime to get into better shape, which has paid off with him becoming one of the best all-around offensive players and the batting champion (.397) in the Big 12 Conference this spring. After dropping 20 pounds, Hardman is displaying better bat speed from the right side of the plate. He tracks balls well, hits high velocity as well as offspeed pitches and draws walks because he isn't afraid to work deep counts (which also leads to strikeouts). With his quicker bat to go with his strength and the leverage in his 6-foot-3 frame, he's better able to translate his at least plus raw power into home run production to all fields. Though he's moving better than ever, Hardman is still a below-average runner who may be limited to first base. He needs to clean up his footwork but projects as an average defender with arm strength to match. He played mostly third base on the Cape but would have a long ways to go to become adequate at the hot corner, while left field could be a more realistic option for expanding his defensive horizons.

Clarke was a bit of a high school pop-up prospect in Virginia at the start of the 2021 spring season, but even though he was a projectable left-hander with glimpses of plus stuff, he wasn’t able to maintain a strong start and faded out of the Draft picture. He headed to Alabama to start his career but after not getting any mound time his first season, he went the junior college route and transferred to State College of Florida. He pitched sparingly in 2023 but was a regular member of the rotation in 2024, finishing among the nation’s junior college leaders in strikeouts. In some ways, Clarke is still the raw and projectable southpaw who opened eyes early in 2021, but with a bit more of a track record. The 6-foot-4 lefty has plenty of fastball, and he relies heavily on the pitch. He can be up to 96-97 mph at times, sitting around 94, though it isn’t thrown with a ton of life right now. His upper-70s curve has the chance to be a real out pitch with power, though he doesn’t always commit to it, and he has a firm, upper-80s changeup that needs work. Clarke’s control has been intermittent, and he walked 4.2 per nine during the 2024 season. While he might best be suited for a relief role, there’s still some ceiling here, though teams will have to balance his upside and arm strength with his lack of resume beyond this spring -- and perhaps his Tommy John surgery in high school -- when deciding if they want to try to sign him away from heading to South Carolina next year.

Draft Spikes draws a lot of comparisons to Ryan Bliss, another 5-foot-9 former Georgia prep shortstop who has developed into a top-three-rounds pick at Auburn, and he's more physical than Bliss was at the same stage and has a stronger arm. He comes from a Parkview High (Lilburn, Ga.) program that has won three national championships in the last decade and has produced four big leaguers, including Jeff Francoeur and Matt Olson. He led the Panthers to another 7-A state title this spring, going 4-for-6 at the plate while saving both ends of the championship doubleheader. Spikes has a compact but strong frame and a quick right-handed swing that produces a lot of hard contact. He generated impressive exit velocities with wood bats on the showcase circuit, though he won't fully tap into his solid raw power until he launches more balls in the air. He hammers fastballs but really struggles against breaking balls, so there are concerns about how well he'll handle more advanced pitching. Though he hadn't played much shortstop before last fall, Spikes has the tools and actions to stay there. The Tennessee recruit has solid speed and quickness and a plus arm that has produced fastballs clocked in the low 90s on the mound. He plays hard and scouts love his makeup.

Spikes doesn't have the physical projection typical of a high school prospect at a compact 5-foot-9, but he's a relatively polished, skills-priented player with some rotational epxlosion in the box. He's tough to beat with velocity because he's so short to the ball and he peppers both gaps with contact. Combine that with advanced defensive feel and instincts and you have a promising utility player's skilset.

A Texas state high school swimming champion in the 50-meter freestyle, David began his college career at McLennan (Texas) CC but pitched just 18 1/3 innings as a freshman and redshirted in 2019 because he struggled to throw strikes. His velocity has picked up since he transferred to Northwestern State and while he still battles the strike zone, he has one of the best curveballs in the 2021 Draft. He had a 72 percent swing-and-miss rate on his breaking ball and hitters went just 5-for-98 with 80 strikeouts against it, the main reason he ranked third in NCAA Division I in whiff rate (15.3 per nine innings). David's curveball can be a plus-plus hammer at its best, sitting at 83-85 mph and reaching 87 with tremendous depth, and he has doubled its usage to nearly 40 percent this spring. When he doesn't stay on top of his breaker, it plays like a mid-80s slider that's just as unhittable. He also can run his fastball up to 99 mph and uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create downhill plane to compensate for a lack of life, though he often dials it back to 92-95 in order to try to throw strikes. David barely uses a changeup and has averaged nearly a walk per inning in college, so he almost certainly will be a reliever in the long run. He pitches without a windup but still struggles to repeat his delivery, which features some effort. He's strong and athletic and scouts praise his competitiveness and intelligence, which helped him graduate in May with a business administration degree and a 4.0 grade-point average.

Lakeland Christian High School in Florida is a national power this year, ranked on a number of Top 25 lists around the country. A big reason for the school's success is Fox, a middle infielder who stood out this spring among Florida prep prospects mostly for his bat, giving him the chance to be the second player ever drafted from his school. Fox can barrel up the baseball with the best of them from the left side of the plate. He has a solid approach and fast hands that generate bat speed using a quick, whip-like swing. There’s some good extra-base authority already with the chance to have some pop in the future. While Fox runs well and shows off good hands, decent instincts and a solid arm, some think he’s destined to move to second base. The good news is he could profile well as an offensive-minded second baseman, reminding some in the area of Colby Halter, currently having a solid freshman year with the Florida Gators -- the school Fox will head to should the Draft not work out.

Fox has a compact swing and tracks pitches really well, guiding the bat head to the ball even when it's at the top of the strike zone. He's not especially projectable and is a better fit at 2B than at sSS, defensively, but he has a carrying offensive tool and projects up the middle, so he's a Cleveland type of prospect.

Temple (Texas) JC has produced one big leaguer in Boone Logan and never has had a player selected in the first 10 rounds, but Stephenson should end that drought this June. The best juco prospect in the Lone Star State this year, he creates some mixed opinions but his biggest backers see him as a third-round talent who's one of the best speedsters available. If he doesn't go high enough to sign, he'll get a chance to prove himself against much tougher competition when he transfers to Tennessee for 2022. Stephenson can post top-of-the-scale run times and gets to top speed quickly, making him a dynamic basestealer. A switch-hitter in the past, he's batting solely right-handed now and is driving the ball more in his second year with the Leopards than he did in his first after adding some strength. He's still a hit-over-power guy, however, and he'll have to prove he can make adjustments and consistent contact against more advanced pitching. A quick-twitch athlete, Stephenson still needs more polish at the plate and in the field. Some evaluators believe he has solid arm strength and the range to get the job done at shortstop as he becomes more reliable with more experience. But most scouts believe he has an average arm and will wind up in center field or possibly second base.

Reed, a toolsy outfielder from northern California, entered the summer as one of the top high school players in the class because of his five-tool potential. The combination of missing some summer events and not performing up to expectations at others, however, led to his stock taking a bit of a hit. At his best, Reed is known as a solid hitter with above-average to plus complementary tools. The left-handed hitter had shown ability to make contact with the kind of future power potential scouts love. But over the summer, he did not show good bat speed and there was more swing-and-miss than there’s been in the past, leaving evaluators questioning his bat impact. Reed also didn’t run as well as he has in the past, perhaps because of a leg injury that sidelined him for a spell. His reads and routes weren’t always sharp, and if that’s more than a temporary backslide, it could mean he would have to be a corner outfielder, putting more pressure on his bat. Reed will have to show he’s the player people thought he could be in the spring or he could be a tough sign away from his Oregon State commitment.

While he has thrown strikes since he arrived at South Carolina-Upstate from Canada, Marks didn't start to thrive until his velocity picked up in 2020. His stuff has continued to get stronger this spring as he set school records for wins (10) and strikeouts (101 in 95 2/3 innings) in a single season en route to the Big South Conference pitcher of the year award. He'll definitely become the second player in school history selected in the top 10 rounds and could go as high as the first, big leaguer Chad Sobotka, who was a fourth-rounder by the Braves in 2014. Marks' fastball has progressed from averaging 87 mph in 2019 to 90 mph a year ago to 92 mph this season, topping out at 98 as he mixes four-seamers up in the zone and two-seamers down. His heater plays better than its velocity because of his ability to locate it, as does his vastly improved 79-82 mph slider, which can get slurvy but has locked up right-handers in 2021. He has good feel for a fading 79-82 mph changeup that elicits more swings and misses than his other offerings. Marks has a simple, effortless delivery that he repeats with ease, allowing him to put his pitches where he wants and maintain the quality of his stuff deep into games. Though he lacks a plus pitch, there are teams who believe his command could make him a back-of-the-rotation starter. If not, he could carve out a role as a middle reliever who pounds the strike zone.

Over the summer, Pena showed off some premium arm strength at events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and in the fall at Perfect Game’s World Wood Bat Association World Championship. He hasn’t missed a step this spring in terms of lighting up radar guns, bringing scouts to Tampa Prep all season. The 6-foot-3 Pena relies heavily on his fastball and he can crank it up to 95-96 mph at times. He missed a lot of bats with his heater at showcases, though scouts were concerned it was a little too true and hittable this spring. His mid-70s curveball has improved this spring and he throws both his fastball and breaking ball with a quick arm, posting high spin rates. He does have a seldom-used changeup, around 78-80 mph. Pena generally is around the zone, though he can struggle landing his secondary stuff for strikes, and he’s definitely control over command right now. Still his size, arm strength and athleticism on the mound could lead teams to take a look at him on Day 2 and try to keep him from attending Florida International in the fall.

Scouts flocked to Silverado HS (Las Vegas) in 2021 to see Tanner McDougal, who signed with the White Sox as a fifth-rounder, and Cortez, who had a better senior season and opted to attend Texas A&M. He has served in a variety of roles for the Aggies, opening this year as a starter before finding more success as a multi-inning reliever and dominating in the NCAA Tournament (1.18 ERA, 29 strikeouts in 15 2/3 innings) as A&M finished second at the College World Series. With little effort, Cortez produces fastballs that park at 96-98 mph and peak at 100 with power sink that makes them almost impossible to lift. Hitters can't try to sit on his heater because he also has a power slider that ranges from 86-92 mph with plenty of horizontal and vertical action. He doesn't have much feel for an upper-80s changeup with modest fade and rarely uses it. Cortez's control has fluctuated wildly in college, as he pounded the strike zone as a freshman before walking nearly a batter per inning as a sophomore. He has thrown more strikes in 2024, though he's doing it by getting chases rather than consistently landing his pitches in the zone. Some clubs may consider trying him as a starter but a more realistic ceiling would be as a high-leverage reliever.

Villanova might be more known for its basketball program, but it has had more than 60 baseball players drafted in the program’s history, though none since 2017 and the last big leaguer to come from the school was outfielder Matt Szczur, a 2010 draftee. Graceffo, who worked his way into the Wildcats’ weekend rotation as a freshman in 2019, had taken a nice step forward as a starting pitcher prospect before the shutdown in 2020 and carried that over to 2021, where his dominance as the school’s Friday night starter gives him the chance to be just the second Villanova product to go in the top seven rounds since Szczur was selected in the fifth. After a big winter workout regimen, Graceffo showed up this spring throwing harder than he had previously, with his fastball now up to 95 mph. He throws it with good sink and that, plus a changeup that could be a plus pitch in the future, elicits a lot of weak contact on the ground. He has an average slider that averages around 81 mph and he can subtract from it to give it more of a mid-70s curve type feel. With the uptick in velocity, the 6-foot-4 Graceffo has actually become a better strike-thrower this spring while missing more bats. He won’t get out-worked in the weight room and gets high marks for his competitive nature on the mound, ingredients teams love in a college performer.

Graceffo, who worked his way into the Wildcats’ weekend rotation as a freshman in 2019, had taken a nice step forward as a starting pitcher prospect before the shutdown in 2020 and carried that over to 2021, where his dominance as the school’s Friday night starter gives him the chance to be just the second Villanova product to go in the top seven rounds since Szczur was selected in the fifth. After a big winter workout regimen, Graceffo showed up this spring throwing harder than he had previously, with his fastball now up to 95 mph. He throws it with good sink and that, plus a changeup that could be a plus pitch in the future, elicits a lot of weak contact on the ground. He has an average slider that averages around 81 mph and he can subtract from it to give it more of a mid-70s curve type feel. With the uptick in velocity, the 6-foot-4 Graceffo has actually become a better strike-thrower this spring while missing more bats. He won’t get out-worked in the weight room and gets high marks for his competitive nature on the mound, ingredients teams love in a college performer.

Neely attended the same high school as Rockies prospect Zac Veen, who was a first-round pick in 2020, but went undrafted in 2021 and headed to the University of Florida. He established himself as a reliable reliever and thrived as the Gators closer in 2023, saving 13 games. He’s largely pitched in relief again in 2024, though he’s been given some opportunities to start, with mixed results, leaving his Draft outlook somewhat cloudy. While most of his collegiate work has come out of the bullpen, many scouts think his best chance at the next level might be as a back-end starter. His bulldog mentality and toughness on the mound stand out more than any of his individual offerings, but he could have a complete starter’s repertoire. While his fastball has been up to 96-97 mph, it’s averaged around 93 mph but misses bats with it thanks to its ride, especially when it’s up in the zone. His slider is his go-to secondary pitch, and the mid-80s breaker can be a tight out pitch with power. He has a curve he doesn’t use, though some think it could be very effective and he mixes in a solid average upper-80s changeup. Neely has never had pinpoint command but tends to be around the plate. Some teams may decide to send him out as a starter and see if something clicks, though he’s lacked the consistency to be seen as a sure-fire future rotation member. He doesn’t necessarily have the kind of plus out pitch teams like to see coming out of the pen. He does tend to step up in bigger moments, something teams considering him on Day 2 of the Draft might be banking on regardless of what role he has.

Part of a Colleyville Heritage program that won a Texas 5-A state title with No. 2 overall pick Bobby Witt in 2019, Smith-Shawver initially was better known for his football exploits. A three-star quarterback recruit who accounted for 29 touchdowns in nine games last fall, he has a brighter future as a pitcher. He has committed to Texas Tech for baseball and may get the opportunity to play football there should he attend college. Smith-Shawver barely pitched at Colleyville Heritage before this spring but attracted attention on the showcase circuit last summer with his strong 6-foot-3 frame and a fastball that reached 95 mph. He has pitched in the low 90s as a senior with some armside run on his heater. He has made encouraging progress with his curveball, improving its shape while still needing to add more power because it parks in the mid-70s. Because of his inexperience, Smith-Shawver is still raw on the mound. He has a methodical delivery and could add some more power to his pitches if he throws with more intent. He has barely begun working on a changeup that he doesn't use in games, but his athleticism should help him get better once he fully devotes himself to baseball.

Prager worked his way into Texas A&M's weekend rotation as a freshman in 2022 but blew out his elbow, had Tommy John surgery that October and redshirted the following year. He returned in 2024 and became the ace of an Aggies team that finished second at the College World Series, pitching his way into the third round of the Draft. But when the Angels wouldn't meet his $1.5 million asking price, he decided to return to College Station for his redshirt junior season. Prager hasn't gained velocity since high school, still averaging 90 mph and topping out at 93 with his fastball, yet college batters have been helpless against it because it comes out of a high release height with plenty of carry and he can locate it where he wants. He complements heaters up in the zone with low-80s sliders with two-plane depth, effectively changing the eye level of hitters. His low-80s changeup features similar movement and gets the most chases and swings and misses in his arsenal. While Prager isn't overpowering, he's a classic crafty left-hander who keeps hitters off balance. He creates deception with his nearly over-the-top delivery, and his pitches play up because he mixes and commands them so well. He has a high floor as at least a back-of-the-rotation option.
