Delgado made some noise over the summer on the showcase circuit, playing well enough to make USA Baseball’s 18 and Under team that won gold. He’s shown some promise with the bat this spring at Calvary Christian Academy, but has been more inconsistent than some scouts had hoped. Delgado’s carrying tool is his bat. A switch-hitter, he has shown a feel to hit from both sides, and his bat speed should give him the chance to hit for average and power as he progresses. There are more questions about his defense. A shortstop in high school, most feel he won’t stay there because his below-average speed limits his range. He’s struggled with the accuracy of his throws this spring, making it tougher to project where his long-term defensive home will be, though he has shown enough arm strength in the past to make some believe he could play third. Otherwise, a future as an offensive-minded second baseman might make more sense. Any team considering Delgado in the top five or so rounds will be doing so because of the bat and the hopes of figuring out his position down the road. Whether or not he can be signed away from his Florida International commitment remains to be seen.

Both of Marusak's parents were noted for their speed as college athletes at Texas Tech, where father Dean was a cornerback on the football team and mother Cyd ran the hurdles on the track team. Max could have a similar future because he's the fastest player on MLB Pipeline's Top 200 Prospects list and considered difficult to sign away from a commitment to the Red Raiders. He's tooled up, but questions about his bat may drop him low enough in the Draft to steer him to Lubbock. Marusak's explosive speed draws top-of-the-scale grades and can change games. He can turn routine groundballs into infield hits, creates havoc on the bases and chase down balls from gap to gap in center field. He also has solid bat speed and arm strength and at least average raw power. While Marusak can do more damage at the plate than a typical speedster, the question is whether he will. He has an aggressive approach, his right-handed swing gets too long and he'll chase pitches well out of the strike zone. A former shortstop who's new to the outfield, he also needs more polish defensively but has the quickness to outrun his mistakes.

Sandlin recorded 20 saves in his first two seasons at Southern Mississippi and dealt in the Cape Cod League last summer, then shifted to the rotation this spring. The move couldn't have gone much better, as he ended the regular season leading NCAA Division I in WHIP (0.71) and ranking second in ERA (1.25). He has high spin rates on his pitches, making him even more attractive to analytically minded clubs. While he's a 5-foot-11 right-hander without overpowering stuff, he makes up for it by mixing five pitches and three arm angles. He'll throw a four-seam fastball and a curveball from a nearly overhand slot and a two-seamer and a slider as a sidearmer, and he'll also work in a changeup and a lower-three-quarters angle. It all adds up to about a dozen combinations of pitches and slots, and he can hit 94 mph with nasty life on his fastball from down low. Sandlin will have to tighten his slider at the next level, because pro hitters won't chase it as much as collegians do. He has the makings of a solid changeup too, and his feel for altering speeds and eye levels while pounding the strike zone gives him the opportunity to continue to succeed as a starter at the next level. His size will lead to durability questions -- he left one April start early and missed the next with shoulder stiffness -- and a pro team could be tempted to move him quickly as a reliever.

While Spillane was a known quantity, with power potential, as he was coming out of the Illinois high school ranks, he wasn't much of a pro prospect because he was coming off of Tommy John surgery and was committed to attend Illinois. Concussions kept him off the field for much of his first two years, but he burst onto the radar with a healthy, and huge, junior season in 2018, when he led Division I hitters in slugging percentage, OPS, while hitting 22 homers through the regular season. The Reds liked his potential with the bat enough to take him in the third round, signing him for below pick value and sending him to the Pioneer League for his pro debut. Spillane has both strength and leverage in his frame, and he combines it well with his bat speed to produce his plus raw power. He showed the ability to drive balls to all fields in college, though it remains to be seen if he'll be able to turn on good pro inside fastballs. There is some length to his swing, so strikeouts will always be a part of his game and he did strike out 41 percent of the time during his summer debut. He does offset that with an ability to draw walks, but he will likely continue to be a power over hit offensive player. A first baseman in college, Spillane is a good athlete and he saw more time in right field than first base during his first summer with the Reds. He could profile as an everyday right fielder if he hits enough and taps into his power consistently.

Deason first put himself on the map as a freshman reliever, one who contributed to Arizona’s long run in the College World Series in 2016. As a sophomore, he was a swingman, then had an outstanding showing in the Cape Cod League over the summer. That catapulted him into the Wildcats’ Friday night role, where he’s been a solid performer this spring. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has a three-pitch mix that could give him the chance to start as a pro. He’ll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range, though it’s fairly straight. His out pitch is his 79-83 mph curve, a plus breaking ball he can land for strikes, and he mixes in an average changeup effectively. While he doesn’t have pinpoint command, he is generally around the strike zone and competes like a closer every time he’s on the mound. Deason has proven he can handle starting and any team taking him will likely send him out in that role until he proves he can’t handle it. His stuff will tick up in shorter relief stints, and some scouts do see him as a seventh or eighth inning setup man when all is said and done.

A year ago, Keirsey looked like perhaps the best college bat in the Four Corners region for the 2018 Draft, but in May of 2017, a collision with the outfield wall resulted in a serious hip injury that required surgery. He returned in time to play all of his junior year, though his speed was initially hampered. Other college hitters in the area may have passed him, but he was coming on strong as the Draft approached. Keirsey has excellent bat to ball skills and makes consistent hard contact. It’s more of a line drive approach at present, though the left-handed hitter has some extra-base thump. While he might run into a few homers along the way, he’s definitely an average over power kind of hitter. Before the injury, Keirsey’s athleticism and speed were by far his best tool, with some putting a 70 on his run tool. It’s more of a 60 now, though it’s trending upward the further removed from surgery he becomes. He’s a solid defender in center field with a decent arm. The more Keirsey looks like his pre-injury self, the more his name was moving up boards, with some buzz as early as the third round. Teams thinking about taking him will have to put aside any worries about long-range questions about his health.

There are three players from New York in MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 200 this year. Mack is the lone hitter of the trio, with enough thump in the bat to interest teams in the top five or six rounds, albeit without a sure-fire defensive home. Mack is stocky and physical at 5-foot-11, but athletic enough to play shortstop capably for his high school team. Few see him sticking at the position, however, because he’s a bit heavy-legged in terms of his range and while he does have some arm strength, he doesn’t always show the ability to throw from different arm angles, a skill needed for the premium position. A move to second might work, with others suggesting third or left field, where his arm would probably play up to average. Playing a corner spot would put more pressure on his bat, and there is some serious raw power for him to tap into. That power, and the hope he’ll hit enough to get to it consistently, is what teams will be banking on should they take the left-handed hitter. Whether a team likes it enough to lure him away from his Clemson commitment remains to be seen.

After hitting 13 homers as a sophomore last spring and then leading the U.S. collegiate national team in all three slash stats at .372/.500/.535 last summer, Koch positioned himself well in a 2018 Draft with a notable lack of catchers. But he has confounded scouts by not making more progress offensively, and they now wonder if his defense might be better than his bat. He still shows decent potential both ways, which along with his track record will make him one of the first backstops selected. Koch's raw power is his best offensive trait, the product of strength and good-not-great bat speed, though there are questions as to how consistently he'll get to it in pro ball. He looks to crush everything to his pull side, leaving him vulnerable on the outer half of the plate. He has managed the strike zone well in college but his approach could get exploited by pro pitchers. Koch has made strides behind the plate this spring, cleaning up his receiving and improving his framing skills. He has average arm strength that plays up a bit because he gets rid of the ball quickly and makes accurate throws. He does a nice job of running a pitching staff.

Rivas went undrafted after a solid high school career in La Jolla, Calif., but a lot has changed in his three years at Arizona. A three-year starter -- with two of those seasons spent as a two-way player -- Rivas’ bat really started coming around as a sophomore. Focusing solely on his hitting as a junior, he’s been an outstanding performer putting him into top five round consideration. The left-handed hitter’s calling card is his bat. He can flat-out hit and makes a ton of contact at the plate while showing solid on-base skills, both for the Wildcats and last summer in the Cape Cod League. The one knock on him offensively has been his power, which hasn’t shown up consistently from his solid 5-foot-11 frame, but some think more can come. That will be important for him to profile at a corner position. He’s playing first base currently, and has good footwork, solid hands and an above-average arm there, but he’s also played the outfield and might prefer playing right field if given the choice. In either spot, his ability to be a run producer will be important for him to profile as an everyday player there. A team taking him early on Day 2 of the Draft could be getting an outstanding bargain.

Rivas went undrafted after a solid high school career in La Jolla, Calif., but a lot has changed in his three years at Arizona. A three-year starter -- with two of those seasons spent as a two-way player -- Rivas’ bat really started coming around as a sophomore. Focusing solely on his hitting as a junior, he’s been an outstanding performer putting him into top five round consideration. The left-handed hitter’s calling card is his bat. He can flat-out hit and makes a ton of contact at the plate while showing solid on-base skills, both for the Wildcats and last summer in the Cape Cod League. The one knock on him offensively has been his power, which hasn’t shown up consistently from his solid 5-foot-11 frame, but some think more can come. After getting shelled by Virginia Military in his first 2018 start, Hill flirted with no-hitters against Charleston Southern and Clemson in his next two outings while striking out 14 each time. That sent his Draft stock soaring, though he hasn't been as sharp since and missed a start in March with shoulder tendinitis. He still has a chance to become the fourth South Carolina right-hander selected in the top three rounds in the last three Drafts, following Clarke Schmidt, Wil Crowe and Braden Webb. Hill's best pitch is his fastball, which sits around 91-93 mph and peaks at 95. He uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create good plane and extension, and has some crossfire in his delivery that imparts running life on his heater. His changeup has been more reliable than his slider this spring, with each showing signs of becoming a solid offering when at their best. Hill is more physical than athletic, and he sometimes struggles to keep his delivery together and locate his pitches where he wants. If he can do a better job of maintaining his velocity into the later innings, improving the consistency of his secondary offerings and commanding his stuff, he could be a No. 3 starter. If not, he might be more of a sixth- or seventh-inning reliever because he lacks an overpowering fastball or a dynamic second pitch.

The Naval Academy has a fairly strong history of producing professional-caliber pitchers, with Oliver Drake and Mitch Harris actually making it up to the big leagues, though no Navy product has been drafted before the 10th round. Based on talent, Song should go way before that, though the military obligations a Naval Academy student has could keep that from happening. Navy’s ace has a strong track record of performance with the kind of stuff and 6-foot-4 frame that looks like a future starting pitcher. He’s shown a strong arm and a solid fastball that will touch as high as 96 mph at timemes. The rest of his stuff is average across the board, though he’ll flash above-average breaking stuff at times. He generally throws strikes, but his overall command fluctuates. A team taking Song in the early rounds of the Draft will be buying the arm strength and the belief that his secondary stuff will continue to come, making him a solid big league starter. That team will also have to be willing to go through the arduous task of finding a way to get him signed given his military commitment.

A three-year starter at Liberty, Artis has probably had his worst season, statistically, in this his junior season. But the speedy outfielder has shown enough where teams that covet college performers will still have interest in the top five rounds It’s not that Artis, a two-time Cape Cod League player, has been bad this spring; it’s just that he set the bar high by winning the Big South Conference’s Freshman of the Year in 2016 and then Player of the Year in 2017. He’s proven he can really hit, albeit from an unorthodox crouch from the left side of the plate. There is some raw power, but he doesn’t tap into it consistently, focusing on line-drive contact and drawing a lot more walks than strikeouts. He’s a plus runner who can handle center field with below-average arm strength, one who could one day hit near the top of a big league lineup. Even in his “down year,” Artis has gotten on base at an impressive clip and stolen bases. That skill set, not to mention his track record, has kept him fairly high on Draft boards.

A three-year starter at Maryland, Dunn has stood out in the wood bat Cape Cod League, being named an All-Star for two years in a row. Some of that offensive performance carried over to his junior season, where he hit for average and more power than he had previously in his career. A left-handed hitter, Dunn has an advanced approach at the plate with very good plate discipline that allowed him to walk more than he has struck out over the course of his college career. The infielder reached double-digits in home runs as a junior, nearly doubling his total over his first two years combined, though his power at the next level is more likely to be of the extra-base, not over-the-fence, variety. With a below-average arm and fringy speed, Dunn is limited to second base. The Terrapins had a middle infielder taken in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft in Kevin Smith, now with the Blue Jays, though he’s a shortstop. Dunn may not go quite as early, but his success on the Cape, as well as his junior year, could get him off the board not long after.

Florence (Ala.) High produced the seventh overall pick in the 2016 Draft in Braxton Garrett and has another quality arm two years later. Henry piqued the interest of scouts when he touched 97 mph and showed a plus curveball in his first outing of 2018, though he didn't maintain that stuff throughout the spring. He could go as high as the fourth round if teams believe that will be early enough to divert him from a Louisiana State commitment. Henry's fastball has ranged from 88-97 mph this year and sat at 92-93 toward the end of his season. His curveball can fluctuate between a slurve and a 12-to-6 breaker in the upper 70s with late bite. He shows some aptitude for throwing a changeup with armside life, though it can get a bit firm at times. While his stuff is inconsistent, Henry can flash two plus pitches and a solid third offering. Of greater concern is his delivery, which features effort and head whack and may make him a reliever in the long run. If he does attend college, he'll be Draft-eligible again as a sophomore in 2020.

Montes de Oca remains one of the biggest enigmas in the Draft, perhaps the biggest. He had Tommy John surgery as a Missouri high school junior in 2013 and ulnar nerve transposition three years later, and he turned down the White Sox as a 14th-rounder in 2014 and the Nationals as a 15th-rounder last summer. While all that is off-putting to a lot of teams, when he's on he might have the most devastating pair of pitches available in this year's crop. Montes de Oca can work at 93-98 mph and reach 100 with exceptionally heavy sink on his fastball, which can get top-of-the-scale grades for both its velocity and its life. His breaking ball has gone from a power slurve to more of a true slider that climbs into the upper 80s and is a wipeout offering at its best. Both pitches were overpowering when he worked the first seven innings of a no-hitter against Maryland-Baltimore County in March, when he struck out 12 of the 23 batters he faced and permitted just two balls to be hit in the air. After continuing to excel in the rotation over the next month, Montes de Oca pitched just 11 innings over the final seven weeks of the regular season without any explanation as to why his role changed. His lack of a reliable changeup and his inability to throw consistent strikes point to a future in the bullpen. With his stuff, he could move rapidly as a reliever and have closer upside if he stays healthy.

It seems more often than not, prospects who play shortstop in college have to move to another position when they begin their pro careers. Pena is an exception to that rule as an infielder who definitely can stick at the premium position. How much a team believes he’ll hit will ultimately determine his Draft status. A product of the Providence, Rhode Island high school ranks who went on to the University of Maine, Pena profiles as a solid to plus defender who can play shortstop at any level. He has good speed that leads to excellent range and possesses the strong arm and footwork necessary to excel at the demanding spot. At the plate, Pena does have some strength and raw power, enough where some see 15 homers annually as a reasonable projection. But that’s only if he makes enough consistent contact to get to that power. There’s length to his right-handed swing, which leads to some swing and miss issues with an at times overly aggressive approach. Some of that can be corrected mechanically once he gets to pro ball, and shortening him up will likely be a primary objective for whatever team drafts him. With his defensive profile, being able to unlock a more consistent bat could produce an everyday big league shortstop.

Holland impressed on the showcase circuit last summer and has established himself as the best up-the-middle position prospect among Texas high schoolers this spring. He could fit in the first four or five rounds, though whether that will be early enough to sign him away from a commitment to Texas remains to be seen. As the son of noted Houston-area hitting coach Sid Holland, it's no surprise that Holland has a quality right-handed swing. He doesn't try to do too much at the plate, satisfying himself with hitting line drives from gap to gap. He has some bat speed but isn't very physical, so most of his power will come in the form of doubles. Holland's best tool is his plus speed, though he's still learning how to get the most out of it as a basestealer and defender. He's a solid center fielder with average arm strength. While he can play all three outfield positions, he doesn't have the pop to profile on the corners.

Moritz won Southern Conference batting titles in his first two seasons with a .400 average as a freshman and a .392 mark as a sophomore. He's well on his way to a third, ranking second in NCAA Division I at .421 at the end of the regular season. As one of the best pure hitters in college baseball, he could surpass Jermaine Mitchell (fifth round to the Athletics in 2006) as the highest-drafted position player in UNC Greensboro history. Moritz possesses a pretty left-handed stroke and uncanny feel for the barrel. With a contact-oriented approach, he easily sprays line drives all over the field. He doesn't have much over-the-fence power but does have a knack for slashing triples. With solid speed and keen instincts that allow him to play even quicker on the bases and in the field, Moritz offers value beyond his bat. He has a good chance to stay in center field at the next level, a key to him profiling as a regular. If he can't, he has enough arm strength to play all three outfield spots and serve as a sweet-swinging reserve.

King High School has had its fair share of high Draft picks, dating back to former big leaguer Derek Bell, a second-rounder in 1987 and up to 2012 supplemental first-round pick Keon Barnum. Barger doesn’t look like a top two round guy at this point, but his skills on both sides of the ball could land him in the top five. Barger is a left-handed hitting middle infielder who has shown some plus bat speed at times this spring. It’s more of a line-drive approach at present, but there is raw power for him to tap into as he progresses in the game. Defensively, Barger has a strong arm and good hands, though with fringy speed, at best, the question remains whether he can stick at shortstop long-term. Scouts think Barger can begin his career at the premium position and let him play his way off, with second or third a more likely landing place. Seeing Barger end up as an offensive-minded second baseman from the left side of the plate might be the best scenario, and he could profile best as a super-utility type who can hit. There is some offensive upside, and that could be enough to entice a team to sign him away from his Florida commitment.

Stowers entered 2018 as a candidate to go in the early rounds of the Draft, but his stock dipped early in his junior season at Louisville when he let the pressure get to him and his swing got out of whack. He recovered to go on a tear as the Draft approached, hitting his way into the second round and a $1.1 million bonus from the Mariners. After his steady pro debut, Seattle swapped him to the Yankees in January for second-base prospect Shed Long, who had just been acquired from the Reds along with a 2019 Competitive Balance A Draft pick in exchange for Sonny Gray and left-handed pitching prospect Reiver Sanmartin. Stowers took off once he smoothed out his right-handed stroke and took a more direct path to the ball. He's at his best when he tries to hit line drives to all fields, and while he isn't a power hitter, he has enough pop to produce 12-15 homers per year as a pro. Stowers has an extremely patient approach and a knack for stealing bases. Scouts give Stowers solid-to-plus grades for his speed, yet there's mixed opinion on whether he can stick in center field at the next level. It's essential that he does so to profile as a regular, because he doesn't have the power to profile on a corner. Stowers' below-average arm will push him to left field if he can't stay in center.

One of the best high school pitching prospects ever to come out of Delaware, Bilous missed his entire senior season following Tommy John surgery but still got offered $600,000 by the Dodgers after they took him in the 29th round of the 2015 Draft. He contributed to Coastal Carolina's 2016 College World Series championship as a freshman and unquestionably has a first-round arm. Yet he has battled the strike zone throughout three years with the Chanticleers and two summers in the Cape Cod League, making it unclear how high he'll get picked this June. Bilous has one of the best pure fastballs among college starters, sitting at 92-95 mph and topping out at 97 with sink. In shorter stints on the Cape last summer, he reached 99. His slider combines mid-80s power and late bite, serving as a wipeout pitch at its best, and he can flash a plus changeup with fade as well. Bilous is athletic but has a long arm action in the back of his delivery that hampers him from repeating his release point and keeping his mechanics in sync. He has averaged at least seven walks per nine innings in each of his three college seasons and may never have more than fringy control. He's probably best suited for the bullpen and has the stuff to handle a high-leverage role if he can find the plate.

Danan Hughes is best known as a wide receiver who played six seasons in the NFL, but he also was the last Iowa position player selected in the first five rounds (third round to the Brewers in 1992). Thanks to an all-star summer in the Cape Cod League last year and a strong finish to his junior season, Neustrom could end that drought. He also led the Hawkeyes in hitting (.387) at the World University Games in August and has set career bests nearly across the board this spring. Neustrom's most attractive tool is his power potential, the product of strength, solid bat speed and loft in his left-handed swing. There are times when he focuses on using the opposite field, and others when he gets pull-happy and vulnerable on the other half. He makes consistent contact and draws his share of walks. While Neustrom is slow out of the box, he moves well for a 6-foot-3, 210-pounder and has at least average speed once he gets going. He plays right field for Iowa and possesses an average arm, though most scouts project him as a left fielder in pro ball. He needs to improve his reads and routes as a defender, and he has the work ethic to get the job done.

Though Kinneman had more success as a pitcher than as a hitter as a Pennsylvania high school senior, North Carolina State recruited him as an outfielder and installed him in its lineup early in his freshman season in 2015. While he provided solid production in his first two years with the Wolfpack, his struggles to make consistent contact with wood bats against top competition in the Cape Cod League depressed his Draft stock. It's on the rise this spring, however, as he has cut his strikeout rate and challenged for the NCAA Division I lead in home runs throughout the first half of the season. Kinneman's surge stems from letting his bat speed and strength produce power naturally rather than worrying about home runs. While he has drawn walks throughout his college career, he's using a more disciplined approach and making hard contact on a more regular basis. He has above-average pop from the left side of the plate, though his slump in Atlantic Coast Conference play probably will keep him out of the top three rounds. Kinneman's speed and arm elicit grades from fringy to solid. A team that believes he's on the high end of that range could try him in right field, though he has played in left at North Carolina State. He's a respectable athlete but most of his value will come from his bat.

Walton High (Marietta, Ga.) is a baseball powerhouse, winning three state titles, sending seven players to the big leagues and getting six players drafted in the top three rounds. Bartnicki entered 2018 as a good bet to increase that last number to seven, but he hasn't thrown as well as he did on the showcase circuit last summer. While he still offers more upside than the typical prep left-hander, clubs don't think they can take him high enough to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment. After sitting at 92-93 mph and touching 95 at times with angle and run on his fastball last summer, Bartnicki has seen his velocity drop 2-3 mph for much of this spring. His slider has similarly regressed, losing some power and bite and rarely looking like the potential plus pitch he flashed in the past. His changeup wasn't quite as deceptive as it had been previously, though he has the makings of an average third offering. Bartnicki has a strong frame and the athleticism to throw strikes, though his control also has wavered this year. His delivery is clean but also somewhat slow and gives batters a good look at his pitches. He has a ceiling as a mid-rotation starter but will need plenty of patience and development to get there.

The Royals have a former First Presbyterian Day School (Macon, Ga.) left-hander knocking on the door of the big leagues in Richard Lovelady and another in their pipeline after signing Cox for an over-slot $447,500 as a fifth-rounder in June. Mercer's best pitching prospect since Cory Gearrin was a Braves fourth-rounder in 2007, he ranked eighth in NCAA Division I with an average of 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings. He broke into pro ball by fanning 23 of the first 46 batters he faced. Cox misses bats with a fastball and curveball that are plus offerings when at their best. He has sat in the low 90s and topped out at 95 mph early in his pro debut, imparting run and sink on his heater. His curveball features power and true 12-to-6 break when he stays on top of it. Cox can throw some backdoor strikes with his slider and also has a decent changeup. With a durable frame, good athleticism and the ability to repeat his deliberate delivery, he's equipped to be a starter. He'll need to avoid nibbling at the plate and challenge hitters more consistently, and has made progress in that regard since signing.

Sean Hjelle and Irvin were the two best high school pitching prospects in Minnesota in 2015, and the tall right-handers both spurned pro interest to attend college. They've blossomed into two of the more dependable starters in power conferences, with Hjelle a possible first-rounder out of Kentucky and Irvin likely to go in the first five rounds. He moved into Oklahoma's rotation midway through his freshman season and has been a mainstay ever since, with the exception of missing two starts with shoulder inflammation as a sophomore. Though he looks the part of a power pitcher at an athletic 6-foot-6 and 225 pounds, Irvin doesn't have overpowering stuff. His fastball parks at 90-92 mph and peaks at 95, featuring armside run and a bit of sink. He relies heavily on his heater and a short slider in the low 80s, rarely using his serviceable changeup. Though he has a long arm action that can affect the consistency of his secondary pitches, Irvin has improved his control and command throughout his college career. There's little effort in his delivery and he repeats it well. His stuff may be as good as it's going to get, making his floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever stand out more than his ceiling.

Martin made an immediate impact at Texas Tech in 2015, leading the Big 12 Conference and all NCAA Division I freshmen with 10 wins, including the Red Raiders' first-ever victory at the College World Series. He enjoyed similar success as a sophomore before missing nearly two months with shoulder tendinitis, then got off to a brilliant start this year only to fade in late April. Scouts aren't sure exactly what to make of a guy they projected as a second- or third-rounder coming into 2018. While Martin doesn't have a true plus pitch, he knows how to mix two versions of a fastball and two effective secondary offerings. He'll usually work with a sinking two-seam fastball at 89-92 mph, though he can reach back for a mid-90s four-seamer a couple of times per game. His tight slider is usually his best secondary pitch, though some scouts prefer his changeup, which he'll throw in any count. Martin has a strong frame that lends itself more to durability than projection. He usually pounds the strike zone, though his control and command deserted him toward the end of the regular season. Scouts love his mound presence and guile, and he'll catch unsuspecting hitters off guard by quick-pitching them.

Projected first-round outfielder Jarred Kelenic (Waukesha West) isn't the only Wisconsin high school position player attracting scouts this spring. Campbell and third baseman Alex Binelas (Oak Creek) also would fit in the first five rounds on talent for some clubs, though they may not get popped early enough to divert from college. An Illinois recruit, Campbell is a better defender but has less power potential than Ben Rortvedt, a Badger State prep catcher whom the Twins drafted in the second round two years ago. Campbell has all the tools to succeed behind the plate. He receives and blocks well, and he makes accurate throws with solid arm strength. He plays with energy and has admirable leadership skills. Campbell has played through a hamate injury that has hampered him at the plate this spring. His strength stands out more than his bat speed, though his right-handed swing is quick enough. He currently employs a middle-away approach that's more conducive to hitting for average than power, though he could have more pop once he starts to turn on more pitches.

Outfielder Mike Siani is the highest-rated player in the state of Pennsylvania, and for good reason. But in many ways Guilbe, a product of Berks Catholic High School in Reading, has outperformed his fellow Keystone State prepster this spring. Guilbe definitely had some helium as the spring finally warmed up and the Draft approached, putting up a season that put him in contention for the state’s Gatorade Player of the Year award. He has legitimate right-handed power coming from a strong, athetic body. He’s more strength over bat speed with a bit of an uphill swing, something he’ll likely need to shorten to ensure he taps into that raw pop consistently at the next level. A below-average runner, there are some questions about his ability to stay at the hot corner because of his hands and lack of range. He is fairly physically mature. There were several teams looking at Guilbe in the top five rounds. Those are the teams that believe his bat will translate and he’ll hit enough to make his power a plus tool and make it worthwhile to lure him away from his University of Tennessee commitment.

Feltner dominated as a full-time reliever in Cape Cod last summer, sharing the league lead with eight saves while not surrendering an earned run in 13 appearances. Though he's one of college baseball hardest-throwing starters, he hasn't had nearly the same success during three years at Ohio State. His fastball velocity and performance in college baseball's top summer league could still get him drafted in the first five rounds, however. Feltner has been clocked as high as 98 mph and can carry a 93-95 mph fastball deep into games, with good downhill plane and some armside run. His changeup can be a plus pitch at times, featuring deceptive arm speed as well as fade. He flashed an improved slider on the Cape last summer but lacks feel to spin and has pitched with a below-average breaking ball for much of 2018. While Feltner generates premium starter velocity without much effort, hitters see the ball well against him and don't miss his fastball as much as would be expected. His control and command lack consistency, which also makes him vulnerable. The consensus is that he's best suited for a relief role as a pro, and he could have a plus-plus heater in shorter stints.

Schaller flashed a low-90s fastball as an Indiana high schooler in 2016, but he went undrafted because he battled injuries during his senior year and was strongly committed to Vanderbilt. He missed all of his first year with the Commodores following Tommy John surgery, and worked just 24 2/3 innings during the regular season this spring. But that has been enough to attract scouts, because he has hit 98 mph as a rare Draft-eligible redshirt freshman. Schaller has worked at 95-98 mph in short stints, generating velocity without much effort. He'll occasionally throw some sharp mid-80s sliders, but for the most part his breaking ball has been below average. He has used his changeup so infrequently that it's best described as a work in progress. Though he has thrown strikes, Schaller has been hit harder than expected for someone with a mid-90s fastball. He needs to improve his command and his secondary pitches to keep batters off his heater. He's far from a finished product and his signability is uncertain, but his fastball alone makes him intriguing.

Whitworth University, a Division III school in Spokane, Washington, has had a grand total of four players drafted from its baseball program, the most recent coming back in 2001. Smith not only is poised to become the first draftee since then, but also the first one ever with the potential to go in the top 10 rounds. The first thing that stands out about Smith is his size, and it’s something that came late to him. The right-hander was reportedly 6-foot-3 and throwing in the low-80s at the end of high school. Now he’s 6-foot-10 and has added a lot of velocity, throwing his fastball up to 97 mph consistently. Because he hasn’t always thrown that hard, Smith has an idea of how to pitch, mixing in his secondary offerings effectively, flashing average sliders and changeups. While he comes across his body with his short-strided delivery, the ball comes out of his hand clean and easy, and he’s thrown strikes this year. Smith has become one of the most intriguing Draft prospects in the Pacific Northwest, if not the country. It’s hard to know exactly what he’ll become, but he’s moved himself firmly into Day 2 Draft status, with teams likely to want to give Smith the chance to figure it out in their system.

Weiss didn't become a full-time pitcher until he was an Illinois high school junior in 2014 and missed his entire first season at Wright State after herniating a disc and fracturing a vertebrae in his back while overdoing weightlifting. He made up for his lost year by leading the Horizon League with a 2.13 ERA and winning conference freshman of the year honors in 2017. He also pitched well in the Cape Cod League last summer and has continued to thrive as a redshirt sophomore this spring, cementing his status as the Raiders' best pitching prospect since Joe Smith was a Mets third-rounder in 2006. The owner of a mid-80s fastball in high school, Weiss now operates at 91-93 mph and can hit 96 with his fastball. His heater can get fairly straight but arrives on a steep downhill plane because he's 6-foot-4 and employs a nearly overhand delivery. He throws his changeup with the same arm speed and it shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch with some fade and sink. Weiss' curveball isn't as reliable as his other offerings but has the makings of an average third pitch. He fills the strike zone but will need to command his pitches better at the next level. Scouts like his mound presence and envision him becoming a No. 4 or 5 starter.

One of the youngest players (17) in the 2018 Draft, Woods Richardson signed with the Mets for $1.85 million after they selected him in the second round. He jumped straight to full-season ball the next year at age 18 and was having a strong campaign in the Class A South Atlantic League when the Mets packaged him with lefty Anthony Kay to get Marcus Stroman from Toronto ahead of the ‘19 Trade Deadline. The Blue Jays promoted Woods Richardson to Class A Advanced Dunedin upon acquiring him, and the young right-hander responded to the challenge by making six impressive starts down the stretch. He continued to add polish while pitching at Toronto’s alternate training site in 2020. The move to Double-A in 2021 had been a bit more uneven, and Woods Richardson was in Tokyo as part of Team USA’s Olympic pitching staff when he was packaged with Austin Martin and sent to the Twins for Jose Berrios at the Trade Deadline. Woods Richardson gets great extension over his front side because he’s an excellent athlete who repeats his clean delivery well. That extension gives Woods Richardson’s 91-95 mph four-seam fastball riding life, and he did a better job of pitching up in the zone with it at the alternate site. He commands his heater better than most, showing the potential for plus command, and it's easy to envision the right-hander adding velocity as he grows into his ultra-projectable frame. Woods Richardson throws two distinct breaking balls in a top-to-bottom, downer curveball in the upper 70s, and a sharp low-80s slider. He can locate the latter down in the zone as a chase pitch and showed better action and command of his curveball in 2020. Woods Richardson completes his four-pitch mix with a plus changeup that is regarded as the best in Toronto’s system. Woods Richardson’s size, stuff and pitchability at a young age all bode exceptionally well for his future development, and he already demonstrates plus control and command of four pitches. He's more advanced and polished than the typical prep hurler and could move quickly as a result, with the potential to grow into a No. 2 or 3 starter.

Though Gomes has one of the best arms and bodies among high school pitchers in the Midwest, teams believe it will be virtually impossible to divert him from playing at Nebraska. His father Justin played with current head coach Darin Erstad at Nebraska in 1995, and Colby gave the Cornhuskers a verbal commitment as a sophomore. Based on talent alone, he could crack the first five rounds. Gomes' fastball velocity fluctuated with the weather during an unusually cold spring, as he would pitch at 87-92 mph on some days and 91-95 on others, holding it deeper into games once it warmed up. He has some feel to spin a curveball with some power and depth, though it lacks consistency. He can throw his changeup for strikes but needs to refine it further. Gomes has a long, lanky frame with plenty of projection remaining. He's athletic and does a nice job of maintaining his three-quarters arm slot. If it doesn't happen this year, he could be an early-round choice in 2021 after three years of adding polish at Nebraska.

Minnesota's top pitching prospect often has the two-way talent to pull double duty at the college level, as was the case with Logan Shore (2012), who blossomed into an Athletics second-rounder after three years at Florida, and Sam Carlson (2017), who signed with the Mariners for $2 million as a second-rounder last June. It's true again this spring with Halvorsen, which may make him follow through on a commitment to Missouri. He wants to play shortstop and pro teams clearly prefer him on the mound. Halvorsen throws harder than most high schoolers, hitting 96 mph while earning a save in the Perfect Game All-American Classic last August and pumping the second-quickest fastball (95.4 mph) at the World Wood Bat Assocation World Championship last October. Though horrible weather this spring delayed his senior season until mid-April, he regularly threw 92-95 once he took the mound. He generates his velocity with arm speed rather than effort and has some armside run on his heater. Halvorsen has decent feel for his curveball and changeup but both are works in progress because he has spent more time on his development as a position player. He threw a slider last summer, which some scouts preferred to his curve. He has the raw power, arm strength and athleticism to profile as a college third baseman but won't get the opportunity to hit if he does turn pro.

After starring as a reliever in his first two seasons at Louisville and in two summers in the Cape Cod League, Wolf has made a nifty transition to starting. He has proven to be a more than capable replacement for Brendan McKay (the No. 4 overall pick in 2017) as the lefty fronting the Cardinals rotation, ending the regular season with seven consecutive quality starts. The key to his success is a pitch he says he learned via the Internet. Wolf wanted to add a cut fastball while he was on the Cape last summer, so he googled \"Mariano Rivera cutter\" and now has a solid one that is his lone above-average offering. His 89-91 mph fastball tops out at 93 and plays up a little bit with some run and sink. He also has a curveball and a changeup that he can land for strikes, and he can morph his cutter into more of a slider. Wolf's 6-foot-6 frame and three-quarters arm slot create deceptive angle that adds to the effectiveness of his modest repertoire. He helps himself by controlling all of his pitches and doing little things like fielding his position well and controlling the running game. If he can't make it as a starter at the next level, he could have a future as a reliever because he's very tough on left-handers.

There are some real high school baseball powers in Florida. Nature Coast Technical High School, where Gates pitches and hits, is not one of them, but Gates made a name for himself by pitching well at a number of showcase events last summer. While Gates plays two ways in high school, his future is most certainly on the mound. The left-hander is fairly physically mature, with a three-pitch mix he uses well. His fastball this spring has been in the 88-91 mph range, sometimes touching a tick higher. He throws a solid breaking ball that sometimes has slider shape and some see more as a power curve and he has shown the ability to throw a changeup with good arm speed. There is some effort in his delivery, which can impact his overall command, and there is a debate about whether his future is as a starter or reliever, where his plus competitiveness would be an asset. A team taking him in the top five or six rounds and signing him away from his Miami commitment will give him every chance to stick in a rotation.

Carranza spent the first two years of his college career at Oregon, but transferred to Division II Asuza Pacific for his junior season. After a strong showing in the Northwoods League over the summer, he has stepped in as the Cougars’ ace and has helped them be one of the top DII teams in the country. Now 6-foot-5, Carranza has some projection, with the chance to add velocity as he adds strength to his frame. He’s already up to 95 mph with his fastball and comfortably sits around 92 mph. His low-80s slider is inconsistent, but shows depth and tilt enough to make you think it can be an average pitch in the future. He’ll flash a solid changeup with fade on occasion as well. Carranza has missed bats this year at a good clip, but command has eluded him, both in and out of the strike zone, leading to a high walk rate and getting hit more than he should. Still, his live arm and good frame could point to a future in the back of a rotation, enough for a team to consider him in the top six rounds.

There are college catchers who can really hit, but might have to move out from behind the plate because of their defensive inefficiencies. Then there are those like Meyer, who undoubtedly have a future as a defensive backstop, with how much they hit truly determining what kind of professional career they have. A three-year starter at Cal Poly, Meyer’s glove also earned him a spot on USA Baseball’s Collegiate National Team. He has excellent hands and moves well behind the plate, allowing him to receive and block well. He has a strong and accurate arm, recording excellent pop times to second base on a consistent basis. Offensively, the right-handed hitter has been less productive. He does make consistent contact and rarely strikes out with decent on-base skills. And he’s having his best offensive season now, albeit without any power. Meyer more than likely profiles as a backup at the next level. If his bat comes around with pro instruction, he could become a defensive-minded regular. In either case, his defensive skillset should have him off the board in the top six rounds.

Plassmeyer quickly worked his way into Missouri's weekend rotation as a freshman in 2016 but pitched his way out of it midway the following year. After working during the offseason to add velocity to his fastball and sharpness to his slider, he rebounded to become the Tigers' best starter in ‘18. The Mariners made Plassmeyer their fourth-round pick that June, then traded him to Tampa Bay during the offseason along with Mike Zunino and Guillermo Heredia. He pitched his way from Class A Bowling Green up to Triple-A Durham in his first full season, finishing second in the Minors (120 IP min.) with a 1.91 ERA. Plassmeyer has below-average velocity on his fastball, which sits 89-90 mph and peaks at 93, but it plays as an above-average pitch because its high spin creates running action and he commands it so well. His slider is average, but he manages to sneak it by more hitters than would be expected. A changeup that has some late fade gives Plassmeyer a third average pitch that he threw with more confidence in 2019. He's not afraid to pitch inside despite lacking swing-and-miss stuff. Plassmeyer’s effectiveness is largely, if not entirely tied to his plus-plus control. After issuing 35 walks in 203 1/3 innings (1.5 BB/9) in three years at Missouri, he’s allowed 27 free passes across 156 frames (1.6 BB/9) as a pro. Plassmeyer’s stuff limits his ceiling, but he has a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter who will compete and gobble up innings.

Wells was a solid prospect at Las Vegas high school power Bishop Gorman, but a combination of him only DHing all year along with his commitment to the University of Arizona took him out of contention to sign. The Yankees did take him in the 35th round in 2018 and he's now back as a Draft-eligible sophomore coming off a solid freshman season and very strong Cape Cod League showing. There is no question that Wells' bat plays. The left-handed hitter has power to all fields, with good timing and a simple setup at the plate. He has strength and bat speed and controls the bat head well to make loud contact. He does strike out a bit, but he also draws a lot of walks. There are more concerns about where he might play defensively. He's adequate behind the plate, and while his arm stroke and release are fine, his throws are inconsistent. He is a decent enough athlete to play first or figure things out in left field. A team taking Wells with its first pick might want to send him out as a catcher until he proves he can't play the position. His bat should play regardless of his eventual defensive position and he could end up following a Kyle Schwarber type path to the big leagues.

It can be difficult for high school players from Hawaii to gain exposure, though Bello was seen at the Area Code Games last summer, Perfect Game’s WWBA World Championship in the fall, and also participated in a Prospect Development Pipeline event in Los Angeles in February. The upside of hailing from Hawaii? Getting to work out with the Cardinals’ Kolten Wong and his brother, Rays prospect Kean, during the offseason. Bello profiles as a top-of-the-order catalyst who can impact the game with his speed on both sides of the ball. The right-handed hitter makes consistent contact and projects to be an average hitter. He needs to add strength, but there is some extra-base pop in his swing. He has the kind of speed to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in the outfield, with the chance to be an above-average defender eventually, and a plus arm to boot. There hasn’t been a top five round pick from Hawaii since Ian Kahaloa went to the Reds in the fifth in 2015, and the last time a high school position player from there went that early was when the younger Wong brother joined Isiah Kiner-Falefa as fourth rounders in 2013. Bello, a St. Mary’s commit, has the chance to join that select group.

Redan High (Stone Mountain, Ga.) has produced six big leaguers, including All-Stars Domonic Brown, Wally Joyner and Brandon Philllips. Scouts came to Redan this spring to check out speedy shortstop Kevin Smith and came away more impressed with Bradley, who entered 2018 more noted as a position player. Now his future clearly is on the mound, though the difference between his present and his projection may make him difficult to sign away from South Carolina. Bradley pitches at 88-91 mph and reaches 93 with sink on his fastball, and his quick arm and athletic frame promise more velocity to come. He'll show flashes of a quality 12-to-6 curveball at times, though it sometimes loses power and shape. He's working on a changeup and needs to create more velocity separation from his heater. Bradley's athleticism and clean delivery bode well for his future control. His stuff and command currently lack consistency, so he might spend two years in Rookie ball if he signs out of Redan. But his upside could make the youngest player on MLB Pipeline's Top 200 (he won't turn 18 until next March) worth the wait.

A three-year starter at Loyola Marymount, Decolati's strong showing in the Cape Cod League last summer had many excited to see what he'd do during his junior season. While the raw tools are there, his performance hasn't measured up, making it a little tougher to place him on Draft boards. A product of the Las Vegas high school ranks, Decolati has a lot of potential weapons he'll bring to the pro game. The right-handed hitter has a ton of bat speed and is capable of making very loud contact. He has outstanding raw power, but his aggressive approach has led to swing-and-miss issues that have hurt his performance this spring, which makes some wonder if he'll hit enough to reach that power consistently. Defensively, Decolati has a strong arm and will show the ability to make tough plays, but will boot routine ones at times. Primarily a shortstop in college, he might be better suited for third base, with some thinking a corner outfield spot would work. It's possible Decolati ends up filling a super-utilty role in the future. How much his bat can develop will determine his ultimate job and the team thinking they can help him tap into his offensive potential will be the one to take him on Day 2 of the Draft.

As a sophomore at the University of San Diego, Richan began as a reliever, but gained confidence when given the chance to move into the rotation. He’s been a weekend starter all year and while he’s had some up-and-down results, he’s far outperformed fellow Draft prospect Nick Sprengel. Richan has missed a ton of bats this spring, while walking very few, thanks to a solid four-pitch mix. He’ll throw his fastball up to 94 mph consistently, complementing it with a pair of breaking balls. His slider will show flashes of being above-average and he’ll fold in a fringy curve as well. His changeup continues to develop and could eventually be average when all is said and done. While he has a high strikeout rate, he’s also been fairly hittable. Richan is more floor than ceiling, though he does have a solid delivery and a good 6-foot-3 pitcher’s frame. His upside is as a No. 4 or 5 starter, one who could come off the board in the top six rounds, which would make him the first San Diego pitcher to be taken that early since David Hill was a fourth-round pick of the Rockies in 2015.

Quezada began his post-high school career at Cypress Junior College, pitching there for two seasons before moving on to Cal State Fullerton. He began the year pitching on Saturdays behind Colton Eastman, but after struggling initially moved to Sundays, where he righted the ship and upped his Draft stock late in the spring. Quezada isn’t the biggest guy in the world at 6-foot-1, but he has a fearless approach on the mound, going right after hitters with his three-pitch mix. His fastball sits comfortably, and consistently, in the 90-94 mph range. His changeup might be his best secondary pitch, though he also has a slider that should be a Major League average breaking ball in time. Quezada throws a ton of strikes with a free and easy delivery, and is at his best when he is commanding his fastball well. The right-hander has the stuff and command of it to potentially be a back-end starter at the big league level. He did look good out of the bullpen while pitching in the Cape Cod League last summer, where his aggressive approach could fit well.

As a 17-year-old with an athletic but thin build, Wrobleski stood out more with his projection than his present stuff for much of the spring. That profile usually lands a high school pitcher in college, but he generated some late helium when he showed improved velocity late in the season. He still might not be easy to lure away from Clemson, where he could get a chance to contribute as a two-way player. Wrobleski's fastball jumped from 88-92 mph to 91-93 mph as the Draft neared, with his low-three-quarters arm slot creating angle and sink. His slider showed more power and flashes of becoming a solid second offering as well. His fading changeup could be equally as effective. Wrobleski shows a willingness to use all three of his pitches, though he sometimes struggles to control them. He has the athleticism and delivery to figure out how to locate his offerings and remain a starter for the long term. His development will require time and patience if he turns pro this summer, though he has a high ceiling as a lefty with three potential solid or better pitches.

Liniak missed most of his junior season with a broken hand, so while he did hit the summer showcase circuit, he was understandably rusty. The speedy outfielder has come back with a strong senior year in San Diego, adding some shine to what is a lackluster crop of SoCal talent this spring. There a lot of tools to like with Liniak, even if you have to dream on them a bit with this long and lanky high schooler. His bat has a ways to go, as he needs to add strength and some scouts would like to see him not as spread out in his setup as he cudrrently is. But he does have a frame to support good weight and there is bat speed and raw power to tap into. His best tool is his speed, which helps him on both sides of the ball. He’s even better once underway, which allows him to cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He has a strong arm to boot, one which would work from a corner, but he has the tools to stick in center field. Liniak is committed to stay at home and attend the University of San Diego, which could be tough to sign him away from. But his tools to go along with his performance this spring could entice a team to take a serious run at him in the top five or so rounds.

The son of seven-time Cy Young Award winner Roger Clemens, Kody is a better prospect than his brothers Koby and Kacy, both of whom entered pro ball as eighth-round picks. He played with Kacy in his first two years at Texas, spending most of 2016 at DH following offseason Tommy John surgery. Fully healthy again this spring, he won Big 12 Conference player of the year honors and led the league with 19 homers in the regular season after going deep just 10 times in 2016-17. A 35th-round pick by the Astros out of a Houston-area high school, Clemens' left-handed power and gritty makeup should get him selected about 30 rounds higher this time around. He has focused on getting stronger and pulling more pitches, managing to retain his control of the strike zone while increasing his pop. He has the upside of a .260 hitter with 20 homers per season, though that comes with the caveat that his track record of production consists solely of 2018. Clemens' below-average speed limits his defensive range, though his instincts and work ethic are assets wherever he's stationed. He played third base as a Longhorns freshman and was erratic there and has lost a bit of arm strength since having his elbow reconstructed, so he's manning second base this spring. He's an adequate defender there and fits the offensive profile better than he does at the hot corner.

Mangum comes from a football family -- his grandfather John Sr., father John Jr. and uncle Kris all played professionally -- but has made his name in baseball. He won the Southeastern Conference's batting title (.408) and freshman of the year award in 2016 and has stayed at Mississippi State for four years despite getting drafted by the Yankees in the 30th round as a sophomore and by the Mets in the 32nd round last year. One of the best seniors in the 2019 Draft, he broke Eddy Furniss' SEC career hits record in April with his 353rd. The scouting report on Mangum has changed little during his college career. A switch-hitter, he has an extreme contact approach that results in a lot of opposite-field singles but few walks and little in the way of power. His best tool is his well above-average speed and he's doing a better job of translating it into stolen bases as a senior. Mangum also has improved as a center fielder during his time with the Bulldogs, showing better reads and routes instead of just relying on his quickness to track down balls. He has a stronger arm than most at his position and touched 93 mph with his fastball when he started five games on the mound as a sophomore. One scout likened him to a faster version of Sam Fuld.

Heading into this year, Hofstra had had just one player get drafted before the 10th round, Bryan Verbitsky, a 2013 third-round pick. The school had also had just one player, Daniel Poma in 2012, be named a Golden Spikes Award semifinalist. Rooney joined Poma in the latter category this spring and the left-hander almost certainly will join Verbitsky in the former in June. The 6-foot-5 left-hander has really come into his own as Hofstra's Friday night starter this spring, using a three-pitch mix to carve up opponents in the Colonial Athletic Association. He'll throw his fastball in the 87-93 mph range, using his size well to create good downhill plane. His slider flashes plus with good bite, a pitch that has improved over time, even from his stint in the Cape Cod League last summer until now. He'll effectively mix in an average changeup with some fade as well, and he's thrown all three pitches for strikes. With a somewhat limited ceiling, Rooney may not go quite as high as Verbitsky, who was the 86th overall selection. But he may not be far behind. After the dominant junior season he's had, he should easily beat Poma, who was a 10th-round pick back in 2012.

He'll throw his fastball in the 87-93 mph range, using his size well to create good downhill plane. His slider flashes plus with good bite, a pitch that has improved over time, even from his stint in the Cape Cod League last summer until now. He'll effectively mix in an average changeup with some fade as well, and he's thrown all three pitches for strikes. With a somewhat limited ceiling, Rooney may not go quite as high as Verbitsky, who was the 86th overall selection. But he may not be far behind. After the dominant junior season he's had, he should easily beat Poma, who was a 10th-round pick back in 2012.

2020 Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. He was deemed advanced enough to jump straight to Class A Kane County for his first full season -- an assignment Arizona seldom gives to its high school pitchers -- and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. He pitches in and out with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggle to square up due to its angle and late life. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. Kelly’s tendency to fall in love with the pitch makes his sequencing too predictable at times, which is why club officials view the right-hander’s changeup development as a key for him to take the next step. While it is currently a distant third pitch, Kelly throws it with splitter-like action that plays nicely off of his fastball. Kelly's max-effort delivery raises questions about his control and command profile and has led some evaluators to peg him as a future bullpen piece. But the big right-hander has already simplified his mechanics and thrown more strikes than expected in pro ball, and the D-backs are quick to praise his determination and work ethic, qualities that could go a long way in helping him remain a starter.

Playing for powerhouse American Heritage, alongside potential first rounder Triston Casas, Acton has gotten a lot of looks from a lot of scouts. Many like his offensive potential, but concerns about his defensive profile as a high school second baseman have limited his Draft stock. Acton isn’t overtly physical, but few doubt his ability to hit. After a bit of a slow start, he’s come on of late, showing a left-handed swing that should allow him to hit for plenty of average at the next level. There’s extra-base ability as well, though it might be more doubles than home runs. He is a solid defender at second with an average arm, but he doesn’t really profile well at other infield positions. And that’s where teams run into trouble trying to place him on a Draft board, as prepsters already at second aren’t typically high Draft picks. Acton is committed to the University of Florida and some see him re-emerging three years later after leading the nation in hitting with the Gators, kind of like a Jonathan India path with less power. It is possible a team will try to buy him out of that commitment in the top five or so rounds.

Cole batted a mediocre .276/.350/.377 with five home runs during his first two seasons at Arkansas, then sat out fall practice with a stress fracture in his back. He has exceeded expectations this spring, hitting .333/.420/.559 during the regular season with a team-best 12 homers. His potential for average tools across the board and his strong makeup could land him in the first five rounds. A switch-hitter, Cole is equally adept from both sides of the plate. He has a history of making consistent contact and has gotten stronger, giving him the chance to hit 15-20 homers per year at the next level. He draws his share of walks and has average speed, not standing out in any particular area offensively but doing a little bit of everything. Cole is a little quicker once he gets going and scouts who like him think he might have a chance to play center field at the next level. He has manned right field for the Razorbacks, displaying average range, arm strength and throwing accuracy. He has the tools to at least fill in at all three outfield spots, enhancing his profile as a backup if he turns out to be more of a tweener than a regular.

Horace Greeley in Chappaqua, NY, has had just one player drafted from its baseball program, back in 2003. Neeck is sure to be the second as an intriguing high school lefty, though it remains to be seen whether he begins his pro career or heads to the University of Virginia. While Neeck isn’t the biggest guy in the world at 6-foot-1, there’s reason to believe there’s more in the tank as he physically matures because he’s athletic with a loose arm. He currently throws his fastball in the 90-93 mph range and has a good little slider that lefties really struggle with and that he successfully gets in under the hands of right-handed hitters. He doesn’t use his changeup much, which is a bit firm, but he does show some feel for it. He repeats his delivery, but he does wrap his arm behind his head, which causes inconsistent demand, something that should be correctable at the next level. It’s been a good spring to check out New York’s Section 1 high school baseball action this spring. Lenny Torres Jr. is likely to go ahead of Neeck, but the southpaw may not be behind by all that much.

An all-state quarterback as a Pennsylvania high schooler, Datres has been a three-year starter for North Carolina at third base and has steadily improved his numbers each season. Draft-eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2017, he went unpicked because of signability concerns. This year, he's arguably the best college third baseman available after lock first-rounders Alec Bohm (Wichita State) and Jonathan India (Florida) and could land in the first five rounds. Datres has gotten in better shape this season, adding strength and bat speed. He shows solid raw power in batting practice but it hasn't translated that way in game action, where most of his pop comes in the form of doubles. He makes consistent contact and draws a decent amount of walks, but he may need to get more aggressive and hit more home runs to fit the offensive profile at third base. Datres has average speed and moves well on the bases and at the hot corner. His arm and defensive ability earn average to solid grades from scouts, and some wonder if he might be able to handle second base. He may be more of a utilityman than an everyday third baseman if he doesn't do more at the plate.

There are college pitchers who are labeled as “performers,” those whose numbers are better than their pure stuff would indicate they’re capable of. Then there are hurlers whose stuff is actually better than the stats they put up. Flynn, who served as Arizona’s Saturday starter in 2018, fits into the second category. Flynn has four pitches, all of which he is capable of throwing for strikes. He’ll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and he’ll back it up with a pair of breaking balls. He’ll throw a curve 79-82 mph and will also mix in a mid-80s slider that has cutter-like action to it. His 83-85 mph changeup gives him a fourth at least Major League average offering. While his command hasn’t been pinpoint, he is generally around the strike zone. Flynn’s ceiling is that of a No. 4 or 5 starter at the next level, though he did put up better numbers largely as a reliever as a sophomore. For him to go in the top five or so rounds, teams will have to look past his numbers and have a feel that his stuff will play in a professional rotation.

An eighth-round pick in the 2016 Ontario Hockey League draft, Ceranatola was the top Canadian pitching prospect in the 2018 Draft but slid to the Rays in the 30th round because of signability and headed to Mississippi State. After pitching sparingly in his first two years with the Bulldogs, he created first-round buzz by showcasing perhaps better stuff than any college pitcher anywhere last fall. But he pitched himself out of Mississippi State's rotation a month into the 2021 season, barely saw action afterward and was left off the College World Series roster of the eventual national champions. During fall practice, Cerantola pushed his electric fastball to 98 mph and his curveball up to 87 with an astounding 3300 rpm. He averaged 95 mph and hit 100 with his heater this spring, but he struggled to throw it for strikes and it got hit when he dialed it back to find the zone. His curve remained devastating if not quite as powerful. Though Cerantola doesn't use his third pitch much, he does show some feel for a low-80s changeup with fade. But he can't succeed in the rotation if he can't dramatically improve his control and command, and the effort and stiffness in his delivery make it difficult to do so. He has frontline starter upside but comes with a lot of reliever risk and Mississippi State didn't trust him in high-leverage situations.

After starring on a pitching staff that included five future high school first-rounders and won a gold medal at the 18-and-under World Cup in Japan in September 2015, Bergner had first-round aspirations of his own. But an inconsistent prep senior season and worries about his mechanics rendered him unsignable, so he headed to North Carolina after turning down the Red Sox as a 38th-rounder in the 2016 Draft. A similar scenario is unfolding this year, when Berger has followed a banner summer in the Cape Cod League with an up-and-down spring and may not get picked high enough as a Draft-eligible sophomore to turn pro. Bergner can show flashes of three plus pitches but doesn't produce that kind of stuff on a regular basis. He often worked with a mid-90s fastball on the Cape but has sat in the low 90s this spring and his heater is hittable because it lacks much life. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s changeup with fade, though he lacks feel to spin and doesn't trust his curveball. The biggest issue with Bergner is his delivery, which is long in back and short in front. It affects the quality and command of his pitches and also allows hitters to get a good look at them. The hope is that he can clean things up and maybe become a mid-rotation starter, but the consensus is that he'll be a reliever who will have to work heavily off his fastball.

North Florida has never had a pitcher taken in the top five rounds of the Draft, with only outfielders Todd Dunn and Donnie Dewees going that early. German, who began the year as the Ospreys' Tuesday starter but worked his way to being their Friday night ace en route to being a Golden Spikes Award semifinalist, has the chance to become the first. German has a solid three-pitch mix that points to a future as a starting pitcher at the next level. He'll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and maintains his velocity, able to reach back for that 94 late in starts when he needs it. His breaking ball is close to a 12-to-6 curve with late and sharp break to it and he throws an effective mid-80s circle change that has the bottom fall out of it. He commands all three pitches well and has thrown a lot more strikes, while missing more bats, this year compared to his sophomore season. German has a limited ceiling, that of a No. 4 or 5 starter. But his performance in his Draft season has had more than GSA voters take notice, giving him a good chance to become the first North Florida pitcher to go in the top six rounds since the Tigers took Tyler Stohr in 2008.

A two-sport standout who has played both wide receiver and safety for the Rutgers football team, Harris has been a three-year starter on the baseball field as well, giving scouts a toolsy if a bit more raw collegiate performer to consider. Harris’ athleticism certainly plays on the field. He has plus speed that allows him to steal a ton of bases and cover a lot of ground in the outfield, where he has the chance to be an above-average defender with an average arm. His ability with the bat is what remains relatively unrefined. He is super short to the ball, more jabs than anything else, and he has a tendency to chase pitches, which leads to an elevated strikeout rate. There is a lot to work with, though, and it should be noted that because he switched focus to football rather than find a league to play baseball in over his summers, he’s had relatively few at-bats. The upside is considerable, something a team is likely to bet on at some point during Day 2 of the Draft.

As a high school standout at Gulliver Prep, Del Castillo was a bat-first catching prospect who was ranked No. 194 on our Draft Top 200 list in 2018. The White Sox took a flier on him in the 36th round that year, knowing he was certain to honor his strong commitment to the University of Miami. He quickly showed his bat would play when he posted a .995 OPS as a freshman. He upped that to 1.025 over his first 16 games in 2020 and while his offensive production was inconsistent this spring, he was still thought of as one of the top position players in the 2021 Draft class. There is a lot to like about Del Castillo’s offensive profile, starting with his outstanding left-handed swing. He has a strong tendency to barrel up the baseball with an advanced approach, leading to more walks than strikeouts over his first two years with the Hurricanes. He hit 14 homers in just under 350 plate appearances at Miami. While Del Castillo didn’t open 2021 with a ton of pop and he didn’t dominate as much with wood during his time in the Cape Cod League in 2019, he did hit five balls over the fence in 37 games that summer. Just like when he was in high school, there are still some reservations about whether he can stick behind the plate long-term. His arm strength has improved and he tends to be accurate, but he’s not quiet enough with his receiving, showing a tendency to snap at balls too frequently. A team that feels he can improve and stick at the premium position will consider him in the top third of the first round, but his offensive profile alone will make him a first-rounder regardless of his defensive home.

Gatorade's 2018 player of the year in Massachusetts, Hajjar turned down the Brewers as a 21st-rounder to attend Michigan, where he was slated to start on Sundays as a freshman. Instead, he tore the ACL in his right knee playing pickup basketball and missed the entire season as the Wolverines came within one victory of a national title. He has been Michigan's best pitcher since returning and led the Big Ten Conference with 110 strikeouts in 81 2/3 innings this spring, though his stuff wasn't as sharp in 2021 after he used his downtime last year to add 20 pounds. When Hajjar is at his best, he works in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which has sinking action and gets on hitters quickly because of the extension he gets with his 6-foot-5 frame. He has sat at 88-91 mph with less life on his heater for much of this season. His best pitch often is his low-80s changeup with tumble, which he sells with fastball arm speed, while his curveball can be solid but has spent most of the spring as a loopy mid-70s offering. Though Hajjar has gotten stronger, he still has some projection remaining. While scouts hoped to see better stuff from him in his Draft year, he does have the makings of three solid or better pitches. He has done a nice job of tightening up his deceptive delivery since arriving in Ann Arbor, though he still can get more consistent with his control and command.

Schwarz seemed like a slam-dunk first-round pick for the 2017 Draft after his freshman season in 2015, but that dunk has somewhat gone off the back of the rim since with up-and-down sophomore and junior seasons. His bat has bounced back in his return for his senior campaign, but there are still questions about his future defensive home. Schwarz’s best tool remains his tremendous raw power to all fields and his home run output kicked back up in 2018, and while he does draw walks, there is a good amount of swing and miss to his game. The son of one-time big league pitcher Jeff Schwarz does have some tools to catch, but his arm and receiving are fringe-average. A team looking to draft him in June will be buying the bat, with the hopes things can work out behind the plate enough for him to be an offensive-minded backstop, or in the belief he’ll hit enough to play first base at the next level. While he is a senior, this may not be the kind of senior discount that has become de rigueur on Day 2 of the Draft.
